sens: man from the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy
H6000.detail: Amal is a man from the tribe of Asher mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:35. He is the son of Helem and the brother of Zophach, Jimna, and Shelesh. His name means "work" or "labor" in Hebrew, which was common in biblical culture where names often carried symbolic meaning.
H6000.origine: The name Amal comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to work" or "to toil." This same root appears elsewhere in the Bible to denote labor and human effort.
H6000.emploi: Amal is mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 7:35, in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher. He is listed among the descendants of this people during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel. This unique mention shows that he was a known man in his tribe, as his name has been preserved in the genealogical records.

sens: one who performs work, a manual trade
one who suffers, who endures pain
man in his state of labor and fatigue
H6001A.detail:
1. The worker is primarily the laborer, the man who practices a trade with his hands — like carpenters or blacksmiths who make the tools of war mentioned in Judges 5:26, where it refers to the "hammer of the workers."
2. This word also designates one who suffers under the weight of pain and affliction: in Job 3:20, God gives "light to the one who suffers," meaning to the one whom life oppresses.
3. More broadly, the worker is the man who earns his bread by the sweat of his brow, motivated by need: in Proverbs 16:26, "the one who works, works for himself, for his mouth urges him on" — his hunger drives him to effort.
H6001A.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of fatigue and hard work. It paints the image of a busy man, engaged in labor that exhausts. The family of the word also includes the verb "to work" and the noun "labor": all share the idea of an activity that costs energy and often involves suffering.
H6001A.emploi: This word appears four times in the Bible, concentrated mainly in the wisdom books (Job and Proverbs) and in the account of Deborah (Judges). In Judges 5:26, it refers to the artisans who make the tools. In Job 3:20 and 20:22, it takes on a more existential tone: the suffering one, the miserable, the one whom life crushes under its weight. In Proverbs 16:26, it returns to the sense of the worker who labors for his sustenance. The word thus unites the idea of physical labor and that of the suffering it entails.
H6001A.portee: This word reminds the reader of the human condition after sin: man must work by the sweat of his brow, and this work bears the mark of fatigue and pain. But it also reveals the dignity of honest work — the laborer, the worker, is not contemptible. For the believer, it invites seeing in every labor an opportunity to depend on God and to seek in Him the rest that work alone cannot provide.

sens: laborious effort, toil
physical or mental fatigue
task, work
usual occupation
sterile preoccupation
H6001B.detail:
1. Painful work is the effort that costs, that requires sweat and perseverance. It is the image of the farmer or worker who struggles to accomplish his task (Ecclesiastes 2:18: "all the work that I have done").
2. Fatigue is what results from this effort: the physical or mental exhaustion that accompanies labor (Ecclesiastes 2:22: "the concern of his heart, the object of his labors").
3. Work also simply refers to the task, the work one accomplishes each day (Ecclesiastes 9:9: "in the midst of your work that you do").
4. More broadly, it is the usual occupation, the trade or burden that fills life (Ecclesiastes 4:8: "his work has no end").
5. The word takes on a bitter hue in Ecclesiastes: work becomes a vain preoccupation, effort without true fruit, when one forgets God (Ecclesiastes 3:9: "What advantage does the one who works gain from his toil?").
H6001B.origine: The Hebrew word עָמֵל (amel) originally designates one who works hard, a man devoted to fatigue. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of effort, of toil. The Bible uses it mainly to describe not work itself, but work experienced as a burden, a difficult load — particularly in Ecclesiastes, where the Preacher questions the meaning of work under the sun.
H6001B.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Bible, exclusively in Ecclesiastes (chapters 2, 3, 4, and 9). It describes the work of the ordinary man, but always with a melancholic or questioning nuance: not work as a task to be accomplished, but as an experience of effort and fatigue. Ecclesiastes uses it to highlight the vanity of human toil when considered without God ("What advantage... does he gain from his toil?") or to remind that one must enjoy life despite the fatigue of work. It is a word that carries a judgment: it is not merely labor, but a burden that weighs.
H6001B.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on his work: is it a mere task emptied of meaning, or a burden carried with trust in God? Ecclesiastes teaches us that work without God becomes a sterile weariness, but that work offered to God, accomplished with gratitude and wisdom, regains its dignity and flavor. This calls us not to be consumed by activism, but to seek rest in Him.

sens: Nomadic people settled in the south of Canaan
Descendants of Amalek, ancestor of this people
Implacable enemy of Israel since the Exodus
Biblical representation of evil and hostility toward God
H6002G.detail:
1. Amalek is primarily a nomadic people who inhabit the southern part of Canaan, in the desert regions. At the time of conquest, it is an organized military force with its own king (Agag in 1 Samuel 15:8) and its cities (1 Samuel 15:5).
2. The term also designates the descendants of Amalek, this founding ancestor of the people — the Amalekites formed a distinct warrior nation, often allied with other enemies of Israel like Midian (Judges 7:12).
3. Amalek represents visceral hostility against Israel: it is the first people to attack Israel without reason during the exodus from Egypt (Exodus 17:8), which provokes the divine order to erase its memory (Exodus 17:14).
4. In biblical understanding, Amalek symbolizes persistent evil and opposition to God Himself — hence the radical order given to Saul to devote Amalek to destruction (1 Samuel 15:3), that is, to annihilate it completely.
H6002G.origine: The name literally means "inhabitant of the valley." Amalek is presented in the Amalekite (עֲמָלֵקִי) as a descendant of Esau according to 1 Chronicles 1:36, making Amalek a figure of genealogical hostility toward Israel (who descends from Jacob, Esau's brother). The people bears the name of this ancestor, as is customary in the ancient Near East.
H6002G.emploi: Amalek appears 37 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Pentateuch and the historical books. Its first act is the attack against Israel at Rephidim (Exodus 17:8-16), a founding event of a perpetual enmity. Amalek reappears as an adversary during the times of the Judges (Judges 6-7), allied with Midian against Gideon. Saul receives the explicit order to annihilate Amalek (1 Samuel 15), a mission he partially executes by capturing King Agag but sparing the spoils — which leads to his rejection by God. David completes the destruction of Amalek (1 Samuel 27:8; 2 Samuel 8:12). The memory of Amalek is invoked in the Psalms as a type of the enemy of God (Psalms 83:8).
H6002G.portee: Amalek teaches that certain forms of evil require radical and uncompromising opposition. The order to erase Amalek reminds us that God does not tolerate deliberate hostility against His people and that partial obedience is not obedience: Saul loses the kingship by sparing the spoils of Amalek. For today's believer, Amalek invites recognition of the spiritual enemies that systematically oppose God and to refuse any compromise with them.

sens: Son of Eliphaz and Timna, grandson of Esau
People or tribe descended from Amalek
H6002H.detail:
1. Amalek is the son born to Eliphaz, son of Esau, and Timna, the concubine of Eliphaz. He is a figure from the time of the Patriarchs, mentioned in Genesis 36:12, which lists the children of Eliphaz.
2. From Amalek will arise a tribe, the people of the Amalekites, who will inhabit the southern part of Canaan and play an important role in the history of Israel, particularly as an adversary during the desert journeys.
H6002H.origine: The name Amalek means "inhabitant of a valley" — a geographical image that perhaps describes the territory where his descendants settled. It is a proper name from the lineage of Esau, ancestor of the Edomites, placing Amalek among the neighboring and rival peoples of Israel.
H6002H.emploi: Amalek appears twice in Genesis as a historical figure: first in Genesis 36:12, where he is named among the children of Eliphaz, and then in Genesis 36:16, where he is listed among the chiefs descended from Eliphaz in Edom. Although these two usages present him as an individual figure from the time of the Patriarchs, Amalek is primarily known in the rest of the Bible as the ancestor of a nation, the Amalekites, who will form a people fighting against Israel.

sens: nomadic people enemy of Israel, descendants of Amalek
warriors who attack Israel in the desert
H6003.detail:
1. The Amalekites are a nomadic people who inhabit the Sinai desert and surrounding regions. They are the descendants of Amalek, grandson of Esau. This people appears as early as the time of the patriarchs: when Abraham pursues the kings who captured Lot, he encounters them in the region of Kadesh (Genesis 14:7).
2. The Amalekites are best known as formidable warriors who harass Israel during its journey in the desert after leaving Egypt. They attack unexpectedly and regularly raid God's people. Moses commands the Israelites not to enter Canaan, for the Amalekites and the Canaanites would defeat them (Numbers 14:43), and indeed they came down from the mountain and struck the Israelites at Hormah (Numbers 14:45).
H6003.origine: The name "Amalekites" comes from Amalek (עֲמָלֵק), himself a grandson of Esau according to Genesis. The ancient definition of the name "Amalek" means "people who lap" or "who drink eagerly," an image that describes a people of desert nomads, greedy and aggressive warriors. The term designates all the descendants of this eponymous ancestor and is used for the tribe, the people, or the territory.
H6003.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the accounts of the struggle between the Amalekites and Israel. They are encountered as early as Genesis 14, and especially during the Exodus and the beginnings of the monarchy. They inhabit the Negev desert and the surrounding mountains (Numbers 14:25; Judges 12:15). Saul is commanded to fight against them and to destroy them (1 Samuel 15:6), which becomes one of the great military campaigns of his reign. David also fights several battles against them (1 Samuel 27:8; 1 Samuel 30:1). The Amalekites embody the relentless and merciless enemy seeking to destroy the chosen people.
H6003.portee: The Amalekites represent in the Bible the determined carnal opposition to the people of God. Their name evokes predation and unrestrained violence. For the believer, this enemy people reminds us that the road to the promised land is fraught with obstacles, and that trust in God and obedience are necessary to overcome them. They symbolize the spiritual battle against hostile forces.

sens: lose its brightness, become dull or dark
be hidden, remain secret or elusive
surpass in brightness, eclipse
H6004.detail:
1. The basic meaning is "to become obscure, lose light." In Lamentations 4:1, gold has "lost its luster" — its shine has darkened, altered — which expresses how Israel's past glory has faded after the destruction of the Temple.
2. "To be hidden" or "to remain in the shadow": what is obscured is not visible, thus remains secret. In Ezekiel 28:3, "nothing secret is hidden" from the king of Tyre means that no mystery escapes him — he cannot keep anything in the dark.
3. "To surpass, eclipse": conversely, if something shines brightly enough to obscure the rest, it dominates in brightness. In Ezekiel 31:8, no tree in the divine garden "surpassed" (could eclipse) the royal tree of Pharaoh in beauty.
H6004.origine: The Hebrew verb עָמַם (ammad) has its root in the idea of obscurity and veil. It is related to words that express what is hidden, closed, or covered. The root evokes the image of a light that fades or a surface that loses its reflection — the gradual darkening that erases clarity.
H6004.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Bible. In Lamentations 4:1, it describes physical and spiritual alteration: the splendor of Israel has darkened. In Ezekiel 28:3 and 31:8, it takes on a comparative or negative turn, expressing what escapes obscurity (remains hidden) or surpasses (eclipses) in appearance. The word thus plays on the contrast: disappearing from view, remaining veiled, or conversely dominating by brightness.
H6004.portee: This word speaks of what tarnishes — glory, beauty, clarity — and of what remains hidden or invisible. For the reader, it reminds us that everything that shines in this world can lose its luster, and that some things remain forever veiled from our eyes. It is an invitation not to place our trust in what passes or conceals itself.

sens: He who bears the prophetic name "God with us"
The son announced by the prophet Isaiah, born of a virgin
Jesus Christ, the Messiah, in Christian interpretation
H6005.detail: 1. Emmanuel literally means "God with us" in Hebrew — a name that expresses the promise that God himself would dwell among his people, not distant and inaccessible, but present and close. 2. The prophet Isaiah announces that a young woman will conceive and bear a son, and he will be called Emmanuel (Isaiah 7:14); this prophetic name characterizes the one who will come. 3. In the Christian faith, Emmanuel is recognized as Jesus Christ, the promised Messiah, who embodies this promise that God is with his people — not as a mere formula, but as a living reality: the incarnate God among men.
H6005.origine: The Hebrew name Emmanuel (עִמָּנוּאֵל) is composed of two elements: "immanu" ("with us") and "El" ("God"). It is a theophoric construction, meaning a name that contains the divine name El. Its literal meaning and initial image express a divine presence among the people — a promise that God would not remain distant but would dwell at the heart of his people.
H6005.emploi: Emmanuel appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in the prophet Isaiah. In Isaiah 7:14, Isaiah proclaims that the young woman will bear a son and will call him Emmanuel, as a sign from the Lord for the house of David in the time of the Assyrian threat. In Isaiah 8:8, the name Emmanuel reappears to designate the threatened land, as if the people bore this name. This double usage emphasizes that the name is prophetic: it announces a saving divine presence in the midst of distress. Christians recognize in Jesus Christ the fulfillment of this prophecy, the God who became man to be truly "with us."
H6005.portee: Emmanuel is a central biblical promise: that God never abandons us, that he comes to us and makes himself present in our human condition. For the Christian, this name reveals that Jesus is not merely a wise man or a prophet, but God himself incarnate, who chose to share our lives. This truth transforms our relationship with God: he is no longer just the distant Creator, but the inseparable companion of our days.

sens: To place a load, a burden on the back or on an animal
To carry a load, a weight
To impose a yoke, taxes, duties on someone
To overwhelm someone under a weight, in a figurative sense
H6006.detail:
1. The most concrete literal meaning: to place a burden on something to transport it. In Genesis 44:13, Joseph's brothers "reload" their donkeys to return home, meaning they put their luggage on the animals. This is a very material act of preparation for the journey.

2. To actually carry this burden, to support it under its weight. Nehemiah 4:17 speaks of those who "loaded the burdens" during the rebuilding of the wall: they were actively transporting construction materials, working with one hand while holding a weapon in the other.

3. Extending to the political and social sense: to impose a fiscal or administrative burden on a people. King Rehoboam in 1 Kings 12:11 says he will "reload" the yoke on the Israelites, meaning he will increase their taxes and forced labor, making their lives heavier and more difficult.

4. In a figurative sense, it means to overwhelm, to overload under the weight of misfortune or suffering. The psalmist says in Psalms 68:20: "When we are overwhelmed," acknowledging that God allows the trials that weigh upon us.
H6006.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the idea of weight and burden. The family of words includes terms related to burden, to what weighs down. The starting image is very physical: to load something on a back or a beast of burden. It is a concrete word, rooted in the daily life of the ancient Near East where transport by donkey was the norm.
H6006.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the historical and poetic books. It is notably found in Genesis 44:13 for loading the donkeys, in 1 Kings 12:11 and 2 Chronicles 10:11 (parallel passage) for imposing a heavy yoke on Israel, and in Nehemiah for the construction work of the wall and the transport of goods. In Psalms 68:20, it takes on a figurative nuance, that of being overwhelmed by trials. In all contexts, the central idea remains that of adding a weight, either physical and tangible, or administrative or emotional.
H6006.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the weight of burdens — both concrete and spiritual. It reminds us that taxes, obligations, and trials weigh heavily on people, and that God sees this burden. For the believer, it is an opening to ask God to lighten our burdens and to give us the strength to bear them, as Jesus offers in Matthew 11:28 ("Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened").

sens: Judah military chief during the reign of King Jehoshaphat
H6007.detail: Amasiah is an officer in the army of the kingdom of Judah under King Jehoshaphat. He is the son of Zichri and commands two hundred thousand valiant warriors. The text emphasizes that he had voluntarily dedicated himself to the Lord, indicating that his military dedication was based on a religious commitment to God. He represents those military leaders of Judah who put their strength at the service of the Lord (2 Chronicles 17:16).
H6007.origine: The name Amasiah means "the Lord is strength" or "Jehovah is strength" (from the Hebrew "amasiah"). It is a theophoric name — that is, it contains the divine name — which expresses trust in God's power. This type of name was common in Judah, particularly among military and religious leaders who sought to proclaim their dependence on divine strength.
H6007.emploi: Amasiah appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:16. He is mentioned during the account of King Jehoshaphat's reforms, when the text lists the mighty army leaders of Judah. This enumeration in an official list of the kingdom indicates his administrative and military importance. His inclusion in this passage suggests that the greatest Judah officers were known for their piety as well as for their valor in battle.
H6007.portee: Amasiah illustrates how, during the time of the monarchy in Judah, military strength and faith in God were closely linked. His voluntary commitment to the Lord, far from weakening his role as a warrior, made him more effective and trustworthy. His example shows that those who place their trust in God and dedicate their talents and strengths become powerful instruments of His purposes.

sens: City located in Asher, mentioned in the division of lands among the tribes of Israel
H6008.detail: Amead is a small city in the mountainous region of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. It is listed in Joshua 19:26 among the cities assigned to the tribe of Asher during the division of the promised land after the conquest of Canaan. In this text, it is named between Allammelech and Mischeal, marking the boundaries of this coastal region in northwestern Canaan that extended toward Carmel and Schichor-Libnath.
H6008.origine: The name literally means "that endures" or "that persists," evoking stability or durability. Although we have only one biblical mention, the name reflects the importance of permanence and solidity in the nomenclature of cities of that time.
H6008.emploi: Amead appears only once in the Bible, in the book of Joshua 19:26. It is included in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Asher during the division of lands among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. Its mention in this geographical enumeration shows that it was a recognized and established locality in the region of Asher, on the western side of Palestine.

sens: Having great depth
Whose meaning or significance easily escapes understanding
That which is hidden, intentionally kept secret or concealed
H6009.detail:
1. In the concrete sense, deep refers to what sinks far down or inward: Isaiah 30:33 speaks of a "deep" pyre, meaning dug or sinking widely into the ground.
2. In the intellectual or spiritual sense, deep qualifies what is difficult to understand, what escapes usual reflection: in Psalms 92:6, the thoughts of the Lord are described as "deep," meaning unfathomable, beyond what man can easily grasp.
3. In a moral or hidden sense, the word expresses the idea of what is buried, concealed, or kept secret: in Isaiah 29:15, those who "conceal" their plans from the Lord act in secret, burying their dark schemes as one buries something underground; in Hosea 5:2, the deeds of the wicked are "deep," meaning hidden, not easily visible but very real.
H6009.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the fundamental idea of digging, sinking, going beyond the surface. Etymologically, it is the image of a well or a pit, something that goes down far. This root has also given rise to words expressing darkness and secrecy, as what is deep is often invisible, hidden from sight. The word naturally applies to hidden thoughts, buried intentions, and mysteries that are difficult to penetrate.
H6009.emploi: The word appears nine times in the provided usages, mainly in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea) and in the Psalms. It is first used in the concrete sense to describe an excavation or a pit (Isaiah 30:33). But its dominant usage is figurative: to express the unfathomability of God and His thoughts (Psalms 92:6), or conversely, the troubling depth of the wicked schemes of men, their hidden intrigues, their secret rebellions (Isaiah 29:15; Hosea 5:2; Hosea 9:9). In Jeremiah 49:30, it takes on the meaning of retreating in secret, hiding far away. In Isaiah 7:11 and 31:6, the word expresses rather a deep request or deviation.
H6009.portee: This word invites the biblical reader to two contrary but complementary meditations. First, it reminds us that God is deep: His thoughts and ways infinitely surpass us (Psalms 92:6), and this should fill us with respect and humility. But it also warns that sin has its hidden depths, its underground intrigues: what is kept secret from human sight is never hidden from God. The moral depth of evil and the unfathomable depth of divine wisdom remind us that nothing can be hidden from the Lord.

sens: depression of the land between heights
expanse of fertile and habitable land
region or territory
H6010G.detail:
1. A valley is a depression in the land, a low area situated between mountains or hills. The valley of Achor, mentioned in the Old Testament, is a well-identified geographical region: it is where Achan and his family were executed (Joshua 7:24-26), and it remains a visible reference point at the time the author writes.
2. A valley also refers to a fertile and habitable region, conducive to agriculture and livestock: this is why Isaiah 65:10 mentions the valley of Achor as a resting place for cattle and a pasture for flocks, an image of prosperity and abundance.
3. The word sometimes takes on a broader meaning of "territory" or "region": it can refer to a land, a country with its inhabitants and history. In Hosea 2:17, the valley of Achor becomes a door of hope and comes back to life, symbolizing the renewal of the relationship between God and His people.
H6010G.origine: The Hebrew word עֵמֶק (émeq) literally means "hollow" or "depression." It comes from a root that expresses the idea of something that sinks or lowers. The word evokes a natural, concrete image: the sinking of the land that creates a low space. In biblical geography, a valley is an identifiable and stable element of the landscape, often named and recorded as a territorial landmark.
H6010G.emploi: The word "valley" appears five times in the provided usages, all related to the valley of Achor, a region of Canaan during the time of Joshua and beyond. In Joshua 7:24-26, the valley of Achor is the scene of divine judgment: it is where Achan, who violated the Lord's ban, is executed along with his entire family. Joshua 15:7 mentions the valley of Achor as a geographical landmark in the description of the borders of the territory of Judah, showing that it is a geographically established and known place. But gradually, the valley of Achor changes meaning in the prophecies: Isaiah 65:10 speaks of it as a place of pastoral abundance, and Hosea 2:17 refers to it as a "door of hope" where the people will sing again, transforming a memory of judgment into a promise of restoration. The word first designates a precise physical space, then it becomes the symbol of a divine transformation.
H6010G.portee: The valley of Achor reminds the reader that God's judgment is real and consequential, but it is never the final word. This cursed geographical space gradually becomes a place of restoration and hope, showing how God turns mourning into joy and guilt into a new chance. For the believer, it is an assurance: the painful and shameful past can be transformed into a door of hope if one turns to God.

sens: depression of the land, space between two heights
low and fertile region, conducive to habitation and agriculture
expanse of land, country
H6010H.detail:
1. A valley is a hollow in the land, an area between two hills or mountains, naturally lower. It is the opposite of a mountain or height: water flows naturally there, and it is a place where travelers can move more easily. In 2 Chronicles 20:26, it is in the valley of Berachah (which means "blessing") that the people of Israel gather after a victory, choosing this open and easily accessible place.
2. The valley is also a fertile and inhabited region, as water is abundant and the soil rich; this is why ancient peoples built their cities and fields in the valleys. The name "valley of Berachah" persists in collective memory, showing that it is a lasting place, marked by a sacred event and divine blessing.
H6010H.origine: The Hebrew word עמק (émèq) literally denotes a depression, a hollow in the land. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of depth and cavity. This word is common in the Bible to describe the geographies of Canaan and the Near East, where valleys are prominent features of the landscape. It corresponds to the Greek word "koilás" (κοιλάς) when the Septuagint translates the Old Testament.
H6010H.emploi: The word "valley" appears once in this specific usage (2 Chronicles 20:26), referenced in the Segond. It designates the valley of Berachah, the place where the army of Israel, under King Jehoshaphat, gathers to thank the Lord after His miraculous victory over the Ammonites, Moabites, and the inhabitants of Mount Seir. This place name, given to the valley that day, remains attached to it for future generations, symbolizing God's power and faithfulness. The valley thus becomes not only a geographical space but a living memorial of a divine intervention.
H6010H.portee: For the Christian reader, the valley of Berachah reminds us that God sometimes chooses ordinary places—a depression in the land—to manifest His power and grace. This place becomes sanctified not by its natural grandeur, but by the act of recognition and worship that the people perform there. The valley teaches us that any place where we turn to God sincerely can become a place of blessing, and that witnesses of divine faithfulness mark the memory of generations to come.

sens: natural depression of the land between two elevations
low and open area conducive to agriculture or gatherings
space of struggle and confrontation
H6010I.detail:
1. A valley is a depression in the land, a low area between heights: it is the opposite of a mountain. In Israel, these valleys are often natural passages or places where one can cultivate the land and raise livestock.
2. The valley can refer to an open and accessible region, unlike the steep mountainous areas. This is why armies gather there to set up camps and prepare for battle: Saul and the men of Israel gather in the valley of the terebinth (1 Samuel 17:2).
3. The valley symbolically becomes the place where confrontation takes place: it is in this same valley that David kills Goliath (1 Samuel 21:9), and it remains the theater of the struggle between Israel and the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:19).
H6010I.origine: The Hebrew word עֵמֶק (émèq) literally means "hollow" or "depression." It comes from a root that expresses the idea of being low and hollowed out. It is a simple and concrete word, very common in the Old Testament to designate all kinds of land depressions, whether fertile or not.
H6010I.emploi: The word appears three times in the Segond, all in the accounts of Saul and David facing the Philistines. The three usages refer to the same valley: the valley of the terebinth (a well-known tree in Israel). It is first the place where Saul gathers his troops to confront the Philistines (1 Samuel 17:2), then where hostilities take place (1 Samuel 17:19), and finally where David kills Goliath with the giant's sword (1 Samuel 21:9). The word thus retains a constant concrete and geographical meaning, but it takes on a historical and theological resonance: this valley becomes the symbol of the victory of God's people over their enemies.
H6010I.portee: The valley of the terebinth reminds the reader that God acts in real history, in concrete places and specific moments. This valley is the theater where David's faith triumphs over the power of the giant Goliath: it symbolizes how God uses earthly circumstances and ordinary places to manifest His power and save His people. Meditating on this place helps the Christian to see that their own life, their daily struggles, also take place on ground that God knows and controls.

sens: Elongated depression of the terrain between two heights
Region of open lowlands or low-lying land
Fertile and habitable territory
H6010J.detail: 1. A valley is a depression in the terrain, a hollow area that extends between hills or mountains: it naturally forms a passage and often a watercourse. 2. By extension, the word also refers to a region of low and open land, habitable plains, particularly in contexts where the lands promised to Israel are enumerated (as in Joshua 18:21, where the valley is part of the land inheritance distributed to the tribes). 3. These low-lying areas, generally well-watered, are fertile territories conducive to human settlement and agriculture, hence their importance in land distribution.
H6010J.origine: The Hebrew word עֵמֶק (emèq) comes from a root that denotes depth or depression of the ground. It is a concrete term that paints the image of a natural hollow in the terrain. It appears in many biblical geographical names, often in composition ("valley of...") to identify a specific territory: valley of Hinnom, valley of the Jordan, etc.
H6010J.emploi: The word appears in the context of the land distribution among the tribes of Israel after the conquest. In Joshua 18:21, it refers to the flat or habitable depressions that fall to Benjamin. It is a practical geographical term for describing the topography and delineating territorial inheritances. The word is used for all types of low areas: from simple depressions in the ground to large regional plains.
H6010J.portee: For the biblical reader, the word "valley" reminds us that the lands promised to Israel were varied, including fertile low areas, and that God was giving His people a concrete and manageable inheritance. It is a word that anchors faith in real geography and in God's material promises to His children.

sens: depression of terrain between two heights
expanse of low and fertile land
H6010K.detail:
1. A valley is a natural depression in the terrain, a low area that extends between hills or mountains. It is a geographical space marked by its relief: unlike a flat plain, the valley is enclosed. In Genesis 37:14, Joseph is sent from the valley of Hebron, which shows that this region, although fertile and inhabited, is characterized by this particular relief.
2. By extension, the word designates a region or territory defined by this hilly landscape, often fertile because water flows naturally there. It is a living space: livestock is raised, crops are cultivated, and people inhabit it. The valley of Hebron mentioned in Genesis 37:14 is a land of pastures and pastoral life.
H6010K.origine: The Hebrew word עֵמֶק (emeq) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "being hollow" or "to sink." It literally designates what is dug out, sunken into the ground. The same root is found in other Hebrew words related to depth and depression of the terrain. The word expresses direct observation of the landscape: a valley is what one sees when the terrain lowers.
H6010K.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond in Genesis 37:14, in the account where Jacob sends Joseph to find his brothers who are tending the flocks. Joseph departs "from the valley of Hebron": the valley is here the starting point, the place where Jacob and his family are located. This mention of the valley of Hebron geographically situates the action and emphasizes that it is a known, inhabited region, with its territorial landmarks. The term anchors the narrative in the reality of the Palestinian landscape.
H6010K.portee: This word reminds us that God acts in the concrete history of men, anchored in real places, living lands. The valley of Hebron is not an abstract backdrop: it is a fertile region where the patriarchs live, where God leads His people. By reading these geographical details, the believer can meditate on God's providence orchestrating events in specific places, including where Joseph's trial begins.

sens: A depression in the terrain between two heights, a hollow in the landscape
A low, open region, fertile or arid
The physical space where water flows and rain accumulates
In a figurative sense, a difficult period, a trial
H6010L.detail:
1. A valley is primarily a geographical formation: a natural depression between hills or mountains, where the terrain lowers. It is a hollow that can be wide and spacious (hence the idea of "open country"), unlike a narrow gorge.

2. The valley is the place where water naturally concentrates. When rain falls, it flows down from the heights and accumulates in the valley, which can make it fertile or, conversely, lead to flooding. Psalm 84:7 illustrates this: as they pass through the valley of Baca, the pilgrims "turn it into a place full of springs" — what may have been arid becomes a source of life.

3. By extension, a valley can simply refer to a low region or an open territory, a space for passage and circulation.

4. In a figurative or spiritual sense, the valley represents a period of trial, difficulty, or mourning — a low moment in life, but also a place where God can intervene and transform things (as in the psalm, where the pilgrims turn the valley into a source of blessing).
H6010L.origine: The Hebrew word עֵמֶק (emek) designates the visible depression of the ground, the sinking of the terrain. It belongs to a family of words related to the idea of hollow, depth. In the Greek Old Testament, this word is generally rendered by the Greek κοιλάς (koilas), which has the same concrete meaning. The word evokes the primary and simple image: when observing a landscape, the valley is what one sees below, between the elevations.
H6010L.emploi: The word emek appears only once in the biblical usages given to us — in Psalm 84:7. There it designates the valley of Baca, a region that pilgrims pass through on their way to the temple in Jerusalem. This valley, identified by some as an arid region (Baca meaning "tears"), becomes a symbol of spiritual transformation. The faith and perseverance of the pilgrims change their difficult passage into a source of blessing. This spiritual context shows how the valley is not just a geographical fact, but also a space of grace.
H6010L.portee: For the believer, the valley of Psalm 84 speaks of those moments when life seems arid or painful. Yet the text suggests that passing through the valley while turning to God transforms the trial: the desert becomes a source, tears become blessings. It is a word of encouragement for those going through a difficult period — not to deny the trial, but to affirm that God can be present and active in it.

sens: elongated depression between heights, low and flat terrain
fertile and habitable region
area of strategic confrontations or divine judgment
H6010M.detail: 1. A valley is a depression in the terrain, a low and flat area between mountains or hills: it is the opposite of a mountain which "is not sufficient" for the available lands (Joshua 17:16). The word simply designates geography, natural relief. 2. In Israel, these valleys are fertile and coveted regions, with an established population and resources: among the Canaanites "who dwell in the valley," there are even "iron chariots" (Joshua 17:16). It is habitable, exploitable terrain, strategically important. 3. In the biblical context, the valley becomes the place where destiny is played out: it is where Midian and the enemies of Israel "gathered" to fight (Judges 6:33), and where God announces that He will "break the bow of Israel" (Hosea 1:5). It symbolizes the place of judgment or trial.
H6010M.origine: The Hebrew word עֵמֶק (émèq) literally means what is "hollow" or "sunken." It comes from a root expressing the idea of depth. It is an ancient and common word in the Old Testament to designate any topographical depression, particularly the famous valley of Jezreel, in northern Israel, one of the most strategic areas of the Promised Land.
H6010M.emploi: The word appears 3 times in the provided passages, always associated with the valley of Jezreel in Canaan. In Joshua 17:16, it is presented as a territory conquered by the well-armed Canaanites, whom the sons of Joseph fear to confront. In Judges 6:33, it becomes the battlefield where Midian and his allies invade Israel. In Hosea 1:5, it is the place where God promises to break the military power of Israel, transforming the valley into a theater of divine judgment. Each time, the valley is a place of conflicts or major strategic stakes.
H6010M.portee: The valley of Jezreel reminds the believer that geographical locations are theaters where God exercises His judgment and sovereignty. Even fertile and well-defended lands cannot resist divine will: only trust in God, and not military strength, allows Israel to endure.

sens: depression of the terrain between two heights
low and fertile region
open space between hills
H6010N.detail:
1. A valley is primarily a natural depression in the terrain: a low area that extends between two higher mountains or hills. It is the opposite of a mountain or height. In Joel 3:2, God says He will gather the nations in the "valley" of Jehoshaphat to judge them: it is a concrete place, a geographical formation where the multitude can gather.
2. The valley is often fertile and habitable, as it is where water accumulates and rich soil deposits. This is why people willingly settle there. In Joel 3:12, the image of the valley becomes the stage for God's final judgment on the nations: a place where all can converge for the final accounting.
H6010N.origine: The Hebrew word עֵמֶק comes from a root that evokes the idea of hollow or depression. It is a concrete word, derived from the observation of relief: any valley is by definition a hollow in the terrain. The word is used in Hebrew to designate any valley, but it becomes symbolic when it refers to the valley of Jehoshaphat, which represents divine judgment.
H6010N.emploi: The word appears twice in the French Bible, both in the book of Joel in chapter 3. Both occurrences speak of the "valley of Jehoshaphat," a place where God promises to gather all nations for judgment. Although "valley" is primarily a simple geographical term, these passages make it a powerful symbol: God's judgment will unfold there, in an open space where nothing can hide. The valley thus becomes the focal point of the eschatological (future) divine justice announced by the prophet Joel.
H6010N.portee: For the believer, the valley of Jehoshaphat is not a geographical curiosity, but a reminder that God's judgment will come one day upon all nations. This symbolic place invites vigilance and repentance: no one can escape God's judgment. At the same time, for those who belong to God, this valley reminds them that their cause is just and that they will be defended by the Lord on the final day.

sens: depression of the terrain between two heights, low place
fertile or habitable region situated in a hollow
open and uncovered space between mountains or hills
H6010O.detail:
1. A valley is primarily a hollow in the terrain, a natural depression between two higher areas: it is a low path that water naturally follows. In Genesis 14:17, the valley of Shaveh (also called the valley of the king) is the low place where the king of Sodom can meet Abram after his victory.
2. The valley is often a fertile and habitable region, because water flows there and the terrain is suitable for cultivation. It is a coveted living space, contrasted with the barren heights.
3. It is also an open and uncovered space, visible, which can serve as a place of passage, meeting, or gathering, as in 2 Samuel 18:18 where the valley of the king is a notable place where monuments are erected.
H6010O.origine: The Hebrew word עֵמֶק (eméq) designates the depression, the hollow: it comes from a root that expresses the idea of sinking, of digging. Its basic image is that of terrain that sinks, gives way, forming an emptiness. It is a common word in the geographical and poetic vocabulary of the Old Testament to speak of low places and spaces between mountains.
H6010O.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided usages, always in the plural or associated with proper names: "valley of Shaveh" and "valley of the king." In Genesis 14:17, it designates a specific place, a determined geographical space where a meeting can take place. In 2 Samuel 18:18, the same place becomes a memorable spot where a monument is raised. Everywhere, the valley is a concrete, identifiable space, often fertile and frequented, contrasted with mountainous or desert regions.
H6010O.portee: Understanding that God created diverse places — mountains and valleys — and that valleys, although low, are no less important: they are places of life, meeting, and even memory. The valley of the king becomes the place where generations remember; it reveals that the humility of the terrain can carry spiritual nobility.

sens: elongated depression of the terrain, low passage between heights
flat and fertile region at the bottom of a valley
open expanse, uncovered terrain
H6010P.detail:
1. A valley is primarily a natural depression in the terrain: an elongated hollow that sinks between mountains or hills. It is the quintessential low passage between heights. The Valley of Hinnom (Joshua 15:8) is such a corridor carved into the relief around Jerusalem.
2. By extension, the word designates the fertile region that stretches at the bottom of this valley, the flat and cultivable land. It is the practical space that is exploited: the place where the Philistines "spread out" (2 Samuel 5:18) to establish their encampment and where David's warriors descended (1 Chronicles 11:15).
3. The word can also simply mean an open and uncovered space, unobstructed — a cleared terrain where one can move, wage war, or harvest. It is the image of a region without obstacles, accessible and approachable.
H6010P.origine: The Hebrew word עמק comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging, making a hollow, sinking down. It naturally designates a depression in the ground. The valley is what sinks, what is "hollow" in the landscape. In Hebrew, this word is very ancient and very common for describing the geography of Canaan.
H6010P.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the concrete sense of depression or geographical region. It mainly appears in texts that describe the borders of the territory of Israel after the conquest (Joshua 15:8, 18:16): the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem is an important boundary. It also appears during battles against the Philistines: the Valley of Rephaim (2 Samuel 5:18, 5:22, 23:13; 1 Chronicles 11:15, 14:9) is the scene of two confrontations where David achieves victory. The context is always that of a precise geographical position, a real region of the land.
H6010P.portee: The valley reminds the reader that the God of Israel knows and masters every corner of the territory He gives to His people. Valleys are not obstacles: it is in them and through them that boundaries are established and victories are played out. For David, the Valley of Rephaim becomes the place where he defeats the enemy not by brute force, but by trust in God.

sens: depression of the terrain between two heights
low and fertile region
open space of plain
H6010Q.detail:
1. A valley is a natural depression in the terrain, an area that sinks between two hills or two mountains. In Genesis 14:10, the Valley of Siddim was "full of pits of bitumen," which shows that it formed a characteristic hollow in the landscape.
2. The valley is often a fertile and habitable region, unlike the barren heights. It is a space where peoples can gather and fight: in Genesis 14:3 and 14:8, the kings of the enemy cities assemble and array themselves for battle there.
3. By extension, the word designates a low, open region of plain — a territory distinct from the mountain, where the inhabitants circulate and meet.
H6010Q.origine: The Hebrew word émèq (עֵמֶק) comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging or hollowing out. It literally designates what is hollow, what sinks — hence the image of a depression in the terrain. This word is ancient and common in the Hebrew Bible for describing the geography of the Levant.
H6010Q.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible, always to designate the "Valley of Siddim" in Genesis 14. This valley is presented as the scene of the battle where Abram intervenes to rescue Lot. It is described as a region rich in resources (bitumen), but also as a place of danger and flight for the kings who are defeated there. The three occurrences show how this valley structures the narrative: it is the terrain where the combatants assemble, where they array themselves for battle, and where some fall or flee.
H6010Q.portee: For the reader, the Valley of Siddim reminds us that the events of sacred history take place in real and geographically precise locations. It also evokes the contrast between the heights where God reveals Himself and the hollows of the terrain where humanity stirs and fights. The mention of bitumen underscores the material wealth of the cities of the Jordan, but also their vulnerability to the powers coming from the north.

sens: depression of the terrain between two heights
open and fertile plain
low region of a country
open space where armies deploy
H6010R.detail:
1. A valley is a natural depression in the terrain, framed by mountains or hills. It is the hollow between the heights. When the Israelites are ordered to go into the desert, they are told that the Amalekites and Canaanites inhabit "the valley" (Numbers 14:25), meaning the low and accessible lands.
2. The word also designates a fertile plain, a low and arable region of the land. In Judges 1:19, Judah can master the mountain but not "the plain" inhabited by people equipped with iron chariots: it is an open and productive terrain, suitable for agriculture.
3. More broadly, it is a region or area, the lower part of a territory. Isaiah 22:7 speaks of the "valleys" filled with chariots, images of the inhabited and organized lands of a kingdom.
4. From a military perspective, a valley is an open space where troops can gather and maneuver. In Judges 7:12, the Midianites and their allies are "spread out in the valley like a multitude of locusts": it is the open terrain where armies deploy and engage in battle.
H6010R.origine: The Hebrew word עֵמֶק (emeq) comes from a root that evokes the idea of being hollow or deep. In biblical Hebrew, it primarily designates the geographical hollow, but it quickly took on a broader meaning to designate any low region or plain. It is frequently found in names of famous places: the Valley of Hinnom (Gehenna), the Valley of Jezreel. The family of words shares this notion of depression or depth.
H6010R.emploi: The word appears 34 times in the Old Testament, especially in the historical books and the prophets. It describes concrete geographical valleys (Numbers 14:25, Joshua 10:12) and regions where peoples live. Frequently, it designates battlefields or military encampments: Judges 7:12 where the Midianites fill the valley, 1 Chronicles 10:7 where the people of Israel flee when they learn of Saul's death. In Job 39:24, the "soil" of a valley is the terrain that the horse traverses. In poetry (Psalms 60:8, Isaiah 22:7), the term takes on an imagery value to speak of the prosperity or vulnerability of a land.
H6010R.portee: The valley in the Bible often embodies human space, both a place of life and of combat. It reminds us that we live in concrete and corporeal realities, not just spiritual ones. The narratives of battles in the valley (Judges 7, 1 Chronicles 10) teach that even in situations where we are numerous and exposed, God can intervene. The word invites us to see our lives as inscribed in a real geography, where God acts and reigns.

sens: characteristic of what extends far back or down, distance between the surface and the bottom
that which is difficult to know or understand, what remains mysterious
H6011.detail:
1. Depth is the distance that measures how far something extends downwards or backwards. In Proverbs 25:3, the depth of the earth is mentioned to evoke the immense expanse of what surrounds us, so vast that our gaze cannot reach it.
2. Figuratively, depth refers to that which eludes understanding, what remains hidden and mysterious. The same verse compares the depth of the earth to the hearts of kings: just as no one can fathom the depths of the earth, no one can truly know the secret thoughts of those who reign.
H6011.origine: The Hebrew word ʿōmeq comes from a root that means "to be deep, unfathomable." It belongs to the same family as other Hebrew words related to depth and what cannot be measured or understood. The original image is that of a well or a pit: something whose bottom remains invisible and inaccessible.
H6011.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 25:3. It is found in a proverb that lists three realities that man cannot scrutinize: the heavens in their height, the earth in its depth, and the hearts of kings. This enumeration underscores the impenetrability of certain mysteries: just as one cannot reach the heavens or measure the depths of the earth, the true intentions of the powerful remain hidden.
H6011.portee: This word reminds us that certain realities surpass us and that there is wisdom in recognizing the limits of our knowledge. In the face of the mysteries of the world and the human heart, the believer learns humility and trust in God alone, who sees what remains deep and hidden.

sens: That which is deep, difficult to fathom or understand
A language or tongue that is not understood, strange and unintelligible
A word or speech that is incomprehensible
H6012.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes that which is deep, in the sense of what eludes understanding — it cannot be fathomed, measured, or reached. In Proverbs 9:18, the "valleys" of the realm of the dead are mentioned, the deep and hidden domain of the dead, which cannot be seen or fully understood.
2. Applied to language or speech, it describes a word that is not clearly heard, that is not grasped. Isaiah 33:19 speaks of a "people of obscure language that cannot be understood": these are people who speak a barbaric language, so foreign that it remains impenetrable to the listener.
3. Ezekiel 3:5 and 3:6 use the word to say that a language is "unintelligible": the prophet is not sent to peoples whose speeches he would not understand. The word emphasizes the impossibility of communication, the gap between the speaker and the listener.
H6012.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be deep," "to go deeply." The image is that of a depth that cannot be fathomed, of impenetrable darkness. In Aramaic, the cognate word "deep" retains this sense of what is hidden or inaccessible. The word thus expresses the idea of a depth that obstructs understanding.
H6012.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in books of wisdom or prophecy. Proverbs 9:18 uses it to refer to the "valleys" of the realm of the dead, an invisible and incomprehensible domain. The other three occurrences (Isaiah 33:19 and Ezekiel 3:5-6) describe a language or tongue that is not heard, that remains unintelligible. In these last two passages, the word emphasizes the linguistic barrier: a language so foreign that it remains impenetrable, closed to the listener.
H6012.portee: This word reminds us that communication requires mutual understanding: an incomprehensible language or word creates a separation. For the believer, it also emphasizes that there are realities — like the realm of the dead — that remain hidden and unfathomable to our present knowledge. It is an invitation to humility before the mysteries of God.

sens: That which extends far down, or penetrates far inside
That which is hidden, secret, difficult to know
That which is mysterious, unfathomable, beyond understanding
H6013.detail:
1. In Leviticus 13, the word describes a skin lesion that sinks into the flesh: if it "appears deeper than the skin of the body," it is a sign of leprosy (Leviticus 13:3). This is a visible, measurable depth that shows the severity of the affliction.
2. In Job 12:22, what is "hidden in darkness" is brought to light — here, "deep" means what is buried, secret, impossible to see without revelation.
3. In Proverbs 18:4, the words of a man are "deep waters," a poetic image of a depth of thought and wisdom that remains partially veiled and mysterious, like a spring that is not fully visible.
H6013.origine: The Hebrew word עָמֹק comes from a root that expresses the idea of digging or sinking. It primarily denotes a physical and tangible depth, then acquires a figurative sense to express what escapes sight and understanding: the hidden, the mysterious, the unfathomable.
H6013.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Bible. In Leviticus 13 (at least 5 occurrences), it is an objective medical term that describes the depth of a leprous sore. In Job 12:22 and in Proverbs (18:4, 20:5, 22:14, 23:27), it takes on a figurative sense to denote what is hidden, secret, or mysterious — the thoughts of the heart, inaccessible wisdom, or hidden traps. In Psalms 64:7, it refers to secret thoughts. The nuance varies according to the context: concrete depth, depth of the heart or mind, unfathomable depth of God or of evil.
H6013.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that not everything is visible on the surface: true wisdom has a depth (Proverbs 18:4), the intrigues of the heart are hidden, and only God truly knows them (Psalms 64:7). It also reminds us that God scrutinizes the invisible and reveals what is hidden, giving to those who walk with Him the necessary light to distinguish good from evil.

sens: To gather and tie together the cut stalks of grain to form a sheaf
H6014A.detail: 1. To bind into sheaves: this is the action of the reaper who, after cutting the ears of grain, gathers them into a tight handful and ties them with a string or strap to make a sheaf, a small bundle of grain. The image is that of field work at harvest time: the one who binds the sheaves loads his arm to carry them (Psalms 129:7).
H6014A.origine: The Hebrew verb עִמֵּר comes from the root עמר which evokes the idea of gathering and tightening. The related noun עֹמֶר (omer) specifically denotes a sheaf of grain. It is an agricultural term, rooted in the rural life of Israel where the harvest was a crucial time of the year.
H6014A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 129:7. It describes the reaper binding the sheaves of wheat or barley, a fundamental act of the harvest. The poetic context evokes abundance or, in this case, its absence: the one who binds the sheaves cannot fill his hand or load his arm, meaning that the harvest is meager and without blessing.
H6014A.portee: This word brings us back to the humble and daily work of biblical farmers, but also to the dependence of God's people on His blessing. In this psalm, binding the sheaves becomes the image of a prayer for God to prosper the work of their hands and the life of His people.

sens: To reduce someone to a state of servitude or forced dependence
To exploit someone by depriving them of their freedom
To mistreat someone by imposing a yoke of domination on them
H6014B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to put someone in a condition of slavery, that is, to submit them to total domination and take away their freedom. In Deuteronomy 21:14, the man who has taken a captive woman cannot "treat her as a slave" — he cannot sell or exploit her at will, for he has already humiliated her by taking her as a wife: the law recognizes her dignity.
2. The verb also refers to the act of reducing someone to slavery through violence or fraud. In Deuteronomy 24:7, "who has made him his slave" speaks of one who steals a man to subjugate him, and this crime deserves death: it is an assault against the freedom of an Israelite brother.
3. More broadly, it is to mistreat someone by exercising brutal domination over them, a yoke of servitude imposed by force.
H6014B.origine: The Hebrew verb עָמַר (amar) expresses the idea of controlling, dominating, reducing someone to a state of total dependence — as one treats a slave. The word carries the image of complete loss of freedom and dignity. Its reflexive form (hitpael) emphasizes the action of behaving towards someone as one would treat a slave: it is a voluntary act of domination.
H6014B.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Deuteronomy, in a context of law and protection of persons. In Deuteronomy 21:14, it prohibits the master of the house from reducing his captive wife to slavery, recognizing a dignity that slavery would deny. In Deuteronomy 24:7, it designates the capital crime of reducing an Israelite to slavery: this act is ranked alongside the most serious theft and human trafficking. The Israelite law thus protects the freedom of each person, especially that of their brothers in Israel.
H6014B.portee: These two verses remind the reader that human dignity cannot be taken away: one cannot treat a person as a thing or a property to be exploited. For the Christian, this reflects the respect for the freedom and value of each individual — a value that God recognizes in every human being created in His image. The law of Moses here protects the weak and the captives against tyranny, echoing the cry for justice of the Gospel.

sens: Textile fiber obtained from the fleece of sheep or other animals, used for weaving clothing and fabrics
H6015.detail:
1. Wool is the soft, curly fiber that covers the bodies of sheep and certain animals. It is spun and woven to make clothing, fabrics, and blankets. In Daniel 7:9, the vision of the Ancient of Days describes His hair "like pure wool": this comparison evokes a brilliant, soft, and immaculate whiteness, suggesting the holiness and majestic dignity of the celestial figure.
2. In the Law, the first sheaf of the harvest had a particular religious significance: it was presented to the priest, who waved it before the Lord to consecrate the entire forthcoming harvest (Leviticus 23:10-11). It was an act of gratitude and trust in God for the entire harvest.
3. Figuratively, the word also refers to the work accomplished, the harvest itself: a man who forgets a sheaf in his field must leave it for the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, for it is the fruit of his labor (Deuteronomy 24:19).
H6015.origine: The Aramaic word עֲמַר (amar) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word צֶמֶר (tsemer), H6785, which also means wool. These two words share the same Semitic root and the same concrete reality: the textile fiber taken from wool-bearing animals. Wool is one of the first fibers that man used for clothing and protection.
H6015.emploi: The word appears only once in the Aramaic New Testament of Daniel 7:9, in the grand vision of the Ancient of Days. Here, wool is not mentioned for its raw material or everyday use, but as an element of mystical description: the hair of the celestial figure is compared to "pure wool". This comparison emphasizes the immaculate whiteness and luminous aspect of the figure, attributes of purity and holiness in biblical symbolism.
H6015.portee: This image of wool white as snow in Daniel's vision reminds us that God's sacred character is manifested through purity. This brilliant and immaculate whiteness invites the reader to contemplate the holiness of the Ancient of Days and to recognize His absolute transcendence over the earthly kingdoms that succeed one another.

sens: A handful of wheat or barley cut and bound during the harvest
Firstfruits of the harvest, offered to God according to the Law
Product of the labor of the harvesters
H6016A.detail:
1. A sheaf is a handful of grains — wheat or barley — that has been cut and tied together during the harvest. It is the natural way to group and transport the cut stalks: Ruth gathers ears and sheaves left by the harvesters (Ruth 2:7).
2. In the Law, the first sheaf of the harvest had a particular religious significance: it was presented to the priest, who waved it before the Lord to consecrate the entire forthcoming harvest (Leviticus 23:10-11). It was an act of gratitude and trust in God for the entire harvest.
3. Figuratively, the word also refers to the work accomplished, the harvest itself: a man who forgets a sheaf in his field must leave it for the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, for it is the fruit of his labor (Deuteronomy 24:19).
H6016A.origine: The Hebrew word עֹמֶר (omer) literally means a handful, a bundle of grain. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of binding or gathering. The same word is used to measure a quantity: a sheaf is also a measure of grain in the ancient Hebrew system. The Feast of the Sheaf, celebrated the day after the Sabbath of Passover (Leviticus 23:11), takes its name from this first sacred bouquet presented to God.
H6016A.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in legislative passages concerning the harvest and crops. The main references are found in Leviticus 23, where the Law prescribes bringing a sheaf of the firstfruits and waving it before the Lord (Leviticus 23:10-15): it is an offering rite that marks the beginning of the harvest. In Deuteronomy 24:19, the word takes on an ethical coloring: leaving a forgotten sheaf for the poor is an act of charity commanded by the Law. Ruth 2:7 shows the ordinary usage: Naomi gleans among the sheaves, working humbly in the field of Israel. In Job 24:10, the sheaf symbolizes the fruit of another's labor, which should not be unjustly taken.
H6016A.portee: The sheaf teaches the Christian two essential lessons: first, that the harvest comes from God and deserves to be consecrated through worship and thanksgiving; second, that the Law commands charity towards the weak and the needy. The act of waving the sheaf before the Lord expresses a posture of dependence and gratitude that every believer can cultivate. This ancient practice also reminds us that faith translates into concrete actions: leaving ears for the poor is to believe that God is sufficient for our needs.

sens: a unit of capacity equal to one-tenth of an ephah, approximately two liters
the daily portion of food measured for each person
H6016B.detail:
1. The omer is a dry measurement unit used to quantify grains, flour, or other foods. It is precisely one-tenth of an ephah (Exodus 16:36), which corresponds to about two liters. During the wilderness journey, God commands Israel to gather manna by measuring one omer per person for the day (Exodus 16:16).
2. The omer also becomes the individual portion that each person must collect or consume. Exodus 16:18 explains that this measure ensures fairness: whoever gathers more than one omer has no surplus, and whoever gathers less does not lack, as the portion remains fixed. The omer kept in a jar (Exodus 16:33) becomes a tangible memorial of divine provision in the wilderness.
H6016B.origine: The Hebrew word omer likely comes from a root meaning "to measure" or "to pile up." In Aramaic, the word has a similar form. It is a purely technical term related to the practices of measuring and distributing food in ancient Israel. The word does not refer to an abstract entity but to a concrete object: the container itself or the quantity it holds.
H6016B.emploi: The word omer appears six times in Exodus 16, all usages focusing on the account of the manna. In this context, it serves three purposes: first, to designate the standard measure for daily collection (Exodus 16:16, 16:22); second, to verify that the distribution is fair (Exodus 16:18); and finally, to preserve as a memorial the testimony of this miraculous food (Exodus 16:32-33). The term does not change in meaning, but its function shifts from the daily to the commemorative. The omer remains a term exclusively linked to this foundational event in Israel's history.
H6016B.portee: The omer reminds Christians how God reliably and fairly provides for the needs of His people. This measure illustrates that divine provision is never excessive for some nor insufficient for others: it corresponds exactly to real needs. The jar of omer kept as a memorial (Exodus 16:33) invites each generation to remember God's faithfulness, which strengthens trust in the face of present uncertainties.

sens: City in the Jordan Valley, twin of Sodom
Symbol of divine judgment against sin
Type of total and irreversible destruction
H6017.detail:
1. Gomorrah is an ancient city in the Jordan Valley, mentioned alongside Sodom as early as the account in Genesis 10:19. It was part of the urban network of the Canaanites and participated in military alliances, as shown in Genesis 14:8 where the king of Gomorrah joins battle alongside other kings.
2. The Bible presents Gomorrah as the very symbol of sin and judgment: "The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah has increased, and their sin is very grave" (Genesis 18:20). Together, these two cities embody the moral corruption that provokes God's anger.
3. Gomorrah and Sodom were destroyed by fire from heaven in an irreversible judgment (Genesis 19:24). The prophets cite them as the archetype of total ruin: "Like Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighboring cities that were overthrown, says the Lord, no one shall dwell in them" (Jeremiah 49:18). Their destruction becomes a lesson of history.
H6017.origine: The name literally means "submersion" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking the complete engulfing of the city. Gomorrah exists only in biblical texts and has no counterpart in known Mesopotamian literature. It is always mentioned with Sodom, its fate being inseparable from that of Sodom: the two cities form a pair in divine judgment.
H6017.emploi: Gomorrah appears 19 times in the Hebrew Bible and the Greek New Testament, always closely linked with Sodom. It is first mentioned geographically in Genesis (chapters 10 and 14), then becomes a theological motif: the prophets Isaiah (1:9-10, 13:19), Jeremiah (23:14, 49:18, 50:40), and Amos (4:11) invoke it to warn against idolatry, injustice, and rebellion. Deuteronomy 29:23 compares the burning of the territory of Gomorrah to the fate of the land if Israel transgresses the covenant. Everywhere, Gomorrah symbolizes the inevitable judgment of the holy God.
H6017.portee: Gomorrah reminds the reader that God judges sin with certainty and severity. It warns that moral corruption and rejection of God lead to absolute consequences. At the same time, the mention of Gomorrah alongside Sodom testifies to God's faithfulness to His words and His justice, which provides a moral anchor for the believer's faith.

sens: King of the Northern Kingdom (Israel) during the divided monarchy period
Father of King Ahab
Military leader who became king after a revolt
H6018G.detail:
1. Omri is a king of Israel who reigned twelve years over the Northern Kingdom (1 Kings 16:23). He is one of the major figures in Israel's history during the time when the people were divided into two rival kingdoms.
2. Omri is the father of King Ahab, who became famous for his unfaithfulness to the God of Israel and for his conflict with the prophet Elijah. Ahab reigned twenty-two years after his father (1 Kings 16:29).
3. Before becoming king, Omri was the commander of the army of Israel under King Ela. When Zimri assassinated Ela and took power, the people proclaimed him king in reaction (1 Kings 16:16).
H6018G.origine: The name Omri means "servant of the Lord" or "child of the Lord." It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains a reference to God. The name expresses a relationship of dependence or spiritual formation toward the Lord, even though ironically, Omri and especially his son Ahab turned away from faith in God.
H6018G.emploi: Omri appears in the historical accounts of the kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 16 and 2 Kings 8) and is mentioned retrospectively by the prophet Micah (Micah 6:16). The biblical texts report his accession to the throne following a political crisis, his twelve-year reign, and his succession by his son Ahab. His significance mainly lies in his role as the founder of an influential royal dynasty, although the Bible mentions little of his personal deeds. His legacy is primarily associated with the spiritual evil that Ahab brought to Israel.
H6018G.portee: Omri represents a critical turning point in Israel's history: his reign and that of his dynasty mark the deepening estrangement of the Northern Kingdom from the God of Israel. By establishing his capital in Samaria, he structured a kingdom that would become the center of idolatry and disobedience. For the Christian reader, Omri serves as a reminder that political power, without submission to God, can only lead to the spiritual ruin of a nation.

sens: Son of Becher, of the tribe of Benjamin
King of Israel in the ninth century B.C.
H6018H.detail:
1. Omri is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Becher, living at the time of the Exodus and the wilderness. He is mentioned in the genealogy of Benjamin alongside his brothers Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, and others (1 Chronicles 7:8).
2. Omri is also the name of the king of Israel in the north who reigned for twelve years. He was captain of the army of King Ela before taking power, and he is the father of the famous King Ahab, known for his unfaithfulness to God.
H6018H.origine: The name Omri means "child of Jehovah" or "one whom God sees." It is a compound Hebrew name that expresses a relationship of dependence or divine protection. Several individuals bore this name in biblical history.
H6018H.emploi: The biblical text mentions at least four individuals named Omri: a son of Becher of the tribe of Benjamin, whose genealogy is recorded in 1 Chronicles 7:8; the king of Israel in the north, who reigned after King Ela and before his son Ahab; a descendant of Pharez, son of Judah; and a son of Michael, chief of the tribe of Issachar during David's time. The Omri mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:8 is simply an ancestor whose name has been preserved in the Benjaminite genealogy.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah during the time of Exile and Return
H6018I.detail: Omri is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:4. He belongs to the genealogy of the sons of Perez, son of Judah. He is the father of Ammihud and the son of Imri. This character is part of those who returned from the Babylonian exile or who lived during the time of the return to the Holy Land. Although little known and rarely cited, his inclusion in this genealogy shows that he represents the continuity of the people of Judah after the Exile.
H6018I.origine: The name Omri means "Jehovah's pupil" or "one whom Jehovah keeps." It comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of divine protection. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God. The same name Omri also refers to the king of the Northern Kingdom of Israel (a much more famous character), but these are different individuals.
H6018I.emploi: This name designates several people in the history of Israel. This one is a man of Judah mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 9:4, in the genealogical list of the families of Judah who settled in Jerusalem after the Exile. His name appears in the lineage of Perez and testifies to the persistence of Judean families. Unlike the king Omri of the Northern Kingdom, this Omri plays no reported political or military role: he is simply an ancestor whose trace is preserved in the genealogical records of the people returned from captivity.

sens: son of Michael, prince of the tribe of Issachar during the reign of King David
H6018J.detail: Omri is a tribal chief mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when King David organizes the administration of his kingdom. He represents the tribe of Issachar among the twelve princes tasked with governing the twelve tribes of Israel (1 Chronicles 27:18). He is a man from the time of the united monarchy, before the division of the kingdom into Northern Israel and Southern Judah.
H6018J.origine: The name Omri means "servant of the Lord" or "disciple of God," composed of a root denoting one who learns or is trained. In biblical history, this name has been borne by several characters, the most famous of whom is King Omri of the Northern Kingdom, but this one belongs to a later period and is not the same man.
H6018J.emploi: Omri appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 27:18, as the son of Michael and chief of the tribe of Issachar. He is listed among the twelve administrators that King David established to govern the twelve tribes. This is a detail of the political and administrative organization of David's reign, with the biblical text providing no further details about his life or actions.

sens: Descendant de Kohath et de Lévi, père de Moïse, Aaron et Miriam
Un des fils de Bani qui avait pris une femme étrangère au temps d'Esdras
H6019G.detail:
1. Amram is a man of the tribe of Levi living in Egypt and in the desert, a direct ancestor of Moses and Aaron. He is the son of Kohath (who is himself the son of Levi) and married Jochebed, his aunt, with whom he had three children: Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. His name means "exalted people." The Bible mentions him to establish the genealogy of the great figures of Israel and the Levitical priests (Exodus 6:18-20, Numbers 3:19).

2. Another Amram, son of Bani, appears at the time of Ezra among those who had married foreign women and who had to repudiate them according to the law of Israel.
H6019G.origine: The name Amram literally means "exalted people" in Hebrew (from "am" = people and "ram" = exalted, elevated). It is a name that expresses dignity and height. The term "Amramite" (Amrami) designates the descendants of Amram, according to the biblical custom of forming clan names from the patronym of an ancestor.
H6019G.emploi: Amram appears thirteen times in the Bible, mainly in the genealogical lists of Exodus, Numbers, and First Chronicles. The first mention (Exodus 6:18) places him among the sons of Kohath; shortly thereafter (Exodus 6:20), the Bible specifies that he married Jochebed and fathered Aaron and Moses, laying the foundations of the priestly and prophetic lineage of Israel. The passages in Numbers (3:19, 26:58-59) elaborate on this genealogy in more detail. The verses in First Chronicles (6:2-3, 6:18, 23:12-13, 24:20) maintain this genealogical trace in the temple records and Levitical organization. A namesake, a son of Bani, is mentioned at the time of Ezra, but he plays no particular role in sacred history.
H6019G.portee: Amram reminds us that Moses and Aaron, the two most important figures of the Old Testament after Abraham, are from a clearly established Levitical lineage. His existence and lineage affirm that God has prepared His instruments of salvation in order and genealogical order, placing them at the heart of the chosen people. For the reader, Amram is a link in the golden chain that God weaves throughout the history of salvation.

sens: homme qui vivait à l'époque de l'exil et du retour, mentionné dans le livre d'Esdras
H6019H.detail: Amram is a man of the people of Israel who lived during the time of the exile and the return from exile. He is mentioned in the book of Ezra as one of the sons of Bani, a group of men who had taken foreign wives and who had to repudiate them at Ezra's order to comply with the Law (Ezra 10:34). It is only on this occasion that his name appears in the Scriptures.
H6019H.origine: The name Amram means "exalted people" in Hebrew (from am, "people," and ram, "elevated"). He should not be confused with the Amram of the Old Testament, father of Moses and a descendant of Levi, who lived many centuries earlier. The Amram in the book of Ezra is a different person, contemporary with the restoration of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.
H6019H.emploi: The name Amram appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:34. He is listed among the men who, at the time of Ezra, had violated the Law by marrying women from other nations. These men had to separate from their foreign wives to restore their faithfulness to the divine covenant. This Amram thus represents a particular case of the problem of mixed marriages that the religious leaders of Israel sought to correct during the return from exile.

sens: descendants d'Amram, un lévite
membres d'une branche de la famille des Kehathites
H6020.detail:
1. The Amramites are the descendants of Amram, a man of the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. Amram was the son of Kohath and the father of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam — three of the greatest figures of the Old Testament. In Numbers 3:27, the Amramites are listed among the families descending from Kohath, forming a recognized branch of the Kehathites.
