2. These families played an important role in the organization of the people of Israel, particularly for the worship and service of the Tabernacle. In 1 Chronicles 26:23, the Amramites are mentioned again as an administrative and spiritual division of God's people, heirs of an illustrious genealogy.
H6020.origine: The Hebrew word עַמְרָמִי (Amramite) comes from עַמְרָם (Amram, H6019), which literally means "exalted father" or "exalted people." Amram himself was a key figure in the history of Israel: son of Kohath, grandson of Levi, and husband of Jochebed. He fathered Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. The suffix "-ite" marks belonging to a family or descent, as in "Kehathite" or "Levite."
H6020.emploi: The term "Amramites" appears twice in the Bible according to the Segond 1910 translation: in Numbers 3:27 and in 1 Chronicles 26:23. These two occurrences are found in contexts of genealogical and administrative classification of the people of Israel. In Numbers 3:27, during the census of the Levites in the desert, the Amramites are listed as one of the four main families of the Kehathites. In 1 Chronicles 26:23, this same group is enumerated again, this time in the context of the organization of service at the Temple. The usage is purely genealogical and administrative, without particular moral connotation.

sens: General of Absalom's army, son of Abigail, David's sister
H6021G.detail: Amasa is a high-ranking military officer who appears during Absalom's revolt against his father, King David. He is the son of Abigail (sister or half-sister of David according to sources) and Jithra. Absalom places him at the head of his army to replace Joab, the general of King David (2 Samuel 17:25). After Absalom's defeat, David forgives him and appoints him commander-in-chief of his armies (2 Samuel 19:13), but Joab, jealous of this rival, kills him shortly after by stabbing him under the pretense of greeting him (2 Samuel 20:8-10). Amasa dies without having had the time to accomplish the mission that David had entrusted to him: to gather the men of Judah in three days.
H6021G.origine: The name means "burden" or "one who carries." Amasa is a historical figure from the time of the united monarchy in Israel, contemporary with King David and his son Absalom, probably in the 10th century BC.
H6021G.emploi: Amasa appears 15 times in the Bible, primarily in the dramatic account of Absalom's rebellion and its aftermath (2 Samuel 17, 19-20) and in retrospective references in 1 Kings 2. His story illustrates the rivalries and power struggles within the Davidic royal court: appointed general by Absalom, he embodies the hope of new loyalty after the rebellion, but his elimination by Joab shows that the old general will not easily relinquish his authority. Amasa's death remains a long-unavenged act of vengeance, which poses a problem for David at the end of his life.
H6021G.portee: The story of Amasa invites reflection on the fragility of human power, political instability, and the violence that marks court relations. It also shows how David, even as king, cannot always ensure justice: he fails to punish Joab for Amasa's murder. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that earthly kingdoms are fragile and transient, and that only the kingdom of God offers lasting and impartial justice.

sens: Prince of Ephraim during the reign of King Ahaz
H6021H.detail: Amasa is a prince of the Northern Kingdom (Ephraim) during the time of the divided monarchy. He appears in 2 Chronicles 28:12 as one of the leaders who rise up against the soldiers returning from a military campaign, demanding that the prisoners from Judah be released rather than enslaved. He is a man of power and influence, capable of taking a stand for justice and compassion.
H6021H.origine: The name Amasa means "burden" in Hebrew. It is a compound name that evokes the idea of carrying a weight. In the Old Testament, several men bear this name: the most well-known is Amasa, son of Ithra, who was general of Absalom's army during King David's time. The one in our entry is his namesake, living several generations later, son of Hadlai.
H6021H.emploi: Amasa appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 28:12. The text mentions him among four Ephraimite leaders who intervene when King Ahaz's troops return after a defeat against Syria and Israel. These princes oppose the enslavement of the captured Judah prisoners during this battle, demanding that the captives be treated with mercy. It is a moment where moral conscience prevails over vengeance and military interest.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, son of Elkana
Ancestor of the prophet Samuel in the genealogy of the Kohathites
H6022G.detail: 1. Amasaï is a Levite, a member of the tribe of Levi responsible for temple service. He is the son of Elkana and has a son named Achimoth (1 Chronicles 6:25). 2. He appears in the genealogy leading to the prophet Samuel: Amasaï is the ancestor of Mahath and is part of the genealogical succession of the Kohathites, an important branch of the Levites (1 Chronicles 6:35).
H6022G.origine: The name Amasaï means "one who carries a burden" or "heavily loaded" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of carrying, supporting a weight. This name recalls the responsibilities that the Levites bore in divine service.
H6022G.emploi: Amasaï appears twice in the text of Chronicles, always in the genealogical lists of the Levites (1 Chronicles 6:25 and 6:35). These two mentions place Amasaï in the lineage of Elkana and make him an important link in the genealogical chain leading to Samuel, the great prophet of Israel. His name appears only in these two places in the Bible, making him a minor but acknowledged figure of Levitical service.

sens: Warrior and chief of Judah who joined David at Ziklag
Levite of the family of Kohath, father of Mahat
Priest who blew the trumpet before the ark
Levite of the family of Kohath during the reign of King Hezekiah
H6022H.detail: The only clear biblical mention is in 1 Chronicles 12:18: Amasaï is a powerful military chief who, clothed with the Spirit of God, proclaims his allegiance to David with a word of peace and encouragement. This is a decisive moment: this high-ranking man abandons his neutrality to join David in exile, recognizing that God supports him. The three other Amasaï mentioned in the Old Testament (Levites and priests) only appear in genealogical lists or enumerations, without detailed accounts of their deeds.
H6022H.origine: The name means "heavy" or "burdensome" in Hebrew, formed from the root that denotes burden or weight. This name evokes a person of substance and weight — one whose presence and influence are felt.
H6022H.emploi: Amasaï appears only once in the preserved biblical text, in 1 Chronicles 12:18. This is a crucial moment in David's history: while he is hiding at Ziklag, an important warrior, Amasaï, comes to him with his troops and, inspired by the Spirit, declares his support with a solemn blessing. This moment symbolizes the gradual rallying of the powerful around David. Three other characters bear the same name in Levitical genealogies, but they are known only by their position in the priestly families.

sens: Priest who blew the trumpet before the ark
H6022I.detail: A priest who played the trumpet during the solemn transport of the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, under the reign of King David. He appears in the procession of musicians and priests who accompanied the ark to the capital, marking this important moment in Israel's history.
H6022I.origine: The name means "one who carries a burden" or "heavy." He is a Levite from the family of the Kohathites, from the tribe of Levi, the tribe dedicated to priestly functions and temple service.
H6022I.emploi: Amasaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 15:24. He is among the priests who sounded trumpets before the ark of God during its transport to Jerusalem. His name appears in a list of sacred musicians — Shebaniah, Josaphat, Nethaneel, Amasaï, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer — who marked this royal and religious procession with their music.

sens: Levite of the family of Kohath, father of Mahath
H6022J.detail: 1. Amasaï is a Levite of the family of Kohath mentioned in the account of the religious reform of King Hezekiah. He appears in 2 Chronicles 29:12 as one of the chief Levites who rose up to purify the temple. He is identified as the father of Mahath, who himself became an ancestor of the prophet Samuel in the genealogy of the Levites serving in the temple.
H6022J.origine: The name Amasaï literally means "burden" or "load" (from Hebrew עמס, "to carry a burden"). It is a theophoric name that expresses the idea of a charge entrusted by God. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament: a warrior who rallied to David at Ziklag, a priest who blew the trumpet before the ark, and this Levite during Hezekiah's time.
H6022J.emploi: Amasaï appears only once in the Bible: in 2 Chronicles 29:12, where he is cited among the Kohathite Levites who took the initiative to consecrate the temple under King Hezekiah. The context shows that he was a high-ranking Levite leader, prominent enough to be named among the chiefs. He is primarily known as the father of Mahath, which establishes his place in the genealogy of Levitical service in the temple.

sens: Priest of Judah during the time of Nehemiah
H6023.detail: Amaschai is a priest from the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of the return from exile to Jerusalem. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:13, where he is presented as the son of Azareel and part of the leaders of the ancestral houses among the priests who returned to dwell in Jerusalem. His name appears in the list of those who reclaimed the holy city after the Babylonian captivity.
H6023.origine: The name Amaschai (עֲמַשְׁסַי in Hebrew) means "who burdens" or "burdensome" (one who imposes a burden). It is a variant of the name Maasaï (מַעֲשַׂי), formed from a Hebrew root evoking weight or load. In the biblical context, the names of priests often reflect qualities or responsibilities attached to their function.
H6023.emploi: Amaschai is mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in Nehemiah 11:13. He is listed among the genealogies of the priests and Levites who resettled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile, around 445 BC. His appearance in this list shows his important role among the leaders of the priestly ancestral houses tasked with rebuilding the religious community.

sens: fortified city in the hill country of Judah
H6024.detail: Anab is a city located in the southern hills of Judah, about 30 kilometers southwest of Hebron. It appears in the account of the conquest of Canaan: Joshua exterminated the Anakim, those giants who inhabited the region, during his campaign in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 11:21). It is also listed among the cities assigned to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:50).
H6024.origine: The name Anab means "fruit" in Hebrew, probably because the region was fertile and known for its crops.
H6024.emploi: Anab appears twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Joshua. First in Joshua 11:21, where it is mentioned as one of the strongholds from which Joshua drove out the Anakim during the conquest. Then in Joshua 15:50, where it is included in the list of cities assigned to the territory of Judah after the land distribution. This presence in both contexts — military conquest and land allocation — shows the strategic importance of this fortified locality in southern Judea.

sens: fruit of the vine, consisting of juicy berries
bunch of grapes
dried grape or fresh grape
wine (the juice of the grape)
vineyard or viticulture production
image of the chosen people or their fertility
H6025.detail:
1. The grape is the fleshy and sweet fruit produced by the vine. In Genesis 40:10, Pharaoh's servant sees in a dream a vine whose blossoms develop and the clusters yield ripe grapes — it is an image of abundance and maturity.
2. The bunch is a collection of grapes attached together. In Numbers 13:23, the spies bring back a branch with a bunch so heavy that they carry it on a pole between two men — it is proof of the fertility of the promised land.
3. Dried and fresh grapes are the two forms the fruit can take: fresh and juicy at harvest, or dried for preservation. Numbers 6:3 mentions both: the Nazarite must not eat fresh grapes or dried grapes, as he abstains from anything from the vine.
4. Wine is the fermented juice of the grape. Deuteronomy 32:14 speaks of the blood of the grape, a beautiful poetic image for red wine — which shows that the grape is also what becomes wine.
5. The vineyard, the harvest, and the trade of grapes represent an important part of biblical agricultural life. Nehemiah 13:15 recounts how the people sold grapes on the Sabbath, which was forbidden — it reflects the wealth and labor of the land.
6. In prophetic language, the vine and its grapes symbolize the people of Israel and their calling to be fruitful for God. Isaiah 5:2 and 5:4 make the vine the image of the people that God has planted and cultivated, expecting a good harvest from them.
H6025.origine: The Hebrew word enav comes from a root that designates the fruit of the vine. The vine and its fruit are at the heart of Israel's rural and religious life: this is why the word is rich and often used figuratively. In biblical Greek, it is translated as "staphylè" (bunch) or "botrus" (grape) — the Septuagint chooses according to the context. The vine itself (guépen) is a central symbol in the Old Testament of blessing and the covenant relationship with God.
H6025.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always referring to the fruit itself, fresh or dried, or what is derived from it (wine, vinegar). The contexts are concrete: the grape harvests in the promised land (Numbers 13:23), the prohibitions of the Nazarite vow (Numbers 6:3), the Sabbath prohibition (Nehemiah 13:15). But very quickly, the grape becomes an image: Isaiah 5 uses the vine and its grapes to depict God's judgment on His unfaithful people — expecting good grapes, He received only bad ones. Deuteronomy 32 and Genesis 49 also use the grape as an image of fertility or, conversely, degeneration. It is a concrete word that easily accesses the figurative, because the grape was a daily reality and a very apparent gift from God in the promised land.
H6025.portee: The grape reminds the reader that God gives fertile land as a promise of covenant. It is also a fruit that invites gratitude towards the Creator for earthly goods. But beware: Isaiah and Deuteronomy warn that the people can bear bad grapes despite God's care — the fruit depends on the faithfulness of the people as much as on the cultivation of the vineyard. Finally, the grape unites all the senses of biblical life: food, joy, commerce, worship (wine offerings), and prophetic warning.

sens: To be delicate, fragile, of extreme fineness
To taste refined joy, a deep pleasure
To rejoice with abundance and satisfaction
To take pleasure in something in an intimate and personal way
H6026.detail:
1. The word first describes a physical delicacy: a tender person, accustomed to comfort and softness, who cannot endure fatigue or harshness. In Deuteronomy 28:56, the "most delicate woman" is one who, spoiled by a life of ease, would tremble at the thought of putting her foot on the ground because she has lived in luxury.
2. It then means to taste a fine and deep pleasure, a true delight: not a simple superficial contentment, but an inner joy that fills the soul. When the psalmist says, "Delight yourself in the Lord" (Psalms 37:4), he calls to savor the presence of God as one savors a delicious dish.
3. The word can also express abundant and serene enjoyment: one who "enjoys peace" (Psalms 37:11) receives a full and continuous satisfaction, an abundance that fills the heart.
4. Finally, it designates the personal pleasure one takes in something: "Delight yourselves in rich food" (Isaiah 55:2) invites to find personal satisfaction, not elsewhere, but in what truly nourishes.
H6026.origine: The Hebrew root עָנֹג (anag) refers to the idea of sweetness and tenderness. It first describes a tender texture, almost soft, then it shifts to the meaning of taking pleasure, of enjoying. The verb is expressed in several forms: simple (to be delicate), passive (to be made delicate), and reflexive (to take delight oneself). It is a word from the intimate vocabulary of pleasure and personal satisfaction.
H6026.emploi: This verb appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the books of wisdom and prophecy. In Deuteronomy, it describes the state of women spoiled by luxury. In the Psalms and Job, it designates the spiritual attitude: to make God one's delight is to choose Him as the source of one's deepest joy, where others seek elsewhere. Isaiah uses it to call Israel to feast on true (spiritual and material) food rather than vain pursuits. The word expresses each time a conscious and savored personal satisfaction, never passive or forced.
H6026.portee: This word invites the believer to a conscious and joyful relationship with God: not out of duty or obligation, but out of true delight. "Delight yourself in the Lord" means choosing Him not as a burden, but as the source of one's greatest joy. It is also a call to find satisfaction in God rather than in vain riches, and to cultivate a deep inner life where peace with God becomes the true pleasure of the heart.

sens: Refined and delicious pleasure, exquisite satisfaction of desire
Object or place of pleasure and enjoyment
Joy and contentment derived from something precious
H6027.detail:
1. The word denotes a delicate and exquisite pleasure, more than mere satisfaction: it is the deep enjoyment experienced in the presence of what is beautiful or good. In Isaiah 13:22, the "houses of delight" of the king of Babylon evoke his sumptuous palaces, places built for relaxation and enjoyment.
2. It can also refer to the very object that provides this pleasure — a place of enjoyment or a precious possession. These houses of delight, before their ruin, embodied the refinement and wealth of the king.
3. The word also carries the idea of conscious and voluntary joy that one cultivates. In Isaiah 58:13, making "the Sabbath your delight" means turning it into not a burdensome obligation, but a source of deep joy in honor of God — finding contentment in holiness.
H6027.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of sweetness and grace. The word is rare in the Old Testament, but it always paints a picture of distinguished and refined pleasure, far from mere carnal satisfaction. It stands in contrast to the selfish "inclinations" mentioned in Isaiah 58:13.
H6027.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 13:22, it describes the splendid palaces of Babylon, destined for desolation — contrasting human splendor with the fleeting nature of earthly glory. In Isaiah 58:13, it takes on a spiritual significance: making the Sabbath a source of delight transforms an outward observance into an inner joy directed toward God. The rarity of the word underscores its importance in the two places where it appears.
H6027.portee: This word invites the reader to reconsider what they seek as pleasure. For Babylon, earthly "delight" collapses; for the believer in Isaiah 58, true delights arise from communion with God and holiness. This transforms the Sabbath and the life of faith: not into a stern obligation, but into sources of authentic joy.

sens: State of one who lives gently, without effort or fatigue
Excessive delicacy, tenderness towards oneself
Easy and comfortable life, far from deprivation
H6028.detail:
1. Softness describes the condition of someone accustomed to comfort and delicacy: it is one who has always lived surrounded by sweetness and well-being. In Deuteronomy 28:54, the man most "accustomed to softness" is one who has grown up in luxury and delicacy.
2. It is also an excessive tenderness towards oneself, an inability to endure effort or suffering. The woman in Deuteronomy 28:56 did not try to set her feet on the ground "out of softness and delicacy" — she was too accustomed to comforts to accept ordinary efforts.
3. More broadly, it is the love of an easy and comfortable life, far from trials. Babylon in Isaiah 47:1 is called "delicate and voluptuous" because it lived in abundance and power, far removed from suffering.
H6028.origine: This Hebrew word evokes the idea of delight and sensual sweetness. It comes from a root that expresses pleasure and tenderness, the image of a life spent in ease and comfort. Softness in Hebrew designates this way of life where one gives in to easy well-being.
H6028.emploi: This word appears three times in the Bible, always in a context of criticism. In the first two uses (Deuteronomy 28:54-56), it describes the richest and most delicate men and women of Israel, who will show no mercy in times of famine — their habitual softness will render them incapable of compassion when they finally suffer. In Isaiah 47:1, the prophet reproaches Babylon for its life of voluptuousness and arrogance before its fall. The word always carries a negative connotation: softness makes one insensitive and vulnerable.
H6028.portee: This term reminds the believer that prolonged comfort can stifle compassion and weaken character. A life that is too easy risks making us hard towards those who suffer and unable to endure trials when they come. It is an invitation to cultivate sobriety and solidarity rather than the love of personal well-being.

sens: To bind something around a part of the body or to an object, in order to fix it securely
To carry an attached item on oneself as a visible sign or ornament
H6029.detail:
1. To attach means to bind, to tie something in a way that fixes it firmly. The image is that of a rope or a band that is wrapped or tied to hold something in place. In Job 31:36, Job imagines attaching the writing of his accuser to his shoulder, as one would fix a garment or an insignia.
2. Attached to oneself, an object becomes a visible sign, something one carries constantly in plain sight. In Proverbs 6:21, one must attach the words of wisdom to one's neck, not in a physical sense, but as an ornament that one always contemplates, something that characterizes the one who bears it and guides their actions.
H6029.origine: The Hebrew root עָנַד (anad) expresses the idea of binding, tying, fixing around. It is related to verbs of the same family that denote the action of wrapping or tightening. The word evokes the concrete image of a bond and attachment, then extends to the figurative sense of what is visibly worn as a mark or testimony.
H6029.emploi: The verb anad appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 31:36, it describes the action of attaching a writing to one's shoulder and forehead, in the context of the oath where Job proclaims his innocence — it is a theatrical gesture that would make his accusation an ornament he would adorn himself with. In Proverbs 6:21, the same verb invites one to constantly attach the commandments of wisdom to one's heart and neck, that is to keep them visibly close, to carry them as a precious possession one holds dear. Both uses blend the physical sense of the bond with a spiritual or moral reality that is made visible and enduring.
H6029.portee: This word teaches us that the words of wisdom and faith must not remain abstract or forgotten: they must be carried constantly on us, visible in our hearts and actions, as a sign that we truly live by them. To attach the word of God to oneself is to make it inseparable from our conduct and daily choices.

sens: To emit sharp and prolonged cries (like an animal)
To shout, vociferate (referring to a person)
H6030A.detail:
1. The verb describes the characteristic cry of wild animals, particularly jackals and wild dogs: a piercing and prolonged howl. It is the natural sound of these creatures, often evocative of desolation or danger. In Isaiah 13:22, the jackals will howl in the ruined palaces of Babylon, an image of total destruction.
2. By extension, howling also applies to humans who cry out forcefully, expressing intense emotion such as pain, rage, or distress. The word then refers to a raw and wild vocalization, devoid of control.
H6030A.origine: The Hebrew word עוּן comes from a root that evokes the emission of powerful and inarticulate sounds. This family of words encompasses various cries: that of wild animals, birds, and also of humans in the grip of violent emotions. The basic image is that of sound bursting forth, inevitable and intense, from the heart or body.
H6030A.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 13:22. It is a judgment oracle against Babylon: the prophet paints a picture of future desolation where ruins become the refuge of wild beasts that howl there. This cry of the jackals symbolizes the end of human greatness and the invasion of the desert. The unique use underscores the dramatic intensity of this prophetic vision.
H6030A.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment transforms human strongholds into solitudes populated by beasts. It invites the believer to meditate on the vanity of earthly power and the reality of divine judgment. The howling of animals in the ruined palaces becomes a lesson in the fear of God and humility before His authority.

sens: To give a response to someone who speaks or calls
To speak in return, to take the floor again
To testify as a witness before a judge or in a hearing
To grant a prayer, a request
To be able to face an accusation or a question
H6030B.detail:
1. To respond means to give an answer to someone who has spoken to you or asked you a question. It is the basic exchange of words: Abraham "answered" and said (Genesis 18:27), or the woman in Judges 19:28 who "did not answer" — she remained silent when her husband spoke to her.

2. The word also refers to the simple act of taking the floor after someone else. The king "spoke up" in 1 Kings 3:27 to announce his decision: he is the one speaking now, taking his turn to speak.

3. To respond also means to testify before a judge: those who accuse must "respond" (Deuteronomy 19:18), that is, present their testimony and justify themselves before the one they accuse.

4. In prayer, to respond means to grant, to give what is asked. Job cries: "You would call, and I would answer you" (Job 14:15) — God would respond by blessing him. But the psalmist complains: "I cry out by day, but you do not answer" (Psalms 22:3) — God does not grant.

5. It is also to have a response to give, to be able to defend oneself: Isaiah reproaches the people, "Why has no one responded?" (Isaiah 50:2) — no one knew or dared to retort when God called them.
H6030B.origine: The corresponding Aramaic verb exists (עֲנָה anah). The basic image is that of a word being heard: the one who responds makes their voice known in return. The word is also used to refer to the formal deposition of a witness before a judge — one "responds" by giving the testimony they must give. In biblical Hebrew, this verb is very common for all verbal exchanges, whether private or public.
H6030B.emploi: Used 305 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, this verb is one of the most frequent for designating any act of speech. It appears in everyday dialogues (Genesis 18:27, Genesis 40:18), in judicial scenes where the witness "responds" (Deuteronomy 19:18, Deuteronomy 21:7), in worship where the people "respond" to God's words (Exodus 24:3, Joshua 24:16), and especially in prayers where the believer asks God to "respond," that is, to grant (1 Samuel 7:9, Psalms 22:3). The Segond translates this verb in various ways depending on the context: "respond" for a simple reply, "grant" for divine listening, "word" or "to take the floor" to indicate the passing of speech to someone else, "to retort" for a comeback.
H6030B.portee: To respond to God is to trust Him and await His intervention. The silence of God — when He does not "respond" — is a trial for faith. Conversely, learning that God "responds" to those who cry out is a promise of hope. For the believer, using this word is to acknowledge that every prayer is an expectation of the divine word, and that faith is nourished by the certainty that God hears us and will respond.

sens: To make a melody, words heard to a musical tune
To express joy or praise through singing
To modulate one's voice while speaking, to respond in a singing manner
H6030C.detail:
1. To make a melody, words heard to a musical tune: this is the primary and most concrete meaning. When Israel reaches the edge of the Red Sea, Miriam "sings" a song in response to deliverance (Exodus 15:21). It is an act of musical expression, intentional and joyful.
2. To express joy or praise through singing: the verb denotes the action of celebrating God or a happy event by raising one's voice. At the foundation of the temple, the Israelites "sang," celebrating and praising the Lord, and all the people shouted for joy (Ezra 3:11). It is joy that gives birth to song.
3. To modulate one's voice while speaking or to respond in a musical way: singing can also be a way of expressing oneself, a particular intonation. Miriam "responded" by singing to the children of Israel, which shows that singing here is closely linked to communication and communal participation.
H6030C.origine: The Hebrew verb עָנָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of "responding" and "making one's voice heard." The family of the word also encompasses the meaning of "to afflict" or "to grieve" (through the cry of the heart). It is a polysemous root: depending on the context, it shifts from the general idea of "emitting a voice" (crying, calling, singing) to emotional nuances. The word is very common in the Old Testament to express all forms of vocal expression, from lament to joyful song.
H6030C.emploi: The verb appears 13 times in the provided references. It is primarily used in the sense of "singing" praise or celebration: after crossing the Red Sea (Exodus 15:21), at the well dug in the desert (Numbers 21:17), at the foundation of the temple (Ezra 3:11). But it also nuances: in 1 Samuel 18:7 and 29:5, they "sing" David's exploits "while dancing," blending song with dance and warrior joy. In the Psalms, it is a song of praise addressed to God (Psalms 119:172, 147:7). The word thus encompasses all solemn or joyful vocal expression: celebration, praise, recounting the wonders of God.
H6030C.portee: Singing is presented in the Bible not as entertainment, but as a natural and profound response to God's acts. It is the means by which the people enter into communion with God and are strengthened in trust. For the Christian reader, this reminds us that sung praise is not an addition, but an essential part of the life of faith: it is through singing that we confess our convictions and encourage one another.

sens: To be occupied with a task, to apply oneself to something
To assign an activity, to impose an occupation
H6031A.detail:
1. To be occupied or absorbed by a task: this conveys the idea of being taken, engaged in an activity that requires effort and attention. In Ecclesiastes 1:13, the Preacher says he "applied his heart to seek" — he submitted, engaged himself in this quest for wisdom.
2. To assign, impose an occupation on someone: this is the same root viewed from the perspective of the one imposing the task. God "submits" the sons of man to occupations (Ecclesiastes 1:13 and 3:10) — not as an arbitrary punishment, but as the very condition of human life: we are all bound to works, searches, responsibilities that we must fulfill.
H6031A.origine: The verb עָנָה (anah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of being bent, curved, engaged — hence "to be occupied" or "to submit to." The word suggests a certain difficulty: occupation is not leisure, but work that requires effort. The same family of roots appears in other Hebrew forms related to effort, fatigue, and personal commitment.
H6031A.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Segond, both in Ecclesiastes (1:13 and 3:10), where the Preacher meditates on the human condition. In 1:13, he refers to his own quest: he has devoted himself, submitted to the search for wisdom. In 3:10, he generalizes: it is the lot of every man — God submits each to an occupation, a task that must be accomplished. The context is one of vanity and human limitation: we cannot escape our occupations; they are part of God's plan for us.
H6031A.portee: This word reminds us that the occupation, work, and responsibilities we bear are entrusted by God Himself — they are not accidents or injustices, but the very fabric of human life. For the Christian, this invites us to see our occupations as a calling from God, not as a curse, and to seek meaning in our relationship with the Creator rather than in the visible result alone.

sens: To subject someone to physical or moral suffering, to mistreat, to oppress.
To reduce someone's pride, to humiliate them before others.
To humble oneself, to voluntarily mortify oneself through fasting or ritual fasting.
To be in a state of sorrow, depression, physical or moral weakness.
H6031B.detail:
1. To afflict primarily means to cause someone to suffer through blows, injustices, or brutal domination. This is what the Egyptians did to the Israelites: "The Egyptians mistreated us and oppressed us" (Deuteronomy 26:6). Affliction is a violence inflicted from the outside.
2. It also means to reduce someone to humiliation, to publicly lower their dignity. When David is weakened, God says: "I will humble the descendants of David" (1 Kings 11:39) — not to destroy them, but to bend them.
3. The word also designates the voluntary act of 'humbling oneself': fasting on the Day of Atonement means 'humbling your souls' (Leviticus 23:27), that is, accepting deprivation to acknowledge one's dependence on God and one's guilt.
4. Finally, it is the state of one who is afflicted: to be prostrated, oppressed by suffering or grief. Joseph "was bound in chains" (Psalms 105:18) — he was constrained, humiliated, in a low position.
H6031B.origine: The Hebrew verb עָנָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of bending, folding, or lowering. It also gave rise to the noun עָנִי (ani), the poor or unfortunate, one who is bent under the weight. Aramaic uses the same root with a similar meaning. The word first paints a physical image — the body bending, collapsing — before describing the state of the soul.
H6031B.emploi: This verb is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible (76 occurrences). It first appears in narratives: the oppression of the Hebrews in Egypt (Exodus, Deuteronomy), the mistreatment of Samson (Judges), the crime against the concubine (Judges 19). It is then found in the cultic Law to describe the fast of the Day of Atonement, where Israel 'humbles its soul' (Leviticus). The Psalms use it broadly: personal affliction or affliction inflicted by God to test or correct. Isaiah 53 applies it to the suffering Servant: he is 'mistreated', 'oppressed', silent. The word thus designates both human violence and a trial ordained by God, as well as an imposed action or a voluntary act of submission to God.
H6031B.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reveals that affliction is never accidental: it comes either from the evil of men or from the hand of God who tests His people to correct them. It also teaches that to afflict oneself — to fast, to acknowledge one's weakness before God — is an act of wisdom and faith, not guilt. Isaiah 53 finally shows that Jesus Himself bore affliction, silent and submissive, which gives a redemptive meaning to the suffering of the righteous.

sens: To give a response to someone who has spoken
To take the floor to start speaking
To resume speaking after an interruption
To declare something as a reaction
H6032.detail:
1. To respond means to address an answer to the one who asked a question or spoke first. In Daniel 3:24, the king asks: "Did we not throw three men into the fire?" and his advisors 'responded' directly to his question by confirming: "Certainly, O king!"
2. To take the floor means to start speaking, to open one's mouth to express oneself. Daniel 2:47 says that "the king spoke to Daniel and said", which means he took the initiative to speak.
3. To resume speaking means to start talking again after someone else has stopped speaking. In Daniel 2:5, "the king resumed speaking and said to the Chaldeans", as if he were expressing himself again after listening to them.
4. To declare something can also be a use of the word: in Daniel 4:19, Belshazzar 'responded' to the king not with a simple reply, but by expressing his interpretation of the dream in a broader way.
H6032.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from a root that evokes the action of opening the mouth and letting out speech. In Hebrew, the related verb עָנָה (anah) has the same fundamental meaning. The word 'response' (עֲנוּ) derives from the same root. This family of words revolves around the idea of giving a verbal reaction: one responds when one opens one's voice in return.
H6032.emploi: The verb עֲנָה appears 28 times in the Aramaic Bible, almost always in the book of Daniel. It is used to describe the exchanges of words between King Nebuchadnezzar and his advisors, his wise men, or the prophet Daniel. Often, several characters 'take the floor' or 'respond' in a royal conversation. The word can mean a strict response (reacting to a question), but also simply 'to start speaking' or 'to continue speaking'. In all cases, it is the action of producing a word after or in response to someone else. The Segond translates this verb as 'respond', 'resume speaking', or 'take the floor' depending on the exact context.
H6032.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of speech in the Bible: to speak is not a trivial act, but a form of action and commitment. When Daniel or the king 'respond', they do not just produce noise: they exercise authority, they confess a truth, they establish a connection. For the Christian reader, this emphasizes that our words matter and reflect our heart and faith.

sens: one who suffers from need, who lacks resources
one who is crushed by poverty or misery
one who is humiliated or lowered in their condition
H6033.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who suffers from material poverty — who lacks food, clothing, security. In Daniel 4:27, King Nebuchadnezzar is urged to have compassion for the 'unfortunate', that is, those whom injustice and exploitation have reduced to misery.
2. More broadly, it refers to one whose condition is low, crushed, humiliated. The basic idea is one of lowering or oppression: the unfortunate is one who 'is brought low'.
3. By extension, the word can also evoke the inner attitude of one who recognizes their nothingness before God — one who is humble, aware of their smallness. This spiritual nuance appears in some prophetic and wisdom contexts of the Old Testament.
H6033.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that originally means 'to be low' or 'to lower oneself'. It is the same radical that generates other Hebrew words related to poverty, humiliation, and lowering. The root conveys the image of a descent, a low position in social or moral order. In Aramaic — the language of Daniel — this word retains this fundamental sense of destitution and lowering.
H6033.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 4:27, in a prophetic context addressed to the Babylonian king. The prophet Daniel advises Nebuchadnezzar to transform his heart by ceasing to sin and showing compassion towards the unfortunate — in other words, to manifest justice and pity towards the poor and oppressed in his kingdom. The usage emphasizes that the king's own well-being depends on his attitude towards the weakest of his subjects.
H6033.portee: This word reminds the reader that God sees and cares for those who suffer from poverty and oppression. For the believer, it invites recognition of the unfortunate around them and to show them justice and compassion, not through distant charity, but through concrete action — one of the marks of a converted heart.

sens: One who suffers from poverty, material need
One who is weakened, oppressed, defenseless
One who is humble, gentle in character, unpretentious
One who humbly accepts their condition before God
H6035.detail:
1. The unfortunate is primarily one who lacks resources, who is in economic need. In Psalms 10:12, the psalmist cries out: "Do not forget the unfortunate!", speaking of those whom no one helps and who are abused.
2. It is also one who is crushed, without strength to defend themselves. In Job 24:4, the poor are driven from the path, the unfortunate are forced to hide — they are victims, without recourse.
3. The word also designates one who is humble, gentle, without pride. In Proverbs 16:19, "to be humble with the humble" evokes a heart attitude, an absence of presumption. Moses embodies this humility: Numbers 12:3 describes him as "more humble than any man."
4. Biblical humility is finally this confident submission to God. In Psalms 25:9, God "guides the humble in justice" — they are not morally weak, but men who recognize their need for God and accept His will.
H6035.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes humiliation, lowering, a low condition. It carries the idea of someone who has nothing to show, nothing to claim — neither wealth, nor prestige, nor personal strength. Material poverty and moral humility are linked in biblical thought: one who cannot elevate themselves learns to bow down.
H6035.emploi: This word appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Psalms (13 times) and Proverbs. The contexts are very diverse: sometimes it describes the material plight of the poor and oppressed (Amos 2:7: "They crush the unfortunate"), sometimes the attitude of one who trusts in God without pretension (Psalms 37:11: "The unfortunate will inherit the land"). The prophet Isaiah uses it to announce the coming of the Messiah: he "brings good news to the unfortunate" (61:1). The word nuances its meaning according to the context: it designates sometimes an economic or social situation, sometimes a disposition of the heart.
H6035.portee: This word challenges the believer on two levels. First, it calls for justice: God cares for the unfortunate and oppressed, and the believer must do the same (Proverbs 14:21: "Whoever despises their neighbor sins"). Secondly, it invites each person to recognize their own need before God — to accept being "unfortunate" and humble rather than proud and self-sufficient. This is the condition for receiving God's grace.

sens: man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H6036.detail: Anub is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:8. He is the son of Kots and the brother of Zobebah and Harum. His name means "associate" or "confederate", perhaps evoking a trustworthy or allied man. He is known only through this genealogy of the house of Judah, where he occupies a place among the descendants of Judah and Caleb.
H6036.origine: The name Anub comes from a Hebrew root meaning "confederate" or "associate". It belongs to the same family of words that designate an alliance or union. In the genealogy of 1 Chronicles, Anub is listed among the descendants of Judah through Ashur, the father of Tekoa, which connects him to the important lineages of the tribe.
H6036.emploi: Anub appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:8. He is mentioned in the context of a detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah during the period of the divided monarchy. This genealogy lists the sons and descendants of Judah, allowing for the tracing of the main families of this tribe. Anub is presented as the son of Kots and the brother of Zobebah and Harum, showing his role in the continuation of the Judean lineage.

sens: Absence of harshness, roughness, aggressiveness in words and actions
Humility, modesty, absence of pride or pretension
Benevolent condescension, gracious attitude of one who could dominate but chooses kindness
H6037.detail:
1. Gentleness is primarily a quality of what is not rough or violent. It is the ability to treat others without brutality, with words and gestures full of grace. In Psalm 45:5, the king must uphold "truth, gentleness, and justice": these three values go together, gentleness being not weakness but gentle firmness.
2. Gentleness also expresses humility and modesty — it is not to boast of one's strengths or rank. In Psalm 18:36, the psalmist says that God "makes me great by Your goodness": true greatness comes from this humble and dependent attitude, not from arrogance.
3. Finally, it is generous condescension, the attitude of one who is strong but bends toward the weak with kindness. When a king or God treats someone with gentleness, it is a deliberate act of grace.
H6037.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of bowing down, bending — hence "to descend" in dignity or position to treat someone as an equal or with compassion. This is why gentleness and humility are so closely linked: gentleness inclines the one who practices it. The Hebrew word contrasts with pride and stiffness.
H6037.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible according to the provided usages. In Psalm 18:36, it describes how God's benevolent action "enlarges" or "makes great" the psalmist — divine gentleness gives him true greatness. In Psalm 45:5, it is a virtue that the just king must uphold and embody, alongside truth and justice. In both cases, gentleness is a strength, not a weakness: it comes from God and transforms the one who receives or practices it.
H6037.portee: Gentleness is not for the Christian a secondary or passive virtue. It is an expression of moral strength and closeness to God. To receive God's gentleness is to truly grow; to practice it oneself is to walk in justice, not against it. It invites everyone to consider that a certain humility and grace in our relationships with others reflect the nature of God Himself.

sens: modesty, absence of pride
gentleness, meekness towards others
deep sense of one's weakness before God
virtue that prepares for glory and God's blessings
H6038.detail:
1. Humility is the opposite of pride: it is recognizing that one is not great by oneself, but becomes great through God's goodness (2 Samuel 22:36). It is true modesty, not a facade.
2. It also means gentleness towards others, absence of pretension or harshness: an attitude of a tender and benevolent heart.
3. It expresses the feeling of one's own weakness before God: recognizing oneself as small and dependent, like a fragile creature. It is primarily a lived reality, not just a moral virtue.
4. It is a protective virtue: it precedes glory and blessings (Proverbs 15:33; 18:12; 22:4). He who humbles himself before God will be exalted by Him; he who exalts himself risks ruin (Proverbs 18:12).
H6038.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be bent, to humble oneself, to be weak." The image is that of a body that bends, lowers, and becomes flexible. A humble person is therefore someone who does not stiffen with pride but allows themselves to be shaped by the wisdom and hand of God. Close variants exist in Hebrew (such as ענוה "gentleness"), which share this idea of flexibility of heart.
H6038.emploi: This word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always with a strongly positive value. It is found mainly in Proverbs (three times), where it is systematically presented as a virtue leading to blessing: it precedes glory (15:33; 18:12), it produces wealth, glory, and life (22:4). It is also linked to the fear of God and to righteousness (Zephaniah 2:3). Only one usage in 2 Samuel 22:36 employs it in a warrior and physical context (to become great), but it retains a moral connotation. Biblical humility is never a shameful weakness, but a spiritual strength.
H6038.portee: Humility is a key to God's plan for our lives. It protects us from falling (18:12) and prepares us to receive His blessings: wealth, honor, and life (22:4). Recognizing one's weakness and humbling oneself before the Lord is to place oneself in a position where God can exalt us. It is a central attitude in the life of faith, transforming our relationship with success, power, and others.

sens: Suffering, distress or physical and moral affliction
State of humiliation or degradation in the face of misery
Situation where one cries out to God in need
H6039.detail:
1. The word designates real suffering, a distress that affects the one who endures it. It is the state of one who suffers, who is in pain. In Psalm 22:25, the psalmist affirms that God does not despise the pains of the miserable: he recognizes that God sees and hears the concrete suffering of the one who cries out.
2. Pain also implies a form of humiliation, degradation — the one who suffers is in a low, exposed condition. It is the state of the miserable who has nothing but their cry to turn to God.
3. This pain drives one to cry out to God: it is the context in which prayer, the call, is born. It is because one is in pain that one seeks help from the one who can hear and respond.
H6039.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes lowering, bending under weight. Pain is what bends a person, what causes them to bow under the burden of suffering and misery. It is a state where the person is reduced, impoverished, in distress.
H6039.emploi: This word appears only once in the provided Old Testament (Psalms 22:25). It describes the situation of the miserable, the poor who suffers. The context shows that pain does not repel God; on the contrary: God has neither contempt nor disdain for it. The psalmist confesses that God listens to the one who cries out from their pain and does not hide His face from them. It is a word of comfort for the one who endures.
H6039.portee: This verse teaches the believer that their suffering is not hidden from God, nor despised by Him. Even in pain, even when one is at their lowest, God listens to those who cry out to Him. It is an invitation to trust: pain does not isolate from God; it can instead become the path where His goodness is revealed.

sens: State of physical or moral suffering caused by misfortunes, poverty, oppression
Condition of poverty or material deprivation
Situation of distress or inner anguish
Difficult work, painful effort
Humiliation or degradation
H6040.detail: 1. Misery primarily designates the suffering that someone endures — whether caused by misfortune, oppression, or circumstances. The angel tells Hagar: "the Lord has heard you in your affliction" (Genesis 16:11), while she flees from her mistress; God sees "the suffering" of the Israelites oppressed in Egypt (Exodus 4:31) and delivers them. 2. It also designates poverty or deprivation: the state of one who lacks resources and lives in hardship. 3. It is also inner anguish, moral distress: the psalmist prays, "For you see my misery, you know the anguish of my soul" (Psalms 31:8), and finds comfort in his misery by remembering God's promise (Psalms 119:50). 4. The word also applies to laborious work, costly effort: David enumerates the resources he has prepared "by my efforts" for the temple (1 Chronicles 22:14). 5. Finally, it evokes humiliation, degradation — the fate of one who is crushed under the weight of their misfortune.
H6040.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of pressure, bending, collapsing. The one who suffers is literally "crushed" or "bent" under the weight of their misfortune. Misery is therefore the state of one who bends under the burden — whether material (poverty), physical (illness, captivity), or moral (sadness, anguish). This concept is very present in the Psalms and in the book of Job, where it expresses the raw experience of human suffering.
H6040.emploi: The word appears 36 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms (11 occurrences), Lamentations (5 occurrences), and the book of Job (5 occurrences) — the books where one cries out to God in distress. It also appears in the account of Israel's oppression in Egypt (Exodus 3:7, 3:17, 4:31), where God "sees" the misery of His people and intervenes to save them. In the Psalms, the supplicant asks God to see or consider their misery, as a call to His compassion. In Lamentations, Jeremiah enumerates the misfortunes of captive Jerusalem: "Judah has gone into exile under misery" (Lamentations 1:3). The word designates both current and visible suffering, as well as the painful memory of the past that must not be forgotten.
H6040.portee: This word teaches the Christian that God does not turn a blind eye to human suffering. When the Psalms or Job cry out their misery, it is so that God hears them and intervenes. The Bible does not hide the weight of distress; it names it frankly — and it affirms that God sees it. For the tested believer, this word says that their suffering is not ignored by God; for those who enjoy peace, it calls for compassion towards the miserable and the oppressed.

sens: one who lacks material resources, goods, money
one who is weak, defenseless against others
one who suffers, who is in misery or affliction
one who is humble, humble in heart, unpretentious
H6041.detail:
1. The poor is primarily one who has no money, no property — this is material poverty. In Israel, the law protected these individuals: prohibition against oppressing them as debtors (Exodus 22:25), obligation to leave gleanings for the harvest (Leviticus 23:22). This is a visible, pressing economic reality.
2. But this word also refers to the person made weak by their circumstances, one who cannot defend themselves alone. The wicked easily take advantage of them (Psalms 37:14); the powerful crush them (Isaiah 3:15). It is a matter of vulnerability and inequality of power.
3. The poor is one who suffers, who bears the weight of their condition — "unfortunate" or "miserable." A psalmist cries: "I am afflicted and close to death from my youth" (Psalms 88:16). Material poverty often leads to distress of the heart.
4. By extension, this word can also describe spiritual humility, a heart poor in pride. Zechariah announces the Messiah who comes "humble" (Zechariah 9:9). It is an inner poverty, an absence of self-sufficiency before God.
H6041.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of bending, of bowing. The poor is one who is bent, crushed by their fate. In Hebrew, several words describe misery — "dal" (weak), "ebyôn" (needy) — but "âni" emphasizes the condition of one who suffers and their lack of resources. The family of this word includes verbs meaning to afflict or to humiliate.
H6041.emploi: This word appears 72 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, the Prophets, and the Law. It occupies a central place in divine justice: God "upholds the cause of the afflicted" (Job 36:6) and cares for their cause (Jeremiah 22:16). The Torah commands the Israelites not to oppress the poor and to treat them with respect. The Psalms plead with God to defend the poor against the wicked who target them (Psalms 37:14). The Prophets angrily denounce those who crush the poor — Isaiah rebukes the powerful who trample the people (Isaiah 3:15), Amos condemns those who take advantage of them (Amos 8:4). This word also has a spiritual dimension: Zechariah announces a humble king riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9), heralding the Messiah.
H6041.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals the heart of God: He does not forget the small, the fragile, those whom the world despises or crushes. It is a call to justice and compassion towards the materially poor, but also an invitation to recognize one's own spiritual poverty — our need for God, our lack of self-sufficiency. True salvation begins when one accepts to be nothing without Him.

sens: Levite musician serving in the temple during the reign of King David
H6042G.detail: Unni is a Levite (member of the tribe of Levi, dedicated to religious service) who appears twice in the account of the transportation of the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem during the time of King David. He is mentioned among the musicians and gatekeepers of the temple: in 1 Chronicles 15:18, he is listed among the second-order Levites who accompany the Ark; in 1 Chronicles 15:20, he is designated as a player of the lyre (a string instrument). His role was thus to participate in solemn religious celebrations and to guard the sanctuary.
H6042G.origine: The name Unni means "afflicted" or "one who suffers" in Hebrew (from the root עָנָה, which speaks of poverty or humiliation). This name contrasts with his elevated function: a Levite bearing such a name reminds us that to God, the humble and the afflicted are precious, and that true dignity comes from the service offered to God rather than from external condition.
H6042G.emploi: Unni appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 15, the passage that recounts how King David transported the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem. In this context of a major national and religious celebration, Unni is presented as one of the privileged Levite musicians, capable of playing the lyre to honor God. His inclusion in this solemn list shows that he was a respected servant of worship, although we know nothing else about his life or ministry.

sens: Levite from the time of the return from exile
H6042H.detail: Unni is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:9. He served a musical or liturgical function alongside his fellow Levites at the time when the Jewish people returned from exile in Babylon. His role was to participate in the service of the restored temple, alongside other musicians and worship servants.
H6042H.origine: The name Unni means "afflicted" or "one who suffers," deriving from a Hebrew root expressing affliction. This name could reflect the trials endured during the Babylonian exile, or simply express a condition of humility before God. No documented connection with other individuals of this name in the Old Testament.
H6042H.emploi: Unni appears only in Nehemiah 12:9, in the context of the return from exile and the restoration of the temple. He is cited alongside Bakbukiah and other Levites who "performed their duties alongside their brothers." This passage is part of the list of Levites responsible for the songs and liturgical service during the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem. His uniqueness in the biblical text suggests a specialized but poorly documented role.

sens: Jewish priest during the Exile and Return
H6043G.detail: Anajah is a priest who lived after the Babylonian Exile, when the Jews returned to rebuild Jerusalem. He appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 8:4, where he stands beside Ezra the scribe during the public reading of the Law before the gathered people. His presence at Ezra's right, among other religious and civil authorities, shows his role as a leader in the restoration of Israel's religious life after the Exile.
H6043G.origine: The name Anajah means "The Lord has answered" or "God has answered" — an expression of gratitude towards the Eternal. This name reflects the faith of the Jewish people after the Exile: God had heard their prayers and brought them back from captivity. The name combines two elements: the root that expresses "to answer" or "to be attentive," and the reference to the Lord (God). It was a common name among Jews of that time to express their hope in divine intervention.
H6043G.emploi: Anajah appears only once in Scripture, in Nehemiah 8:4. He is listed among the thirteen priests and scribes who stood beside Ezra when he read the Law to the people after the Return from Exile (around the 5th century BC). This ceremony, a significant occasion for renewing the covenant with God, shows that Anajah was a recognized and trusted religious leader in the reconstituted community of Jerusalem.

sens: Priest who signed the covenant under Nehemiah at the time of the return from exile
H6043H.detail: Anajah is a priest who lived at the time of the return from exile after the Babylonian captivity. He appears in the list of religious leaders and notable figures who solemnly signed the renewed covenant with God under Nehemiah's leadership (Nehemiah 10:22). This moment was crucial: the people, returning to Jerusalem, committed to observing the Law of Moses and remaining faithful to the Eternal. As a signing priest, Anajah represented the clergy in this communal pact and personally committed to holiness and obedience.
H6043H.origine: The name Anajah means "the Eternal has answered": it expresses confidence in divine listening. It is a typical name from the post-exilic period, composed of the divine name Yah (abbreviated from Yahweh) and a verb meaning "to answer." This name reveals the faith of the parents who gave it: they recognized that God had listened to and answered their prayers.
H6043H.emploi: Anajah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:22, in the list of priests and leaders who signed the covenant treaty. This context shows that he was a religious figure significant enough to be named among the official signatories. His name appears alongside other priests and Nehemiah himself, testifying to his role in the religious restoration of Jerusalem after the exile.

sens: City of Judah in the southern mountains
H6044.detail: Anim is a small town located in the mountains of the southern region of Judah. It appears in the biblical text as part of the territory allocated to the tribe of Judah during the division of the promised land (Joshua 15:50).
H6044.origine: The name literally means "fountains" in Hebrew, likely evoking the presence of water sources in this mountainous region where water was precious.
H6044.emploi: Anim appears only once in the Bible: in Joshua 15:50, where it is listed among the cities that Joshua distributed to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. This mention is part of the detailed list of cities in the Judean territory, showing the administrative organization of the newly occupied land.

sens: work, task that must be accomplished
concern, worry of the mind
set of circumstances, situation one is living in
burden, responsibility or lot assigned to someone
H6045.detail:
1. Occupation is primarily a work, a concrete task that must be done. It is the labor of everyday life, the task we accomplish. In Ecclesiastes 1:13, the Preacher speaks of the "painful occupation" to which God subjects the sons of man: it is the effort required to explore and understand all that is done under heaven.
2. By extension, it is what occupies the mind, what concerns us: worries, thoughts that hold us back. In Ecclesiastes 5:2, when dreams arise from the multitude of occupations, the text refers to these mental concerns that agitate the mind before sleep.
3. It is also a matter, an event, a particular situation one goes through. In Ecclesiastes 4:8, the isolated man is engaged in a bad "thing": his condition, his lot of solitude and endless work.
4. Finally, it is the lot, the share, the responsibility that falls to someone. In Ecclesiastes 2:23, the "share" of the rich is nothing but pain and grief: it is his assigned portion, his condition of life.
H6045.origine: The Hebrew word inyan comes from a root that evokes the idea of being occupied, being engaged in something. The family of the word produces variants that emphasize either the aspect of work or that of concern. It is a typical term in the vocabulary of Ecclesiastes, which particularly uses it to explore the vanity of all human endeavor.
H6045.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in Ecclesiastes (7 occurrences, except 1 in Nehemiah). Ecclesiastes uses it to designate the work imposed on men, the concern that arises from it, and the ambiguous lot represented by human existence. In Ecclesiastes 1:13 and 3:10, it is the painful task assigned by God. In Ecclesiastes 2:23-26, it is the painful share of the rich who accumulates, and the consuming care of gathering goods. In Ecclesiastes 5:2, it is the multitude of concerns of the mind. The word thus oscillates between concrete action (work) and mental state (concern), united by the idea of exhausting engagement.
H6045.portee: For the Christian reader, this word summarizes a truth that Ecclesiastes discovers: all human work, all concern, all activity without God leads to vanity. It invites the believer not to place his trust in his own strength or accomplishments, but to recognize that it is God who gives meaning and rest. The word also calls to examine what truly occupies our hearts: are our occupations trivial, or do they serve the glory of God?

sens: city of Levites in Issachar
city designated for the descendants of Gershom
H6046.detail: Anem is a city that the people of Israel assigned to the Levites, specifically to the sons of Gershom (a branch of the Levites). It was located in the territory of the tribe of Issachar. The Bible mentions Anem along with its suburbs, that is, the fields and lands that surrounded it, a right granted to all Levitical cities for the maintenance of the priests and the servants of the worship (1 Chronicles 6:73).
H6046.origine: The name Anem means "fountains" in Hebrew, suggesting the presence of water sources in this place. It is the same city as En-gannim, another Hebrew name meaning "spring of gardens," which highlights the abundance of water and the fertility of the site. These two names refer to a single location, recognized for its water resources.
H6046.emploi: Anem appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:73, in an official list of Levitical cities distributed to the various priestly families. It is among the cities given to the Gershonites, an important branch of the Levites responsible for transporting and guarding the furnishings of the sanctuary. This mention underscores the territorial organization of Israel and the care with which each Levitical family received cities distributed across the different tribal territories.

sens: Egyptian people descended from Mitsraïm
H6047.detail: The Anamim are an Egyptian people mentioned in the biblical genealogies as one of the nations descended from Mitsraïm (Egypt), alongside the Ludim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, and other peoples. They appear in the table of nations in Genesis 10:13 and are recalled in 1 Chronicles 1:11, listed among the Egyptian descendants without further details about who they were or where they lived.
H6047.origine: The Hebrew name עֲנָמִים (Anamim) would mean "affliction of the waters" according to some commentaries, although the exact etymology is uncertain. It is a proper name designating an ancient Egyptian clan or tribe, passed down through the biblical tradition of genealogies of the peoples descended from Noah.
H6047.emploi: The Anamim are cited twice in the Scriptures, only in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:13 and 1 Chronicles 1:11, which reproduce the same enumeration of Egyptian peoples. They always appear in a formulaic enumeration, without narrative or particular historical detail. Their presence in these tables indicates that the biblical authors recognized this nation as a distinct people descended from Egypt in ancient times.

sens: A pagan deity worshiped by the inhabitants of Sepharvaim, a region of Assyria
H6048.detail: 1. Anammélec is a false god introduced into Israel during the divided monarchy. His name means "image of the king" in Assyrian. It was a deity worshiped by the people of Sepharvaim, a region of the Assyrian territory. Not much is known about this god except what the biblical text reports: his worshipers offered children as sacrifices in the fire, an abominable practice similar to that of the god Molech. Anammélec was associated with another false god called Adrammélec, and together they formed the religious pantheon of Sepharvaim. When the Assyrians deported the inhabitants of the Northern Kingdom and replaced them with foreign populations, these pagan cults were brought into the land of Israel, corrupting the faith of God's people (2 Kings 17:31).
H6048.origine: The name Anammélec comes from Assyrian vocabulary: "anan" or "anu" means "image" or "effigy," and "melech" means "king." This god was thus known as "the image of the king" or "the royal effigy." He typically represented the type of deity characteristic of Mesopotamian polytheism, where kings and celestial powers were often conflated in popular religion. The god was part of the religious arsenal that Asian empires imposed on the subjugated peoples.
H6048.emploi: Anammélec appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 17:31. This passage recounts how, after the fall of the Northern Kingdom of Israel in 722 B.C., the Assyrians deported the Israelites and implanted foreign peoples in their lands. These new inhabitants brought with them their national gods, including Anammélec. The text shows them burning their children as offerings to Anammélec and Adrammélec, highlighting the horror of this idolatry and its total incompatibility with faith in the one true God of Israel.
H6048.portee: The mention of Anammélec reminds the Christian reader how false gods spread when the people of God stray from their faithfulness, and how the impious cults of surrounding nations constantly threaten the purity of faith. This passage warns that even practices as abominable as child sacrifice can seduce those who have abandoned the Word of God. It is a call to vigilance and adherence to revealed truth.

sens: To make clouds appear, to produce clouds
To gather clouds in the sky
H6049A.detail:
1. The verb literally means to make appear or produce clouds — it is the action of God assembling the clouds above the earth. In Genesis 9:14, God says to Noah: "When I gather clouds above the earth, the bow will appear in the cloud"; He speaks of His power to form the clouds which are the sign of rain and life returning after the flood.
2. The word evokes the concrete image of clouds gathering, coming together in the sky — a visible and natural action, but which the Bible attributes solely to God. It is God who masters the elements and creates the conditions for life on earth.
H6049A.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root עָנַן (anan), which fundamentally means "cloud." The form used here is the Piel, a verbal form that intensifies or makes active the meaning: not simply "to be a cloud," but "to make clouds" or "to gather clouds." The same root appears in words designating the clouds themselves in other passages of the Bible.
H6049A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible in Genesis 9:14, in the context of the covenant that God establishes with Noah after the flood. God promises that the rainbow will appear when He gathers the clouds — a permanent sign of His goodness and faithfulness. This passage shows God as the absolute master of meteorology and creation, capable of gathering or dispersing clouds according to His will.
H6049A.portee: This verse teaches that God fully controls natural phenomena, including rain and clouds. The rainbow, announced by this gathering of clouds, is a sign of God's eternal covenant — His promise not to destroy the earth by flood again. For the Christian, this reminds us that God is faithful to His promises and that His hand governs all creation.

sens: Observing the signs of nature — clouds, snakes, the flight of birds — to make predictions about the future
Practicing magic, enchantment, astrology, or spiritism
Habitually engaging in these occult practices
H6049B.detail:
1. Observing the signs of nature — clouds, snakes, the flight of birds — to make predictions about the future. This is the concrete image of the word: looking at natural phenomena as hidden messages that reveal what is to come. Manasseh "observed the clouds and the snakes to make predictions" (2 Kings 21:6), seeking answers about his fate in these signs.
2. Practicing magic, enchantment, astrology, or spiritism. This encompasses the techniques of the occult through which one claims to communicate with the invisible or dominate events. The Law denounces the one "who practices divination, astrology, augury, or magic" (Deuteronomy 18:10).
3. Habitually engaging in these occult practices. The verb evokes a habit, a lifestyle turned towards these forbidden inquiries. Manasseh "engaged in magic" (2 Chronicles 33:6), immersing himself more and more in it to provoke the Lord.
H6049B.origine: The primary Hebrew root fundamentally means "cloud." The word has shifted from the concrete meaning (observing clouds) to the figurative meaning (practicing divination), as in the religions of Israel's neighboring peoples, the future was read in cloud formations, the flight of birds, and other natural signs. This shift shows how occult practices hide behind supposedly revealing "natural" observations.
H6049B.emploi: This verb appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the books of the Law (Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in a context of condemnation. Moses formally prohibits it to Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10, 14), classifying it among the abominations of the nations. But kings of Israel, like Manasseh, succumbed to it despite the prohibition (2 Kings 21:6; 2 Chronicles 33:6), which led them towards evil. The prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Micah also denounce it as infidelity: the people "engage in magic like the Philistines" (Isaiah 2:6).
H6049B.portee: This word reminds every Christian that the temptation to seek the future elsewhere than with God — by scrutinizing it in signs, dreams, or occult practices — is a serious fall. It expresses a lack of trust in God's wisdom and Providence. The Bible invites the believer to place their hope in God alone, not in artifices or supposed hidden revealers.

sens: An oak reputed to have divinatory properties or related to witchcraft
A place name or geographical landmark in the region of Shechem
H6049G.detail: 1. It is an oak, a large tree, to which the inhabitants of Shechem attributed magical powers or presaging qualities. The Hebrew word ענן (a.nan) suggests practices of divination or augury — the idea that one can read the future or consult spirits there. In Judges 9:37, Gaal describes to Abimelech a troop arriving "by the way of the oak of the diviners," showing that this tree served as a well-known landmark in the landscape of Shechem. 2. Geographically, it is an identifiable and named place, a landmark that people used for navigation and communication, as one might say "near the big rock" or "next to the bridge."
H6049G.origine: The word ענן (a.nan) comes from a root that designates divination, witchcraft, or augury — the observation of signs supposed to reveal the future. It is not an ordinary verb, but a noun that describes a practice or magical belief. An oak bearing this name indicates that this place was associated with superstitious practices, perhaps a spot where diviners were consulted or where it was believed one could receive omens.
H6049G.emploi: This name appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 9:37, during the account of Abimelech's revolt at Shechem. Gaal, the leader of the rebels, describes the enemy troops descending from the heights and arriving by this "way of the oak of the diviners." It is simply a topographical landmark, a detail of the narrative that shows how people oriented themselves in the terrain. The text neither justifies nor approves the divination practices associated with this name: it uses it solely as a location.
H6049G.portee: This passage reminds us that even in the Promised Land, the Israelites dealt with pagan beliefs and practices — here, a cult or superstition related to a tree. For the Christian reader, it is a subtle reminder that faith in God contrasts with these human attempts to control the future through magic or divination.

sens: A visible accumulation of water vapor in the atmosphere
A dense mass or multitude of something
The sign of divine presence
The dwelling or vehicle of God and celestial beings
H6050.detail:
1. A cloud is literally a mass of water droplets suspended in the sky, what we call a cloud. This is the concrete image of the word.
2. By extension, a cloud refers to a compact crowd, a tight multitude — like a cloud of locusts invading a field.
3. In the Bible, the cloud becomes the visible sign that God is present and active: it veils His glory, which is too dazzling for human eyes, while revealing it (Exodus 13:21-22, the pillar of cloud guides the people in the desert).
4. The cloud is the living throne of God: in the vision of Daniel 7:13, one like a son of man comes "on the clouds of heaven" — not despite them, but through them, for the cloud is the chariot and royal garment of the Heavenly Father and His Son.
H6050.origine: The Aramaic word עֲנָן (a.nan) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word עָנָן (a.nan), both meaning "cloud" or "cloudiness." They share the same root and image: a visible accumulation in the sky. In Hebrew, the "cloud of glory" is often mentioned when God manifests His presence. This vocabulary of the cloud runs throughout the Bible, from Sinai to the Gospels.
H6050.emploi: The word appears only once in Aramaic in the Greek New Testament, but it is in one of the greatest visions of Scripture: Daniel 7:13, where the prophet sees, during his night visions, a figure like a son of man coming to the Ancient of Days — that is, to God the Father — walking on the clouds of heaven. This apocalyptic image announces the coming of the Messiah in glory. It recalls a classic image from the Old Testament: God traveling on the clouds like a chariot, a sign of His omnipotence and kingship.
H6050.portee: This vision reveals that Jesus, the Son of Man, comes in the glory of the Father and with the right to judge. The clouds are not an obstacle between heaven and earth: they are the way, the sacred atmosphere where God's reign is exercised. For the Christian, this image affirms that Jesus will return in the same glory, and that the disciples will see Him coming on the clouds (Matthew 24:30, Revelation 1:7): it is the promise of His definitive coming.

sens: A mass of visible water vapor in the sky
H6051.detail: 1. A cloud is a mass of vapor floating in the atmosphere that can be seen from afar (Genesis 9:13). It is the natural phenomenon observed after rain or before a storm. 2. In the Bible, the cloud takes on a religious meaning: it is the visible sign of God's presence and power. God manifests through a cloud to show that He is there and that He is acting (Exodus 24:18: Moses enters the cloud on Sinai and meets God). 3. The cloud guides the people of Israel in the desert: it rises for them to depart, it stops for them to camp (Numbers 9:17). It is a living cloud, obedient to God, that protects and leads them. 4. The cloud hides and protects: it covers the tabernacle to manifest the glory of the Lord, it envelops the prophets like Ezekiel to reveal divine mysteries (Ezekiel 1:28). 5. Sometimes the cloud symbolizes God's anger or judgment: it brings darkness, it hides His face and makes His presence inaccessible (Lamentations 3:44). It can also veil divine light in the days of the end (Joel 2:2).
H6051.origine: The Hebrew word עָנָן comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering or enveloping. It first designates the natural phenomenon, but in the Old Testament, it quickly acquires a religious charge: the cloud becomes the vehicle of divine presence, the visible form of God who draws near. It is a common word throughout the Hebrew Bible to speak of these mysterious appearances where God is shown veiled but present.
