H6051.emploi: The word is used 80 times in the Old Testament, especially in Exodus and the prophets. After Exodus, it constantly returns to describe the pillar of cloud that guides Israel in the desert (Exodus 13:21-22, Numbers 9:15-22). During great theophanies (appearances of God), the cloud envelops Sinai (Exodus 19:9), the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-38), and the temple (1 Kings 8:10-11). The prophets see it in their visions: Ezekiel sees the glory of God surrounded by a luminous cloud (Ezekiel 1:28), while others speak of dark clouds as an image of judgment (Joel 2:2, Zephaniah 1:15). Its meaning varies: sometimes it is protection, sometimes veiling, sometimes judgment.
H6051.portee: The cloud teaches the believer that God is present even when He is not clearly seen. It shows that the divine is both near and mysterious, guiding and enveloped in secrecy. Trusting in the cloud means believing that God walks with His people, even in darkness, and that He leads them toward His promise. It is a call not to judge God by what we see, but to follow Him by faith.

sens: Leader of the people at the time of the Exile and the Return
H6052.detail: Anan is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return of the Judeans from exile in Babylon. He is among the leaders of the people who signed the solemn covenant with Nehemiah to commit to obeying the Law of Moses (Nehemiah 10:26). His name means "cloud" in Hebrew, an image of lightness and movement in the sky. He thus represents one of the spiritual and civil leaders who renewed the people's commitment to the Lord at the critical moment of the reconstruction of Jerusalem.
H6052.origine: The name Anan literally means "cloud" (עָנָן). This image evokes what rises toward the sky and often symbolizes divine presence in the Old Testament — like the cloud that guided Israel in the desert or filled the Temple.
H6052.emploi: Anan appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:26. He is named among the leaders of Judah who affixed their seal to the covenant document signed with Nehemiah after the return from exile. This context shows that he was a man of influence and responsibility within the restored people, tasked with publicly witnessing the commitment to obey the Law.

sens: Mass of water vapor suspended in the air
Darkness caused by clouds
Veil or curtain that hides or obscures
H6053.detail:
1. A cloud is an accumulation of water droplets floating in the air, what we commonly call a cloud. This is the most direct image of the word: something visible yet immaterial, floating between heaven and earth. In Job 3:5, the poet speaks of clouds that settle above someone, creating an atmosphere of darkness and oppression.
2. By extension, a cloud refers to the darkness or shadow produced by clouds, particularly that distressing twilight of a covered sky. Job associates it with the darkness and shadow of death to depict a desperate situation, as if light were completely obscured.
3. Figuratively, a cloud can evoke anything that veils or hides: it is an immaterial yet real veil that interposes itself between the observer and what he seeks to see. This idea of hiding and obscuring is evident in the poetic use of the text.
H6053.origine: The Hebrew word עֲנָנָה comes from the root עָנַן, which describes clouds and everything related to cloud enveloping. It is a concrete word derived from the observation of the sky: clouds are what rises and envelops the sky. The feminine form here (with the suffix -ה) emphasizes the palpable nature of these celestial formations.
H6053.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 3:5. It is a passage where Job, in his lament, wishes that the day of his birth be erased: he invokes darkness, the shadow of death, and asks the clouds to settle above him. This poetic and desperate context shows that the word does not simply refer to mundane meteorology, but to a force capable of suffocating and darkening. Its unique use makes it a rare word, chosen by the poet to reinforce his image of horror and darkness.
H6053.portee: For the Christian reader, this evocation of clouds teaches that darkness and despair can seem to envelop and overwhelm us. The word reminds us that difficult circumstances can obscure our vision and peace, like a thick cloud. However, in biblical theology, clouds are not the final word: they are often a sign of God's presence (like the cloud at Sinai or the one that filled the temple). Seeing this unfamiliar word prompts meditation on trusting God amid apparent darkness.

sens: Son of Elioenai, descendant of David
H6054.detail: Anani is a man from the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Old Testament. He is one of the seven sons of Elioenai, himself a descendant of King David. His name appears in the genealogy of the kings of Judah, highlighting the importance of his family in the history of Israel after the division of the kingdom.
H6054.origine: The name Anani literally means "my cloud" in Hebrew. It evokes the image of a cloud or a celestial covering, perhaps symbolizing divine presence or God's protection. This type of theophoric name (which contains a reference to God) was common among the Hebrews.
H6054.emploi: Anani is cited only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:24, in the genealogical list of David's descendants after the Babylonian exile. He is presented as the seventh son of Elioenai, alongside his brothers Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, and Delaiah. This genealogical mention establishes his place in the continuity of the royal line of Judah.

sens: Man who lived during the time of Exile and Return
Father of Maaséja, ancestor of Azaria
H6055G.detail:
1. Anania is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile. He appears as the father of Maaséja and the grandfather of Azaria (Nehemiah 3:23), who contributed to the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership.
2. His name means "Jehovah is cloud" or "cloud of Jehovah": it expresses trust in divine protection, the presence of God as a cloud that covers and protects His people.
H6055G.origine: The name Anania comes from two Hebrew elements: "ana" (cloud) and "yah" (Jehovah, the Lord). This composition evokes the biblical image of the divine cloud that guided Israel in the desert and symbolized God's presence and protection among His people.
H6055G.emploi: Anania is mentioned only once in Scripture, in Nehemiah 3:23. He is presented as an ancestor of Azaria, one of the builders of the wall of Jerusalem during the return from exile to Babylon. Although Anania himself is not described as participating in the reconstruction, his name appears in the genealogy that establishes the identity and heritage of those who worked on this important task of restoring the holy city.

sens: Benjaminite city located northwest of Jerusalem
H6055H.detail: Hanania was a small town in the territory of Benjamin, located northwest of Jerusalem. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from the Babylonian exile, when the people of Judah were rebuilding their land. Members of the tribe of Benjamin resettled there, indicating that this locality had been inhabited before the deportation and that its former residents were able to return (Nehemiah 11:32).
H6055H.origine: The name Hanania means "Jehovah clouds" or "the Lord is cloud," combining the divine name Yah with the Hebrew word for cloud. This name evokes the protective presence of God, who guided the Israelites by a pillar of cloud in the desert.
H6055H.emploi: Hanania appears only once in the Old Testament, in Nehemiah 11:32, in a list of cities recolonized by the descendants of Benjamin after their return from exile. This mention occurs in an administrative and genealogical context, where the text enumerates the cities that Israel was rebuilding after its captivity in Babylon. The passage shows the importance of this city in the geography of the people's return.

sens: Ramification of a tree that comes from the trunk or a larger branch
Subdivision of a tree-like structure
Part of a whole that divides like the branches of a tree
H6056.detail: 1. The branch is the part of a tree that grows from the trunk or from another branch, bearing leaves and fruits. In King Nebuchadnezzar's vision, the gigantic tree has branches so abundant that the beasts of the field take shelter in them and the birds make their nests there (Daniel 4:12). It is the concrete image of a natural structure that divides into ramifications. 2. The word can also metaphorically refer to any part that subdivides like the branches of a tree, particularly in symbolic visions or descriptions of power and radiance, such as the tree representing the majesty of a kingdom or authority.
H6056.origine: The Aramaic word עֲנַף (anaph) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word עָנָף (anaph, H6057), which also means "branch" or "twig." It comes from a root that evokes the idea of spreading out, extending. The Hebrew word is used to describe the branches of the burning bush or those of the trees in the temple; the Aramaic takes up the meaning in the prophetic visions of the Book of Daniel.
H6056.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, exclusively in the Book of Daniel in chapter 4, where it designates the branches of the great tree in Nebuchadnezzar's vision. In each occurrence (verses 12, 14, and 21), it reinforces the idea of the magnificence and power of this cosmic tree: the branches are so numerous and robust that they provide shade and food for all living beings. The term contributes to the symbolism of the passage, where the tree represents the kingdom and its earthly splendor before its fall.
H6056.portee: This vision of generous branches that shelter and nourish all beings reminds readers that true greatness lies in giving and protecting rather than dominating by force. It invites reflection on the fragility of even the greatest human empires, which can be toppled, and on the only eternal kingdom that remains.

sens: part of a tree that grows from the trunk or from a main branch
leafy or flowering branch of a tree
that which extends and develops like the branches of a tree
H6057.detail:
1. The branch is literally a living part of the tree: a branch that grows directly from the trunk or a main branch. In Leviticus 23:40, branches of palm trees and other leafy trees are gathered to celebrate the feast: these are the young green, flexible, and leafy shoots that can be held in the hand.
2. By extension, branch refers to any visible and ornamental branch of the tree, the one that stands out. Ezekiel 31:3 illustrates this well: speaking of the great cedar of Assyria, the prophet admires that "its branches were beautiful" — it is the majestic and spread-out appearance of the vegetation.
3. The word takes on a figurative meaning when the Bible uses it to speak of growth and prosperity. In Ezekiel 36:8, the mountains of Israel "will produce your branches": the image means to become fertile and fruitful, to renew like a tree that greens again in spring.
H6057.origine: The Hebrew word עָנָף comes from a root that denotes the action of pushing, growing, and extending. The corresponding verb evokes the natural unfolding of a plant. This image of growth and abundant foliage is central: a branch is what shows that a tree is alive and growing. The Aramaic uses the same word with the same meaning.
H6057.emploi: The word appears about seven times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the prophets (especially Ezekiel) and the Psalms. In Leviticus 23:40, it has a concrete and liturgical meaning: the branches are tangible elements of the celebration. In Ezekiel's visions (17:8, 17:23, 31:3, 36:8), the branch becomes an image of the power, growth, and prosperity of a reign or a nation. The prophet speaks of nations or majestic cedars whose branches "bear fruit" or extend majestically. This transition from the concrete to the figurative shows how the tree with its branches symbolizes flourishing life.
H6057.portee: The branch speaks to us of living growth and renewal. For the believer, this image reminds us that true spiritual development, like that of a tree, is organic and progressive. Ezekiel 36:8 applies this promise to the restored people of Israel: the Lord regenerates what was barren. This image of greenness and fruitfulness encapsulates the hope of renewal and divine blessing.

sens: That bears many branches
That is lush and thick
That manifests great vigor and fertility
H6058.detail:
1. The word literally describes a tree or plant covered with a multitude of dense branches. It is the image of abundant and vigorous vegetation: Ezekiel describes the mother of Israel as a vine "loaded with branches," capable of bearing much foliage and fruit.
2. By extension, it is a sign of fertility and prosperity. A plant "loaded with branches" is well-nourished, well-established near waters, and it manifests its strength through this visible abundance.
3. The image also evokes a density, an impressive thickness: it is not a thin isolated branch, but a profusion that fills the space and attracts the eye.
H6058.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that means "branch." The adjective "loaded with branches" takes this fundamental idea and enriches it: it is not just about having one branch, but being covered with them, weighed down by their number and density. It is a term that paints a picture of overflowing and thriving life.
H6058.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 19:10. There, the prophet uses this image to describe the mother of several kings of Israel as a powerful vine. This unique occurrence shows how Ezekiel resorts to botanical metaphor to evoke the strength, fertility, and lasting establishment of the people — before showing its rupture and downfall (the branches are "torn off"). The context is that of a funeral song that contrasts past prosperity with present ruin.
H6058.portee: This word invites meditation on the visible signs of divine blessing: a plant loaded with branches symbolizes a life rooted, nourished, and fruitful. For a believer, it is a call to seek this spiritual density, this fullness that comes from a deep connection with God, the living source of all prosperity. But Ezekiel also reminds us that even this richness can be lost if one turns away from the Lord.

sens: To serve as a necklace or ornament around the neck
To endow someone with a precious ornament
To clothe, surround as a figurative adornment
H6059.detail:
1. The concrete meaning of the word first evokes an ornament worn around the neck, a necklace or an ornament that beautifies. This is why in Deuteronomy 15:14, the Lord commands Israel to make "gifts" to the freed slave: literally, to adorn him with goods, as one adorns someone with a precious ornament.
2. By extension, the verb denotes the action of clothing someone with wealth or honors, surrounding him with what distinguishes and beautifies him. It is an image of benevolent generosity.
3. In a figurative sense, the word can refer to what envelops a person morally or spiritually. Thus in Psalms 73:6, pride "serves as a necklace" for the wicked: that is to say, it adorns them, embellishes them, in a way defines and distinguishes them, like a visible ornament they wear with arrogance.
H6059.origine: The verb comes from a Semitic root that denotes the ornament and adornment of the neck. The word evokes the image of something that wraps or is placed around the neck. This root is related to the Hebrew word for "neck" (עֹנֶק, 'onèq), which shows the close link between the verb and its concrete application domain.
H6059.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, with two distinct nuances. In Deuteronomy 15:14, it is used in a concrete and generous sense: the master who frees a slave must provide him with gifts, as one adorns him with honorable wealth. In Psalms 73:6, it shifts to the figurative and critical: the pride that "adorns" the wicked becomes an accusation, showing how they boast of their vices as if they were an ornament they wear shamelessly. These two uses illuminate how the biblical language employs the image of adornment, sometimes to express generosity, sometimes to stigmatize arrogance.
H6059.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on generosity towards those in need. Giving gifts to one who is freed from slavery is to clothe him with dignity and respect, recognizing him as a precious person. Conversely, understanding that pride and violence are an "ornament" for the wicked highlights how these vices define and dishonor them in the eyes of God: what shines in the world is often just guilty vanity.

sens: Ornament of precious metal worn around the neck
Valuable jewelry that adorns and beautifies the wearer
Image of that which adorns, honors, or seduces
H6060B.detail:
1. The necklace is a piece of precious metal jewelry — gold or silver — that is worn around the neck. When Gideon asks the Midianites for the ornaments of the defeated kings, he lists "the gold rings... and the necklaces that were on the necks of their camels" (Judges 8:26): the necklace was an attribute of dignity and wealth.
2. The necklace adorns and beautifies the wearer, making them more attractive. In Proverbs 1:9, wisdom and instruction are compared to "a crown of grace for your head, and a necklace for your neck," with the necklace symbolizing the embellishment that wisdom provides.
3. Figuratively, the necklace represents that which seduces, that which charms irresistibly. When the lover in the Song of Songs says, "You have stolen my heart... with one of the necklaces around your neck" (Song of Songs 4:9), the necklace becomes the image of feminine beauty that captivates and enchants.
H6060B.origine: The Hebrew word עֲנָק comes from a root evoking the idea of "suspend" or "hang" — a natural image of an object worn suspended around the neck. In Hebrew, this same word also designates a giant (Anak, Numbers 13:33), probably based on the imposing shape of the neck of a very tall man.
H6060B.emploi: The word appears 3 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in singular or plural depending on the context. Twice it designates a real piece of jewelry: among the Midianites (Judges 8:26), where it marks their wealth and power, and on the beloved in the Song of Songs (Song of Songs 4:9). Once it is used figuratively (Proverbs 1:9), where it symbolizes the honor and attraction of wisdom. The word does not vary much in its uses: it always designates something precious that adorns or seduces.
H6060B.portee: The necklace reminds the reader that true beauty and true adornment of the soul do not come from external ornaments, but from wisdom and virtue. When Proverbs compares wisdom to a gold necklace for your neck, it invites us to seek first the inner riches that will truly honor us.

sens: Father of the giants of Egypt and the desert
Ancestor of a tribe of Canaanite giants
Symbol of superhuman power that inspires fear
H6061.detail:
1. Anak is a tall man living at the time of the Exodus from Egypt and in the desert. He has three sons: Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, all of strong stature, mentioned for the first time during the exploration of Canaan (Numbers 13:22). His name means "neck" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking an imposing silhouette.
2. Anak is the chief or ancestor of an entire tribe of giants living in Canaan, collectively called "the sons of Anak" or "Anakim." These giants terrified the Israelites: the explorers reported feeling "like grasshoppers" in their eyes (Numbers 13:33). Only Caleb and Joshua showed faith to conquer the land despite this threat.
3. Anak represents in Scripture the humanly insurmountable obstacle, the enemy power that exceeds human strength and requires absolute faith in the Lord to be defeated. His name becomes synonymous with a feared giant.
H6061.origine: The name Anak (עֲנָק) literally means "neck" in Hebrew, a name that perhaps underscores the remarkable stature or pride of this man. The plural form "Anakim" (עֲנָקִים) designates all his descendants. Although we do not know the complete genealogies, Anak appears as the founder or leader of a lineage of giants established in Canaan long before the Israelite conquest.
H6061.emploi: Anak is mentioned 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the accounts of the conquest of Canaan. He first appears in Numbers 13:22 during the report of the spies, where his three sons are named. The following passages (Numbers 13:28, 13:33) show how the mention of the "sons of Anak" terrifies the explorers and discourages the people. In Deuteronomy 9:2, Moses reminds Israel that God Himself said: "Who can stand against the sons of Anak?" But Joshua 15:13-14 recounts how Caleb, son of Jephunneh, conquers Hebron and drives out the three sons of Anak. Judges 1:20 confirms this victory. Anak remains the biblical symbol of the giant, of terrifying human power, but defeated by faith and divine power.
H6061.portee: Anak and his descendants teach the reader that faith in the Lord triumphs over all humanly insurmountable obstacles. Caleb and Joshua, the only ones to say "we can go up" (Numbers 13:30), inherited the promised land, while the fearful generation perished in the desert. The name Anak thus becomes an invitation not to fear the "giants" in our lives, but to believe in the power of God.

sens: A tribe of giants descended from Anak
A tall people who inhabited the south of Canaan
Fearsome warriors compared to other peoples of giants
H6062.detail:
1. The Anakim are the descendants of a man named Anak, who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert: it is a race or tribe of giants. Anak had three sons (Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai) who were the ancestors of this people.
2. They were very tall men who had settled in the south of Canaan, particularly around Hebron, Debir, and Anab. Their name literally means "long-necked," evoking the image of creatures of exceptional and impressive stature.
3. In the Bible, the Anakim are presented as fearsome warriors and a threat: the Israelites who saw them said, "Who can stand against the sons of Anak?" (Deuteronomy 9:2). Joshua exterminated them during the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 11:21).
H6062.origine: The word "Anakim" comes from the root "Anak" (עֲנָק), which literally means "long-necked" or evokes the idea of a long and majestic neck. This etymology reflects the major physical characteristic of this people: their very great height. The word designates not only the ancestral father but also his descendants, an entire tribe recognized for its exceptional dimensions.
H6062.emploi: The word "Anakim" appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Deuteronomy and Joshua. The Israelites first encounter them during the reconnaissance of Canaan: ten spies return terrified and declare that the people cannot conquer the land because the Anakim dwell there (Deuteronomy 1:28). The Bible also mentions them in comparison with other giant peoples (the Emim, the Rephaim) to emphasize their strength and remarkable stature (Deuteronomy 2:10-21). Under Joshua's command, the Israelites systematically destroyed them during the possession of Canaan (Joshua 11:21), although some survived and found refuge among the Philistines (Joshua 11:22 and 14:12).
H6062.portee: The Anakim represent in Scripture a human fear and an apparent impossibility against which only God can grant victory. Their presence tests the faith of the Israelites: the report of the ten spies shows how fear can paralyze and prevent obedience to God. But the destruction of the Anakim by Joshua shows that God's promise is stronger than any enemy, no matter how terrible. This story encourages the believer to trust in God even when the adversary seems invincible.

sens: Amorite chief allied with Abraham
H6063G.detail: Aner is an Amorite chief who lived at the time of Abraham. He was the brother of Mamre and Eshcol, and all three made an alliance with Abraham to help him fight four invading kings from the north (Genesis 14:13). After the victory, Abraham acknowledged their share of the spoils, refusing to enrich them with his own goods (Genesis 14:24).
H6063G.origine: The name literally means "boy" or "young man" in Hebrew. Aner designates a political and warrior chief of Canaan during the patriarchal period, a member of a family of Amorites well established in the region of Hebron.
H6063G.emploi: Aner appears twice in Genesis, during the same event: the defeat of the four invading kings. He is a minor but significant historical figure to show how Abraham integrated politically and militarily into the Canaanite context. He, Mamre, and Eshcol form a group of three Amorite brothers who enter into an alliance with Abraham, which grants them a certain dignity and autonomy in the narrative.

sens: City of Manasseh, in the West Bank, assigned to the Levites of the family of Kohath
H6063H.detail: 1. Aner is a city located west of the Jordan River, in the territory of the tribe of Manasseh. It was given to the Levites of the family of Kohath for them to dwell in. In 1 Chronicles 6:70, Aner is mentioned among the Levitical cities that the Israelites distributed among the descendants of Levi — these cities were important religious and administrative centers, where the priests and temple servants resided.
H6063H.origine: The name Aner means "boy" in Hebrew. This city bears a simple and direct name, likely given in antiquity in reference to some local characteristic. Aner is another name for Taanach, an important city of Manasseh. Like many Israelite cities, it had several names throughout historical periods.
H6063H.emploi: Aner appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:70. The context is that of the distribution of Levitical cities: after the conquest of the land, Moses and Joshua distributed cities to the Levites according to their families. Aner, a city of Manasseh, was assigned to the Kohathites, one of the three major Levitical families. This mention is part of a long list enumerated in chapter 6 of 1 Chronicles, which summarizes the status and possessions of the priestly families.

sens: Impose a fine or monetary penalty
Condemn someone to a sanction
Tax or levy a contribution
Chastise or correct through discipline
Suffer a punishment or condemnation
H6064.detail:
1. Impose a fine or monetary penalty: the word primarily denotes the financial sanction imposed by judges. In Exodus 21:22, when men in conflict cause a pregnant woman to give birth prematurely, the husband receives a fine imposed by the judges; in Deuteronomy 22:19, a man who damages the reputation of a virgin is condemned to pay one hundred shekels of silver to the girl's father.
2. Condemn someone to a sanction: this is the act of declaring someone guilty and imposing a penalty, as in Proverbs 17:26 where it is unjust to condemn the righteous to a fine.
3. Tax or levy a contribution: the word can denote the imposition of a financial burden, as in 2 Chronicles 36:3 where the king of Egypt taxes the land with a contribution of one hundred talents of silver.
4. Chastise or correct through discipline: beyond the fine, the word evokes correction that transforms, as in Proverbs 21:11 where chastising the mocker makes the fool wise.
5. Suffer a punishment or condemnation: the passive form of the verb denotes one who receives the penalty, as in Proverbs 22:3 where the simple advance without prudence and are punished for their lack of discernment.
H6064.origine: The Hebrew verb עָנַשׁ (a.nash) comes from a root that expresses the idea of striking or reaching. The word family includes terms related to penalty and repression. The initial image is that of a blow struck, but it has extended to all forms of sanction: first the fine (monetary sanction), then more broadly condemnation and punishment. It is a typical word of the legal and sapiential language of the Old Testament.
H6064.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is concentrated mainly in the legislative and sapiential books: Exodus and Deuteronomy (laws on damages and offenses), 2 Chronicles (tributes imposed by kings), and especially Proverbs (which use it to speak of correction and moral discipline). In Exodus and Deuteronomy, the word is technical and denotes fines imposed by judges for restitution of damages. In Proverbs, it broadens: chastising the mocker produces wisdom in the fool (21:11); he who sees evil and hides escapes punishment (22:3). In Amos 2:8, oppressors do not fear being punished. The word thus remains attached to a concrete penalty or moral correction, never purely spiritual.
H6064.portee: This word reminds Christians that actions have consequences: divine or human justice does not leave unpunished one who wrongs another. For the wise, the punishment of the mocker is a lesson that benefits those who see it; prudence consists of discerning danger and avoiding it before being chastised. It is an invitation to take commandments and morality seriously: not out of servile fear, but because sin carries its own retribution.

sens: Financial penalty imposed by an authority
Seizure of property as punishment
Strict fine
H6065.detail: 1. The word denotes a financial penalty, that is, a sum of money that an authority imposes on someone who has committed an offense or violated the law. In the context of the decree of King Artaxerxes in Ezra 7:26, those who refuse to obey the Law of God and the laws of the king will receive a confiscation — a strict monetary punishment. 2. By extension, the word can also denote the seizure of property: confiscation is then the forced deprivation of what one possesses as punishment. It is a form of material punishment, more radical than a simple fine.
H6065.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "punishing" or "penalizing." It is related to concepts of justice and retribution: one who commits an offense must bear the material price. Confiscation was a common form of punishment in ancient Near Eastern judicial systems, where the property of the offender passed to the royal treasury or the community.
H6065.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 7:26, in the context of the decree of the Persian king Artaxerxes. The king orders that those who do not respect the Law of the God of heaven and the law of the king will incur various punishments, including the confiscation of their property. This usage shows how the term fits into an official legal framework, where financial penalties were a tool for enforcing the law.
H6065.portee: This word reminds us that sin and disobedience to God's law have material and concrete consequences. For Ezra and his people, it underscores the importance of obeying the commandments: neglecting the service of God was not without cost. It is a call to take our commitment to God seriously, knowing that our choices have real repercussions.

H6066.fr: contribution levée à titre de punition
sens: Tax or sum of money imposed as punishment or compensation
Penalty or consequence suffered for an offense
H6066.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a financial contribution imposed as punishment. It is a kind of tribute or fine that a victor demands from the vanquished: in 2 Kings 23:33, Pharaoh Necho imposes on the land of Judah a contribution of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold, as punishment for disobedience. It is a penalty paid in money.
2. More broadly, the word can denote the penalty or consequence of a wrongdoing. In Proverbs 19:19, one who is carried away by anger must "suffer the penalty": the image evokes the natural or justified retribution that follows the offense, like a debt that cannot be avoided.
H6066.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to impose a fine" or "to punish." Aramaic has a related term (עֲנָשׁ anash) that means "confiscation" — that is, the act of seizing or removing what belongs to someone as a form of punishment. This root is linked to the idea of sanction and retribution.
H6066.emploi: The word is infrequent in Hebrew: it appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Kings 23:33, it describes a contribution imposed on the vanquished as a political and military sanction. In Proverbs 19:19, it takes on a more general and moral sense: the penalty or price one must pay for one's actions, without necessarily being a fine paid. The word always evokes the idea that a fault or crime never goes without consequence.
H6066.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that sin has a price to pay, whether through an external sanction or through the natural consequences of our actions. It invites caution and wisdom: to avoid anger and rebellion against God or against established authority, for retribution is inevitable. In the background, it prepares to understand how Jesus submitted to the penalty that was due to us.

sens: father of Shamgar, a deliverer of Israel during the time of the Judges
H6067.detail: Anath is the father of Shamgar, a man who rose up to deliver Israel from the oppression of the Philistines (Judges 3:31). His son Shamgar struck down six hundred Philistines with a simple ox goad and became a deliverer of Israel, marking a time when the roads were dangerous and travelers had to take detours (Judges 5:6). Anath himself is mentioned only as the father of the hero, with the Bible not reporting his own deeds.
H6067.origine: The name "Anath" means "answer" in Hebrew, suggesting the idea of intervention or deliverance. This name was known in the ancient Near East. Anath is mentioned only in the context of his fatherhood, which was the common way in antiquity to identify a person.
H6067.emploi: Anath appears only twice in the Bible, always to designate the father of Shamgar. In Judges 3:31, he is named at the moment Shamgar undertakes to drive out the Philistines. In Judges 5:6, the same patronymic recalls the troubled time when the people were under this oppression. These two mentions frame the account of Shamgar's judgment in the book of Judges, one in narrative prose and the other in the song of Deborah and Barak.

sens: city of Benjamin, in Israel, near Jerusalem
priestly city assigned to the Levite priests
hometown of the prophet Jeremiah
H6068G.detail:
1. Anathoth is a city located in the territory of Benjamin, about 5 kilometers from Jerusalem (Jeremiah 1:1). It regularly appears in lists of biblical cities, especially when enumerating the possessions of the tribes of Israel (Joshua 21:18; 1 Chronicles 6:60).

2. The city was assigned to the priests of the tribe of Levi, making it a holy place (Joshua 21:18). This is why the prophet Jeremiah, who was born there, belonged to a priestly family.

3. Anathoth is especially famous as the birthplace of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:1). It is also where the prophet faced opposition: his fellow townspeople of Anathoth demanded that he stop prophesying in the name of the Lord, threatening to kill him (Jeremiah 11:21).
H6068G.origine: The Hebrew name עֲנָתוֹת (Anathoth) literally means "answers to prayer." It comes from a root evoking God's listening and responding to the requests of His worshipers. This name reflects the hope that God listens and responds to those who call upon Him.
H6068G.emploi: Anathoth appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and prophetic books. It first appears in lists of priestly cities assigned to the Levites (Joshua 21:18; 1 Chronicles 6:60). It reappears during the time of reconstruction, particularly in the census of inhabitants returning from exile (Ezra 2:23; Nehemiah 7:27; Nehemiah 11:32). But Anathoth is most closely associated with the prophet Jeremiah, who was from there (Jeremiah 1:1) and who encountered hostility from his fellow citizens (Jeremiah 11:21-23). The prophet also owned a field there (Jeremiah 32:7-9), symbolizing his trust in God despite the siege of Jerusalem.
H6068G.portee: Anathoth reminds us that God's prophets are not always honored in their homeland. Jeremiah, though the son of a priestly family from a holy city, had to face rejection and threats from his own compatriots. This serves as encouragement for those who faithfully serve God despite opposition.

sens: Son of Beker, of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned during the time of Egypt and the desert
Leader of the people who signed the covenant with Nehemiah
City of Benjamin, priestly seat, about 5 km from Jerusalem, hometown of the prophet Jeremiah
H6068H.detail:
1. Anathoth is primarily a man: son of Beker and grandson of Benjamin, he is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:8 as one of the many sons of his family, all named one after the other in the genealogy of the tribe.

2. Another Anathoth, a namesake of the first, is among the leaders of the people who signed the solemn covenant with Nehemiah upon returning from exile; he thus represents the restoration of Israel.

3. Anathoth is also a city: located in the territory of Benjamin, about 5 kilometers northeast of Jerusalem, it is assigned to the priests of the tribe of Levi. It is where the prophet Jeremiah was born and raised, making it a major prophetic site in biblical history.
H6068H.origine: The name Anathoth means "answers to prayer" or "he answers prayer," an image of a God who listens and responds. The name is connected to the biblical idea of prayer being heard and communion with God. For the city, the name may also evoke a height or an exposed place.
H6068H.emploi: The only usage provided names Anathoth as the son of Beker in the genealogy of Benjamin. However, biblical tradition recognizes at least three bearers of this name: a tribal ancestor, a leader of Nehemiah's covenant, and especially a priestly city in the territory of Benjamin. The city of Anathoth is famous in biblical history: it hosted the priests who served there and, more importantly, it is the birthplace of the prophet Jeremiah, who received God's call there. This city remains a major geographical and spiritual landmark in archaeology and biblical history.

sens: Leader of the people who signed the covenant with Nehemiah
H6068I.detail: 1. Anathoth is one of the leaders of the people of Israel who affixed their seal to the covenant document concluded with Nehemiah after the return from exile (Nehemiah 10:19). He appears in the list of important signatories, alongside other religious and civic leaders.
H6068I.origine: The name means "answers to prayer" or "answered by God," evoking a divine intervention in response to a request. This name was borne by several figures in ancient Israel: a descendant of Benjamin and a distant ancestor, but especially by this leader of the people at the time of Nehemiah, who embodies the restoration of Israel after the exile.
H6068I.emploi: Anathoth appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:19, where he is named among the "heads of the people" who signed the covenant during the restoration of Jerusalem after the return from Babylon. This context shows his role as a religious or civic leader participating in the renewal of the covenant between God and His people. His inscription in this official document attests to his importance in the communal reconstruction.

sens: inhabitant or native of Anathoth
warrior or leader from this city
prophet or priest of the lineage of Anathoth
H6069.detail:
1. An Anathothite is a person from or native to Anathoth, a city in Israel. This term simply designates an inhabitant of this locality. For example, Abiezer is described as "from Anathoth" (2 Samuel 23:27), indicating his geographical origin.
2. The term particularly applies to warriors and military leaders from Anathoth. Several of them are listed among David's men: Abiezer appears as an officer (1 Chronicles 27:12), and other Anathothite warriors are mentioned among David's recruits (1 Chronicles 12:3).
3. The term is also used for prophets or religious figures from this city. Jeremiah, who was a priest and prophet, came from Anathoth (Jeremiah 29:27 refers to him as "Jeremiah of Anathoth"), highlighting the spiritual significance of this community.
H6069.origine: Anathothite comes from the name Anathoth (עֲנָתוֹת), a city in the territory of Benjamin in Israel. The proper name Anathoth means "affliction" or "answer" according to ancient interpretations. The term Anathothite follows the usual pattern of Hebrew patronymics and demonyms: it designates belonging to a geographical or familial group, similar to how one would refer to "Judeans" or "Galileans."
H6069.emploi: This term appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in historical and military or prophetic contexts. It first designates warriors and officers in the service of King David: Abiezer is mentioned several times (2 Samuel 23:27 and 1 Chronicles 11:28, 27:12), confirming that several Anathothites served as military leaders. The term also applies to the prophet Jeremiah, who lived in Anathoth and whose ministry is attested there (Jeremiah 29:27). These usages show that the Anathothites were not merely a rural population, but men of significance: renowned warriors, administrative leaders, and prophetic figures.
H6069.portee: Anathoth reminds us that in Israel, faith and service to God were rooted in concrete places and real families. The fact that Jeremiah comes from Anathoth shows how God calls His prophets from among ordinary people. The military importance of the Anathothites to David underscores how God chooses faithful individuals from all ranks of society to accomplish His work.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H6070.detail: Anthothija is a Benjamite, a member of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in Scripture. He was one of the sons of Shashak and the brother of Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Iphdeiah, and Penuel (1 Chronicles 8:24).
H6070.origine: The name Anthothija means "answer of Jehovah" or "Jehovah answers." It reflects the faith of the parents who saw in this son an answer from the Lord to their prayer. This type of theophoric name (which contains the name of God) was common in Israel, expressing dependence on God and His goodwill.
H6070.emploi: Anthothija appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:24, in a genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. This passage lists the descendants of Shashak, ancestors of the inhabitants of Jerusalem after the exile. Although we know nothing of his personal life or deeds, his mention in the genealogical record shows that even minor figures in Israel had their place in God's history.

sens: Fresh grape juice, before or after fermentation
Sweet, sugary wine, in the process of fermentation
Image of abundance and divine blessing
Wealth and material prosperity
H6071.detail:
1. Must is the juice obtained by pressing grapes at harvest: it is the sweet, thick liquid that flows directly from the press. In Joel 1:5, the drunkards weep because "the must is taken away from your mouth," indicating that this fresh, delicious juice is consumed before it becomes wine through fermentation.
2. Once it begins to ferment, must gradually becomes wine: it is an intermediate stage where it still retains its sweet flavor and intoxicating power. In Isaiah 49:26, the text speaks of men who "will be intoxicated with their blood like must," showing that this fermenting juice easily intoxicates.
3. In prophetic visions of messianic prosperity, must flowing from the mountains symbolizes divine abundance: in Joel 3:18 and Amos 9:13, these images of must flowing from mountains and hills evoke a land so fertile and blessed that the grapes produce more than can be processed.
4. Thus, must represents wealth, well-being, and complete satisfaction: when one is deprived of it (Joel 1:5), it is a serious loss; when it abounds (Joel 3:18), it is a sign of total restoration of the people and their communion with God.
H6071.origine: The Hebrew word עָסִיס comes from a root that evokes the idea of pressing, extracting by force. Must is therefore literally "that which is pressed" from the grape: it is the juice obtained under the press. This term specifically designates the moment when the grape has just been crushed and where the juice is still fermenting, full of sugar and strength, before becoming stable wine.
H6071.emploi: This term appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always referring to grape juice or the harvest. Three usages are in the prophets of restoration (Joel and Amos): they use the must that "flows" as an image of unmeasured blessing, signs of renewal after judgment. One usage in Isaiah (49:26) mentions it in a somber context, as an image of carnage and forced drunkenness. One usage in the Song of Songs (8:2) presents it as a drink of celebration and intimacy. Each time, it is a valuable product, a symbol of agricultural wealth.
H6071.portee: Must reminds us that God knows the simple joys of ordinary life: the harvest, the grapes, the new wine. When the prophets speak of must flowing from the mountains, they teach us that divine blessing is not spiritual and distant, but concrete, abundant, touchable — it fills the mouth and life of the people. It is also a call: let us rejoice in what God gives, not only in material goods but in His presence made tangible in the ordinary.

sens: To walk on something, to crush it underfoot
To reduce to nothing, to completely annihilate
H6072.detail:
1. To tread means to walk on something with force to crush or reduce it to dust. The image is that of the foot pressing and grinding: one treads grapes to extract juice, one treads grass by walking on it. In Malachi 4:3, the righteous "will tread" the wicked, meaning they will completely crush them underfoot like dust.
2. Figuratively, to tread means to annihilate, to reduce to nothing. It is not a mere failure, but total and definitive destruction. The wicked will be "like ashes": not only defeated but reduced to nothing, pulverized.
H6072.origine: The Hebrew verb עָסַס (asas) literally means "to press" or "to crush." It evokes the action of the foot or a force exerted from above to reduce something to crumbs. It is a concrete verb, related to physical work: treading grapes in a vat, walking on grain to strip it of its husk. The word expresses brute force and total crushing.
H6072.emploi: The verb עָסַס appears only once in the Old Testament, in Malachi 4:3. It is used in a prophetic vision of final judgment: the righteous will tread the wicked on the day of judgment. It is a language of apotheosis and divine vengeance: the weak become strong, and the one who oppressed is crushed like dust. The context is that of the consummation of the ages, when God restores justice.
H6072.portee: This word speaks of the definitive victory of the righteous over evil. For the Christian, it reminds us that God's judgment leaves nothing standing: evil will not only be defeated, it will be annihilated, reduced to nothing. It is a promise of comfort for the oppressed and a serious warning for the wicked. The vision of the foot that treads symbolizes the total and irreversible crushing of sin.

sens: Branch or leafy tip of a tree
Place where birds perch
H6073.detail:
1. The word refers to the branches of a tree, particularly the tips adorned with foliage. It is the place where leaves grow and where light penetrates. In Psalm 104:12, the birds of the sky "dwell on their edges," meaning on the branches of the tree.
2. By natural extension, the "edge" becomes the refuge where birds settle to nest, sing, and live. It is a lively place, vibrant with the song of birds, which is part of the created work where God allows His creatures to dwell.
H6073.origine: The Hebrew word עֳפָיִם (ophaïm) is related to roots that express the idea of covering, of foliage that hides and protects. There is a very close Aramaic form, עֳפִי (ophi), which also means "foliage." The word evokes the concrete image of branches laden with leaves.
H6073.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 104:12. In this passage celebrating creation and divine providence, it describes the natural habitat of birds. The context is that of a hymn to the glory of God for having provided each creature with an appropriate place to live. The psalmist sees in this simple detail a reflection of the wisdom and goodness of the Creator.
H6073.portee: This verse invites the reader to contemplate how God cares for each creature, even the birds of the sky. Recognizing that the Lord has provided a refuge for every animal is to learn to trust His providence for oneself. It is also an invitation to admire creation and to see it as the work of a caring and benevolent God.

sens: The entirety of the leaves of a tree
The branches of a tree with its leaves
What gives the green appearance of a tree
H6074.detail:
1. Foliage refers to the entirety of the leaves covering the branches of a tree. In the dream of King Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:12), the giant tree has "beautiful foliage," meaning abundant and healthy leaves that make it attractive.
2. The word also evokes the complete branching — the branches and foliage together — as they together provide shade and shelter. When one cries, "Shake the foliage, and scatter the fruits" (Daniel 4:14), it refers to the entire visible and productive part of the tree.
3. Foliage characterizes the beauty and verdant life of a tree: beautiful foliage shows the health and prosperity of the tree (Daniel 4:21), while losing it or having it removed signifies its decline.
H6074.origine: The Aramaic word עֳפִי (ophi) comes from the same root as עֳפָיִם (ophayim, "branches"), the Hebrew word that designates the twigs and branching of a tree. The root evokes the idea of growth and branching — what grows, what extends. The word appears in the Aramaic context of the book of Daniel and reflects this notion of visible and productive plant vigor.
H6074.emploi: The word appears only three times in Aramaic in the book of Daniel (4:12, 4:14, 4:21), all in the same section: the prophetic dream of King Nebuchadnezzar. The tree in the dream is described as gigantic, with beautiful foliage that provides shade, food, and refuge to all living beings. The foliage characterizes the power, prosperity, and dominion of the king symbolized by this tree. When the foliage must be shaken and scattered, it announces the king's downfall. The word is always used in a concrete and literal sense: there is no complex figure of speech, but a simple and visual description.
H6074.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that visible and impressive beauty and prosperity are never definitive or independent of God. The lush foliage of Nebuchadnezzar's tree symbolizes a power that seemed eternal but falls at the divine word. This invites us to seek our trust not in the apparent strength of this world, but in the one who truly reigns.

sens: To inflate, to expand (in a physical sense)
To be filled with pride, arrogance (in a moral sense)
H6075A.detail:
1. The word first evokes the action of swelling, of expanding like a balloon or a sail in the wind. It is the image of the body or a part of the body increasing in volume.
2. Figuratively, to swell describes the soul or heart that fills with pride and self-sufficiency. In Habakkuk 2:4, the soul of the wicked "has swelled": it is puffed up with itself, filled with pride and self-confidence, whereas it should be upright, that is, honest and humble before God. This is the opposite of the faith of the righteous, who relies on God and not on themselves.
H6075A.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that paints the image of swelling, of expansion. The word belongs to the family of words describing volume and shape, as seen in other Semitic languages. The basic image — something that takes on volume — naturally extends to the moral: pride swells the soul as air swells a skin.
H6075A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Habakkuk 2:4. It describes the moral state of the wicked whose soul has swelled with pride. This passage sharply contrasts the puffed-up heart of arrogance with the life of the righteous based on faith in God. The context of the book of Habakkuk — a call to trust in God in the face of the powers of evil — shows that this swelling of the soul is a symptom of rebellion against God.
H6075A.portee: This word invites the believer to be vigilant against pride and self-sufficiency. To swell with pride is to turn away from God and rely on one's own strength. In contrast, the righteous live "by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4): a humble soul, attached to God, not puffed up with itself. It is a timeless warning against spiritual arrogance.

sens: to act with boldness and carelessness in the face of a warning
to persist in an action despite opposition or danger
H6075B.detail:
1. The word evokes the attitude of one who acts boldly and without fear, deliberately ignoring warnings. In Numbers 14:44, the Israelites are obstinate in their assault on the promised mountain, despite Moses' order and the absence of the ark of the covenant — an image of foolish presumption in the face of divine will.
2. More broadly, to be obstinate means to persist in a decision or action without regard for danger or opposition: it is the misplaced tenacity of one who refuses to back down or listen.
H6075B.origine: The Hebrew verb עָפַל (aphal) expresses the idea of "showing boldness" or "acting lightly." Its root suggests a certain audacity or insolence, the attitude of one who ignores the limits imposed on them. The word belongs to the semantic field of rebellion and refusal to obey.
H6075B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Numbers 14:44. The context is rich: after the Lord declared that the generation of Israel that came out of Egypt would not enter the promised land (because of their unbelief), the Israelites obstinately attempt to ascend anyway. This obstinacy is presented as contrary to the word of God and in the absence of the very sign of His presence — the ark was not with them. The verb thus captures the tragedy of one who knows God's will and transgresses it anyway.
H6075B.portee: This word reminds us of the spiritual danger of presumption: it is the attitude that believes it can succeed without God or against His revealed will. The Israelite who obstinately attempts to ascend without the ark and despite the warning embodied by Moses serves as a warning for us: there is wisdom in recognizing one's limits and welcoming divine guidance, even when it contradicts our desires.

sens: A small mountain, a natural elevation of the terrain
A fortified or defended position overlooking a place
By poetic extension, the people or territory it overlooks
H6076A.detail:
1. It is primarily a simple height of land, a small mountain that rises from the landscape (in 2 Kings 5:24, Gehazi retreats to the "hill" to hide the gifts, a secluded and elevated place).
2. It can also refer to a fortified site: a hill is naturally a good defense, hence its connection with towers and fortresses. In Isaiah 32:14, the "hill" and the tower are mentioned together to evoke the ruins of abandoned cities.
3. In poetic and prophetic language, the hill represents the people or the territory itself. In Micah 4:8, the "hill of the daughter of Zion" does not just refer to a geographical height, but to Jerusalem and its people, whose power will return.
H6076A.origine: The word comes from a root that originally means "to rise" or "to be high." In ancient Hebrew, a hill is what stands up, what dominates. The word can refer to both the natural relief and the fortified site that inhabitants built on heights for protection. The same idea appears in many biblical place names: cities rose on hills.
H6076A.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible. In 2 Kings 5:24, it is a secluded place where Gehazi hides. In Isaiah 32:14, the hill is among the ruins of a city judged and abandoned. In Micah 4:8, the phrase "hill of the daughter of Zion" is a poetic image of the kingdom of Jerusalem. The term thus shifts from the concrete meaning (a height of land) to the figurative meaning (a place of power or the people themselves).
H6076A.portee: The hill reminds us that the places where people live are never neutral: a height is both a refuge and a place of vigilance, strength and fragility. In particular, when Micah speaks of the "hill of Zion," he invites the reader to see in the people of God a community that must remain steadfast and visible, a restored place of dominion. It is also an invitation not to forget that all power and security come from God alone.

sens: Fortified hill of Jerusalem
Part of the city wall
Residential area of Jerusalem
H6077.detail: 1. Ophel is a hill or ridge of hills located in Jerusalem, which was fortified to protect the city. It is a natural defensive position, overlooking certain access points to the capital. 2. The term also refers to the part of the wall or fortification built on this hill to strengthen Jerusalem's defenses. During the repairs under Nehemiah, "the gate of Ophel" and "the wall of Ophel" are mentioned (Nehemiah 3:26-27), showing that it is a well-identified area of urban fortification. 3. Ophel also served as a residential neighborhood, as Nehemiah 11:21 speaks of the people who lived in Ophel and the temple servants who resided there.
H6077.origine: The Hebrew word עֹ֫פֶל (ophel) comes from a root meaning "hill" or "elevation." It describes a natural geographical relief, hence the image of defense: heights offer better protection. It is a geographical name specific to Jerusalem, but its principle (fortifying heights) was common in ancient urban planning.
H6077.emploi: Ophel is mentioned five times in the Old Testament, only in the books of Chronicles and Nehemiah, which focus on the reconstruction of Jerusalem. Hezekiah strengthens the fortifications of Ophel (2 Chronicles 27:3); Hezekiah also adds fortifications to Ophel (2 Chronicles 33:14). During the reconstruction of the wall under Nehemiah after the exile, "the wall of Ophel" and "the gate of Ophel" are specifically restored (Nehemiah 3:26-27); finally, temple servants reside there (Nehemiah 11:21). Thus, Ophel symbolizes the repeated efforts to secure and populate Jerusalem.
H6077.portee: Ophel reminds us that the security of a city, both material and spiritual, rests on solid foundations and constant vigilance. The presence of temple servants at Ophel shows how the urban organization of Jerusalem integrates religious life. For the reader, it is an invitation to reflect on the relationship between physical protection and trust in God.

sens: Small town in the territory of Benjamin
H6078.detail: Ophni is a locality that belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, listed among the cities of the territory assigned to this tribe. It was located about four kilometers northwest of Bethel, in the central region of Canaan. The site likely corresponds to the current locality called 'Jifna.'
H6078.origine: The Hebrew name עׇפְנִי (Ophni) would mean "moldy" or "rotten," an etymology that is surprising for a city, but place names often retain forgotten ancient images. The name has been consistently transmitted in Hebrew and Greek tradition (Ophni in Greek).
H6078.emploi: Ophni is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the book of Joshua. It appears in the list of cities in the territory of Benjamin, enumerated in chapter 18 when the tribes receive their inheritance in Canaan. This unique mention shows that it was a recognized and defined locality within the Benjaminite territory, even though it played no notable role in later biblical narratives.

sens: Mobile membrane that covers and protects the eye
Gaze, what the eye sees or shows
Rays or light of dawn (poetic image)
H6079.detail:
1. The eyelid is the skin membrane that covers the eye and protects it by opening and closing. This is the literal meaning of the word: Job 16:16 speaks of tears that have altered the face and the shadow of death on the eyelids, showing how eyelids can express the fatigue or suffering of the body.

2. By extension, the word also refers to the gaze itself, the ability to see or the expression of what one looks at. Psalms 11:4 says that "his eyelids test the sons of man": these are not eyelids that act physically, but the gaze, the vigilance of God that scrutinizes hearts. Similarly, Proverbs 4:25 commands that "your eyelids look straight before you," which means to direct one's attention and gaze straight ahead.

3. In poetic language, the "eyelids of dawn" (Job 3:9 and 41:9) refer to the first rays of the sun that pierce the darkness of morning, as if dawn opens its eyes to the day. It is a beautiful image to speak of the light that is born.
H6079.origine: The Hebrew word עַפְעַף (aph'aph) likely comes from a root expressing something fine, light, and mobile. Its reduplication (aph-aph) emphasizes the double and symmetrical nature of the eyelid — there are two, one above and one below the eye. The structure of the word well reflects the nature of the thing it designates: something loose that opens and closes.
H6079.emploi: The word appears 10 times in biblical Hebrew, almost always in the books of wisdom or poetry (Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Jeremiah), where the image of the eyelid becomes a means of speaking of gaze, vigilance, or illumination. In the literal sense, it evokes the action of sleeping or staying awake (Psalms 132:4: "I will not give sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids"). In a figurative sense, it becomes an image of divine vigilance (Psalms 11:4) or light (dawn). This richness of usage shows how the Bible plays with body images to express spiritual realities.
H6079.portee: The eyelid, in biblical language, reminds us that gaze and vision are not neutral: they reveal what we seek, what we accept to see, or what we flee from. The calls to direct one's eyelids (Proverbs 4:25) invite the believer to watch over their attention and heart. The image of God's eyelids that test hearts (Psalms 11:4) affirms that nothing escapes His vigilant attention — a source of reverent fear and trust.

sens: to kick up, scatter dust
to stir up, raise in a cloud
H6080.detail:
1. To kick up or scatter dust — this is the image of fine powder that flies up as a result of a gesture or movement. In the only example provided (2 Samuel 16:13), Shimei accompanies David on his way and 'kicks up' dust while walking or gesturing, likely to insult and dishonor him. It is a gesture of contempt and cursing, as dust symbolizes humiliation.
2. To stir up or raise in a cloud — the word evokes the action of stirring the air or ground so that dust rises and envelops someone, as a visible manifestation of anger or dishonor.
H6080.origine: The Hebrew verb עָפַר (a.phar) comes from the root עפר which denotes dust, pulverized earth. In the Piel (the form used here), it means causative: 'to make fly' or 'to kick up' dust. It is a concrete word, an image of movement and dispersion. The root evokes fragility and humiliation, since dust is what covers and soils.
H6080.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 16:13. It is a dramatic moment: David flees Jerusalem after Absalom's revolt, and Shimei pursues him, cursing him and throwing stones at him — gestures of public hostility and humiliation. Kicking up dust adds to this picture of insult: it is a visible demonstration of contempt, reinforcing the shame inflicted on David. The context shows that this gesture accompanies other signs of malice (the stones, the curses).
H6080.portee: This word reminds us that public humiliation, even when suffered unjustly, can be a path of trial for the believer. David, anointed king by God, endures this contempt without retaliating. Understanding this gesture of dust helps the reader to gauge the depth of David's suffering during his exile and temporary abandonment, and shows the strength of his perseverance in the face of insults.

sens: Son of Midian, one of the ancestors of the Midianites
Man bearing the name 'Epher' mentioned twice in biblical genealogies
H6081G.detail:
1. Epher is the second son of Midian, born of the union between Abraham and Keturah after Sarah's death. His name literally means 'a calf', possibly evoking fertility or strength. He is the brother of Epha, Henoch, Abida, and Eldaa, and these five brothers are the ancestors of the Midianite peoples (Genesis 25:4).
2. Epher appears a second time in the genealogies of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 1:33) as an important ancestor in the lineage of the descendants of Keturah, confirming his place in the history of ancient Middle Eastern peoples.
H6081G.origine: The name Epher means 'a calf' in Hebrew, an animal image that conjures vigor and fertility. This name belongs to the patriarchal generation where Abraham, having become a father for the second time with Keturah, sees the birth of a new lineage that will become a distinct people. The repetition of the name in two genealogical records shows its importance in tracing the origins of the Midianites.
H6081G.emploi: Epher is mentioned exactly twice in the Bible, both in genealogical lists: first in Genesis 25:4 as the son of Midian and brother of Epha, Henoch, Abida, and Eldaa, and then in 1 Chronicles 1:33 in a parallel genealogy of the descendants of Keturah. These two occurrences confirm his role as a founding ancestor of the Midianite people. The Midianites, of whom Epher is an ancestor, play an important role in the history of Israel: they are sometimes allies, sometimes adversaries of the Hebrews, particularly during the time of the Judges.

sens: son of Ezra, of the tribe of Judah
H6081H.detail: Epher is a man of the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Ezra and the brother of Jether, Mered, and Jalon (1 Chronicles 4:17).
H6081H.origine: The name Epher literally means 'a calf' in Hebrew, possibly evoking an image of strength or youth. This name also belonged to other biblical characters, notably the son of Midian in patriarchal times, but it is the son of Ezra that the provided usages refer to.
H6081H.emploi: Epher is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:17, in a genealogy of the descendants of Judah. He is listed among the four sons of Ezra (with Jether, Mered, and Jalon), with no further details given about his life or actions. He is a minor character in the Old Testament, known only through this genealogical list.

sens: head of a family of the tribe of Manasseh during the divided monarchy
H6081I.detail: Epher is a man of the people of Israel, one of the important family heads of the tribe of Manasseh who lived east of the Jordan. He is presented in 1 Chronicles 5:24 as a 'valiant man' and a notable figure among the leaders of his tribe.
H6081I.origine: The name Epher means 'a calf', evoking the image of a young beast. It is a Hebrew name among the descendants of Israel, also borne by other biblical characters such as one of the sons of Midian (Genesis 25:4).
H6081I.emploi: Epher appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:24. He is listed among the family heads of Manasseh who lived during the divided monarchy. His enumeration alongside other notable leaders indicates that he held an important responsibility in the internal governance of his tribe.

sens: young deer or young gazelle
grace and lightness in movement
delicate and graceful beauty
H6082.detail: 1. The fawn is the young of a gazelle or deer, a slender and light animal whose movements evoke speed and agility (Song of Solomon 2:9). 2. In the Song, the beloved is compared to a fawn for his grace and agility — he moves quickly and lightly, like this leaping animal (Song of Solomon 2:17). 3. The breasts of the beloved are compared to 'two fawns, twins of a gazelle': this image evokes not the shape but the delicacy, symmetry, and beauty of two young twin animals, soft and graceful (Song of Solomon 4:5).
H6082.origine: The Hebrew word denotes the young of the gazelle or deer. It is a concrete and poetic term, frequently used in ancient Near Eastern love literature to evoke grace and lightness. The root evokes the idea of youth and tenderness.
H6082.emploi: This word appears only in the Song of Solomon, five times, and always in a poetic context of love and beauty. The beloved is 'like a gazelle or a fawn' (2:9, 2:17, 8:14), an image of his speed and irresistible charm. The breasts of the beloved are 'like two fawns, twins of a gazelle' (4:5, 7:4), a metaphor for their delicate beauty and symmetry. The usage is entirely figurative and poetic: it is never about describing the animal for itself, but evoking grace and tenderness in the language of love.
H6082.portee: The fawn, in the Song, teaches us that the Bible sees beauty and grace, including physical beauty, as reflections of the order and delicacy of divine creation. This image also suggests that the joyful love between spouses is worthy, innocent, and beautiful — a theme that Christians too often forget.

sens: dry and fine earth, in light particles or powder
debris, ruins, materials reduced to powder
mortar, mixture to bind stones
that which is vile, fragile, of no value
H6083.detail:
1. Dust is the earth reduced to fine and dry particles, which easily flies away or settles on the ground. It is the material from which God formed man at the beginning: "The Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground" (Genesis 2:7). This ordinary, humble material becomes a living body when God breathes His breath into it.
2. Dust also refers to debris, ruins reduced to fragments, as when a weapon or a city is destroyed. Isaiah speaks of enemies whose sword is reduced to "dust" and the bow made of straw that flies away (Isaiah 41:2).
3. The mortar used to seal the stones of a house or wall is also called dust; thus, one "removes the dust" from a leprous house to cleanse it (Leviticus 14:41-42).
4. Figuratively, dust symbolizes humility, death, and human helplessness. Job weeps in the dust, and the prophet cries: "I am reduced to dust" (Job 2:12; Psalms 119:25). It reminds us that man will return to the earth from which he came.
H6083.origine: The Hebrew word expresses the idea of a fine, powdery material, something that detaches or rises. It comes from a root related to the action of sweeping or shaking. Dust is everywhere in the dry land of the East: it rises with the wind, covers the roads, and seeps into homes. It is a daily reality and a powerful symbol of transience.
H6083.emploi: This word appears 103 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poetry and historical narratives. It primarily denotes the concrete material: the dry earth from which the body is formed (Genesis 2:7; 3:19; Psalms 103:14), the mortar of constructions (Leviticus 14:41-45), the debris of destruction (2 Samuel 22:43; Isaiah 41:2). Figuratively, it expresses ritual humiliation when one throws dust on oneself as a sign of mourning or repentance (Job 2:12; Joshua 7:6), or human fragility before God (Job 4:19; 10:9). Finally, it symbolizes helplessness and death: one returns to dust (Genesis 3:19; Ecclesiastes 3:20).
H6083.portee: This word reminds the believer that he is created from humble material, that he has no strength in himself, and that his life depends entirely on the breath of God. Dust, far from being contemptible, becomes God's means to form a living being endowed with consciousness. It also invites humility: we come from the earth and return to it, which should detach us from pride and turn us towards divine mercy.

sens: City of the tribe of Benjamin, located east of Bethel
H6084G.detail: 1. Ophrah is a small city belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, about eight kilometers east of Bethel. It appears in the list of cities of Benjamin at the time of the division of the territory among the tribes (Joshua 18:23). In the time of King Saul, it served as a point of devastation during Philistine incursions: an enemy detachment headed towards Ophrah to ravage the region (1 Samuel 13:17).
H6084G.origine: The name Ophrah means "young doe" or "fawn" in Hebrew. It is a name derived from the animal world, likely evoking the wooded landscapes of the region. The place is also called Beth-Leaphrah, which literally means "house of dust."
H6084G.emploi: Ophrah appears twice in the Bible. First, it is listed in the administrative list of Benjaminite cities at the time of the land division after the conquest (Joshua 18:23). Then, it is mentioned during a military campaign in Saul's time, when the Philistines send raiding troops into this region (1 Samuel 13:17). These two mentions show that Ophrah was a border town, exposed to external threats.

sens: Place of Manasseh in Canaan, homeland of Gideon
H6084H.detail: Ophrah is a city of the tribe of Manasseh, located near Shechem, famous as the birthplace of Gideon. It is where the angel of the Lord came to find him while he was threshing wheat (Judges 6:11), and where Gideon built an altar after his encounter with God (Judges 6:24). Ophrah belonged to the family of Abiezer and became the center of Gideon's life and governance: it is where he placed the ephod that attracted Israel's idolatry (Judges 8:27), where he was buried after his death (Judges 8:32), and where his son Abimelech committed the massacre of his brothers (Judges 9:5).
H6084H.origine: The name Ophrah means "young doe" or "fawn," evoking lightness and agility. Although this etymology is poetic, it may reflect the character of the site or a notable feature of the local landscape.
H6084H.emploi: Ophrah appears five times in the book of Judges, always in the story of Gideon (chapters 6 to 9). It is mentioned as the place where Gideon's family lived, where major events of his life took place — the appearance of the angel, the construction of the altar, the placement of the problematic ephod, his burial — and where the drama of Abimelech occurred. Ophrah embodies both the home of a God-sent savior and the place where an idolatrous temptation took root, bringing a curse upon Gideon's house.
H6084H.portee: The story of Ophrah shows how a blessed place can become a spiritual trap. Gideon receives a divine call and wins victories there, but it is also from Ophrah that the idolatrous ephod radiates, leading Israel away from God. For the reader, this reminds us that proximity to God does not guarantee faithfulness, and that one generation can abandon what the previous generation received.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah
H6084I.detail: Ophrah is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, during the divided monarchy (after the split of the kingdom of Israel). He is the son of Meonothai and appears in the genealogy of the sons of Judah.
H6084I.origine: The name Ophrah means "fawn" in Hebrew, evoking the image of a young deer. It is a poetic and personal name, borne by this individual from the tribe of Judah.
H6084I.emploi: Ophrah is mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 4:14, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Judah. The text notes that he was the son of Meonothai and that his descendants included craftsmen and workers. This brief mention places him in the continuity of the Judah lineage, but without further detail about his life or role.

sens: Hittite man, son of Zohar
Owner of the field of Machpelah that Abraham bought to bury Sarah
H6085G.detail: Ephron is a Hittite who lived in the time of Abraham. He was the son of Zohar and owned the field of Machpelah, near Mamre, along with the cave that was there. When Abraham sought a place to bury his wife Sarah, he negotiated with Ephron and bought this field for four hundred shekels of silver (Genesis 23:16). This transaction, conducted in the presence of the city's elders, allowed Abraham to establish a lasting family burial site: it is where Sarah, Abraham himself, Isaac, Rebekah, and Jacob were buried (Genesis 49:29-30 and 50:13).
H6085G.origine: The name Ephron means "like a gazelle" or "who has the agility of a doe." It was a name borne by a Hittite, one of the Canaanite populations with whom Abraham dealt directly. The character remains memorable especially for this sale that marked Abraham's appropriation of land in Canaan.
H6085G.emploi: Ephron appears ten times in Genesis, all in chapter 23 and its subsequent references. In the account of chapter 23, Abraham first approaches him before the sons of Heth (Genesis 23:8), then Ephron publicly responds and agrees to sell his field (Genesis 23:10, 23:14). Abraham weighs the money before Ephron and the witnesses (Genesis 23:16), and the property is then designated as "the field of Ephron" (Genesis 23:17). Later, Jacob and Joseph refer to this same field purchased from Ephron when they speak of their burial place (Genesis 25:9, Genesis 49:29-30, Genesis 50:13).
H6085G.portee: This figure of Ephron reminds us that Abraham's faith was also expressed in the acquisition of land where his loved ones could rest. The honest negotiation and the witnesses present show how God inscribed Abraham's heritage in law and concrete reality. This field became a foundation of the promise of a lasting possession in Canaan.

sens: Mountain or locality on the border of the territory of Benjamin
H6085H.detail: 1. Éphron refers to a mountain or locality located on the borders of the territory of Benjamin, in the land of Canaan. It is mentioned as an important geographical landmark for delineating the territory of the sons of Judah. Its name evokes the idea of lightness or grace ("fawn"), a poetic image typical of place names in ancient Israel.
H6085H.origine: The name "Éphron" comes from a Hebrew root suggesting the image of a light and graceful creature, like a fawn. It is a proper name of a place, not a common word used in a figurative sense. Its usage in the Bible is limited, indicating that it is a well-identified geographical site but infrequently cited in the preserved biblical texts.
H6085H.emploi: Éphron appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:9, where it is listed as a landmark in the precise description of the borders of the territory of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. This mention is part of a long passage enumerating the boundaries and territorial limits, showing that this place served as a recognized border between the tribes. Its appearance solely in this administrative and geographical context indicates that it was a well-known site among the ancient Israelites for marking territorial divisions.

sens: Border city of the territory of Benjamin
Site where Abijah defeated Jeroboam
H6085I.detail:
1. Éphron is a city located on the borders of the territory of Benjamin, in ancient Israel. It appears in the account of the war between Abijah, king of Judah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel in the North (2 Chronicles 13:19).
2. During this battle, Abijah achieves victory and conquers several cities of the Northern kingdom, including Éphron, which he takes from Jeroboam along with the localities dependent on it. This site thus marks a key moment in the conflict between the two kingdoms.
H6085I.origine: The name Éphron means "little fawn" or "like a fawn" in Hebrew, an image that evokes grace and lightness. This place name appears in the Bible to designate this fortified city of ancient times, one of the strategic points on the borders of Israel and Judah.
H6085I.emploi: Éphron is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 13:19, as one of the cities conquered by King Abijah during his military victory over Jeroboam. It is listed among the conquests — Bethel, Jeshanah, and Éphron — which mark the extent of Judah's victory and the strengthening of its authority over the Northern borders. This context shows that Éphron was an important locality from a strategic and administrative perspective.

sens: Solid plant material that constitutes the trunk and branches of trees
