Piece or board of wood intended to be worked or used in construction and craftsmanship
Firewood or fuel for maintaining a fire
Tree standing, considered as a source of wood
Figuratively, object of worship or representing an idolatrous power
Instrument of torture or punishment
H6086G.detail:
1. Wood is the solid material of trees, which constitutes their natural framework. When a tree is cut down, wood is obtained — the very substance that formed its trunk and branches. The Bible often mentions specific trees: gopher wood for Noah's ark (Genesis 6:14), acacia wood for the furniture of the Tabernacle (Exodus 37:1), cedar wood for the construction of the Temple (1 Kings 6:10).
2. Wood becomes a raw material that is worked: it is cut into boards, beams, and bars. These pieces of wood are used in the making of worship furniture, doors, and house walls. Exodus 25:5 lists the woods required for building the Tabernacle.
3. Wood also serves as fuel for fire: it is burned to cook offerings on the altar (Leviticus 1:7-8) or to perform purification rites (Numbers 19:6 mentions cedar wood thrown into the flames).
4. Sometimes the word refers to the living tree, the source of wood. Genesis 22:3 recounts that Abraham "cut wood" for the sacrifice — it is wood that he cut himself.
5. Figuratively, wood represents idols and false gods: Deuteronomy 4:28 warns that idols are "the work of the hands of men, of wood and stone."
6. Finally, wood can refer to an instrument of punishment or death, such as the gallows.
H6086G.origine: The Hebrew word עֵץ (ets) comes from an ancient root that designates the hard substance of wood. The same root appears in several Semitic languages. In Hebrew, this word encompasses both the living tree (as a source of wood) and the shaped wood (raw material). No complex family of words directly derives from it in the Bible; the concept remains simple and concrete, rooted in the daily experience of the people who worked wood to build and create.
H6086G.emploi: The word ets appears 139 times in the biblical text, mainly in historical and legislative books. Its usage varies according to context. In construction narratives — the ark, the Tabernacle, the Temple — it almost always refers to wood as a worked material: boards, beams, bars of acacia or cedar wood (Exodus 25:10, 1 Kings 6:10). In sacrifice and purification rituals, it is burned (Leviticus 1:7, Numbers 19:6). Some uses are more abstract or figurative: wood becomes an image of idolatry (Deuteronomy 4:28) or simply represents the tree before transformation (Genesis 22:3, Abraham cuts wood).
H6086G.portee: For today's believer, this word reminds of solidity and stability: wood is what one builds upon, what supports and sustains. It is also the material that God gives to man to create, build, and fulfill his worship. Conversely, wood becomes a warning against idolatry — it symbolizes the futility of carved idols. Finally, the mention of wood in rituals and offerings underscores the importance of concrete material in the service of God: it is with real wood, real fire, that one honors the Lord.

sens: Woody plant with a trunk, branches, and leaves
Wood used as raw material (beam, board, log)
Wooden structure erected to hang a condemned person
Image of stability, growth, or life (figurative sense)
H6086H.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the plant itself: a woody plant with a solid trunk, branches, and leaves, which bears fruit according to its kind (Genesis 1:11). God planted a garden at creation, where the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil were located (Genesis 2:9), central trees in the account of the fall. It is the fruit tree that is cultivated, like those in the plantations of Ecclesiastes 2:5.
2. By extension, the word refers to the wood itself, the material derived from the trunk: boards, beams, logs for fire. When cedar wood was sent from Lebanon for the construction of the temple (Ezra 3:7), it referred to this transformed material, usable for the framework. This also extends to firewood or fuel.
3. In the ancient Near East, the tree served as a gallows: a criminal was hoisted onto a tree to be left to die or after death as an additional punishment (Joshua 10:27; Deuteronomy 21:22-23). This terrible image has marked the vocabulary of executions.
H6086H.origine: The Hebrew word etz comes from an ancient root meaning that which grows and stands upright, particularly the woody plant. Its basic image is one of solidity and duration: a tree is a stable living being, anchored to the ground. In the Old Testament, remarkable trees (oak, cedar, palm) are often landmarks or symbols of power and prosperity. The word applies to both the fruit tree of the orchard and the raw wood or the structure made from it.
H6086H.emploi: The word appears about 125 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the accounts of Genesis, the Law (Leviticus, Deuteronomy), and the historical books. In the first three chapters of Genesis, the tree is central to the creation and fall narrative: God creates the trees (1:11-12), Adam and Eve inhabit them and eat their fruit (2:9, 3:1-3), and the tree of knowledge becomes the instrument of disobedience (3:6). The Law regulates the use of fruit trees (Leviticus 19:23) and their cutting down in times of war (Deuteronomy 20:19-20). In the Psalms and Proverbs, the tree becomes an image of life, strength, or wisdom: a righteous man is like a tree planted by the waters (Psalms 1:3), and the tree of life symbolizes wisdom (Proverbs 3:18). Ecclesiastes refers to tree plantations as human vanity (2:5).
H6086H.portee: The tree unites several dimensions in Scripture: it is first a gift from the Creator God, a source of life and food (Genesis 1:11-12), and recalls the order and beauty of the created world. Next, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil crystallizes the fundamental ethical issue: the choice of obedience or disobedience to God, and its consequences (Genesis 2-3). Finally, the image of the planted and rooted tree, which naturally bears fruit (Psalms 1:3, Proverbs 11:30), invites the believer to be rooted in God for a fruitful life. It is also an image of strength and duration that reinforces trust in divine providence.

sens: the living tree, with its trunk and branches
cut, sawn, or split wood: log, board, beam
an object made of wood: utensil, stick, written piece of wood
wood as material, for construction or fuel
H6086I.detail:
1. The living tree is the primary image of the word: a being that grows and stands upright. Ezekiel 37:16-20 asks the prophet to take two pieces of wood and write the name of the two kingdoms on them; this image of inscribed wood, hard and durable, carries the message that God wants to unite the separated kingdoms.

2. Cut, split, or worked wood: piece of log, board. In 1 Kings 17:12, the widow of Zarephath tells Elijah that she is gathering "two sticks" to light the fire and cook a last meal. Ecclesiastes 10:9 warns: "He who splits wood will experience danger" — the manual labor of the woodsman involves risk.

3. An object or part made of wood: the "stick" of flax under which Rahab hides the spies (Joshua 2:6) is the dry fiber of flax bundled together. The piece of wood inscribed in Ezekiel is a durable support for writing.

4. Wood as raw material and resource: Moses throws a "piece of wood" into the bitter water to make it sweet (Exodus 15:25), an image of a simple yet divine action. Wood is used for heating, construction, and cooking. It is an essential resource for the daily life of the ancients.
H6086I.origine: The Hebrew word ets (עֵץ) primarily denotes the living tree that stands, with its sense of elevation and solidity. The same root appears in other words related to worked wood or growth. In Hebrew, wood and tree form a single reality: the tree is the living source, wood is what is derived from it. The word also evokes the durability and firmness of wood, which resists and remains.
H6086I.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the provided passages. It primarily refers to cut and worked wood for practical use: gathering wood for fire (Numbers 15:33, 1 Kings 17:12), splitting wood (Ecclesiastes 10:9). It can also be a piece of ordinary wood thrown into water (Exodus 15:25) or a piece serving as a writing support (Ezekiel 37:16-20). In this latter case, the wood is not just raw material, but a symbol of the identity and unity of the tribes. Wood is the humble object of daily life, always useful, durable, and concrete: this is why it can become a prophetic image.
H6086I.portee: For the reader, wood recalls divine providence over the simple needs of life: fire, food, warmth. It is also a symbol of durability and unity — the two pieces of wood in Ezekiel carry the hope of restoration. Wood also confronts human fragility and the limits of labor: the woodsman faces danger, the widow gathers her last strength. The word invites recognition of simple things as signs of God's presence and power.

sens: Tree standing or cut down
Material derived from a tree: lumber for construction, heating, or crafting
Object shaped from wood: handle, shaft, post
Gallows or hanging post
H6086J.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the living tree or the tree that has just been cut down. This is the most natural and common meaning in Hebrew.
2. It can also refer to the wood itself — the raw or worked material. Thus in 2 Samuel 23:7, it designates the wood of a spear, meaning the wooden shaft that constitutes this weapon of war.
3. More broadly, the word applies to any wooden object: a handle of an axe (Deuteronomy 19:5), a shaft, a post. This is the most precise meaning when talking about a shaped piece of wood.
4. By serious extension, it designates the gallows or the hanging post — a wooden structure where condemned individuals were executed. Esther 7:10 is the most famous example: Haman is hanged on the wood he had prepared for Mordecai. This meaning, among Jews and later among Christians, will take on major theological significance.
H6086J.origine: The Hebrew word עֵץ (ets) comes from a root that evokes the idea of rigidity or firmness. In Hebrew, there are related words, such as אֵצָל (etsal, "beside"), which share an ancient root. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word was often translated as ξύλον (xylon), which has the same meaning and range of uses. The Hebrew word fundamentally means "that which is hard, durable, stable" — an essential characteristic of wood.
H6086J.emploi: This word appears at least twelve times in the provided usages, with a remarkable concentration in the book of Esther (five occurrences around the wood prepared for Haman). It primarily designates everyday objects: the handle of the axe that accidentally kills in Deuteronomy 19:5, the shaft of the spear in 2 Samuel 23:7. But its most dramatic and meaningful use is that of the gallows: in Esther, the wood becomes the instrument of the death sentence — a wood that Haman builds to kill Mordecai, and on which he himself dies. This reversal of fate, where the prepared becomes the cause of his own ruin, gives the word symbolic force. The wood, an inert material, thus becomes the vector of hidden divine justice.
H6086J.portee: For the believer, this word embodies first the material, the humble reality of the created world. But especially, in the context of the gallows or the execution wood, it opens up to a deep meditation: the New Testament will speak of Christ being attached to the wood (Acts 5:30; 10:39; 13:29; 1 Peter 2:24), exactly using this Hebrew language. The wood thus becomes the place where judgment is fulfilled and grace is unfolded. That is why this small note on a simple word invites us never to separate the material from the spiritual.

sens: one who works with wood, who builds or repairs wooden structures
the skilled craftsman who uses carpentry and woodworking tools
H6086K.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the worker who works with wood to make objects or structures: furniture, houses, or any wooden element. It is a specialized trade that requires skill and experience. David brought in carpenters from Tyre to build his house (2 Samuel 5:11), and King Joash employed them to restore the temple (2 Kings 12:11).
2. The carpenter is a trusted worker, often grouped with other specialized artisans (stone masons, laborers). Solomon gathered a large number to build the temple (1 Chronicles 22:15). The text of Isaiah 44:13 shows him at work: he marks, measures, shapes the wood with his tools (line, pencil, knife, compass), even sculpting human figures.
H6086K.origine: The Hebrew word ʿèṣ primarily means the tree or wood (the raw material). The carpenter is thus literally "one of the wood" or "one who works the wood." It is a derivative that designates the professional due to his raw material. The same root encompasses the tree, construction wood, firewood, and the one who shapes it.
H6086K.emploi: This word appears 4 times in the Segond in reference to the carpenter. It is always used to designate workers engaged in major works: construction or restoration of royal houses, building of the temple. Carpenters are clearly distinct professionals from other trades (stone masons, laborers). The passage from Isaiah 44:13 enriches the portrait by showing the carpenter not only as a builder but also as an artist and sculptor, capable of measuring precisely and creating human forms. The usage is always honorable and linked to significant projects.
H6086K.portee: The carpenter in Scripture represents the skilled worker, one whose trade requires skill, prudence, and creativity. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that every well-done work — every honest and careful labor — honors God. Furthermore, the carpenter of Isaiah 44:13 becomes an image of idolatry: man makes wooden gods in his image, forgetting that he himself is created in the image of God. It is an invitation to recognize the true craftsman: it is God.

sens: Cause physical or moral pain to someone
Experience pain, sadness, or grief oneself
Be in a state of suffering or torment
Offend or harm someone
H6087A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to make someone suffer, to cause them injury or pain. It is an act directed against a person to hurt them: in Ecclesiastes 10:9, the one who moves stones "will be injured," meaning will receive a blow that causes suffering.
2. The word also expresses the emotional state of the one who suffers: to be saddened, to be in grief or remorse. In Genesis 6:6, the Lord "was afflicted in His heart" over His creation, which shows profound moral pain, a painful regret.
3. Sometimes it designates an inner affliction, a pain that weighs on the heart without necessarily coming from an external aggression. In 1 Samuel 20:34, Jonathan "was afflicted because of David" because his father had offended him.
4. The word can also mean to offend or outrage someone. In 1 Kings 1:6, it is said that the father "had never reproached him," meaning had never offended him with a rebuke.
H6087A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that paints the idea of striking, injuring, causing harm. It is linked to the concrete notion of physical pain that has extended to moral pain and grief. Aramaic has preserved the same root with the same meaning: "to do harm." This root thus expresses everything that causes harm or suffering, whether it be physical or from the heart.
H6087A.emploi: The verb appears 15 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical books, the Psalms, and the wisdom literature. It often describes the emotional affliction of a person: God can be afflicted (Genesis 6:6), a person can be afflicted by the actions or words of another (1 Samuel 20:34), or one can afflict oneself by refusing to rejoice (Nehemiah 8:10-11). The verb nuances according to whether it describes suffered pain, felt grief, or received offense. In several passages, it designates the heart's pain in the face of injustice or misfortune.
H6087A.portee: This word helps to understand that moral suffering and affliction are real and that God Himself can be touched by them. It shows us that refusing comfort (Nehemiah 8:11) or remaining in sadness can be a lack of trust in God. It also reminds us that our actions afflict or rejoice the hearts of others, especially that of God, and that true freedom comes from accepting grace rather than remaining in reproach.

sens: To shape, mold a material to give it a form
To create, shape a living being, especially in its body
To honor, worship by forming offerings or acts of devotion
H6087B.detail:
1. To form primarily means to shape or mold a raw material — like a potter who kneads clay or a craftsman who works wood — to give it a specific and useful shape.
2. The word is also used to create and shape a living being: in Job 10:8, God tells Job, "Your hands have formed me," meaning He carefully shaped his body, like an artist shapes his work. It is the image of a delicate and intentional creation.
3. To form can also mean to honor or worship: in Jeremiah 44:19, the women ask if they can "honor" the queen of heaven by preparing cakes and offerings for her. Here, to form means to make or prepare the acts and offerings that show respect and devotion.
H6087B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of shaping, molding, or giving a form. This root belongs to the family of verbs related to creation and manual work: it is found in words that designate the work of a potter, sculptor, or any craftsman who gives shape to material. The basic image is that of hands working the material to transform it.
H6087B.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Bible in Hebrew according to these uses. In Job 10:8, it describes God's creative action in forming man's body with His hands, depicting it as a carefully molded work. In Jeremiah 44:19, it is used in the context of idolatrous worship, where women prepare offerings to the queen of heaven to honor her. The verb consistently retains the fundamental idea of creating or making something with one's hands, but the context refines the meaning: divine and respectful creation in Job, cultic act of devotion in Jeremiah.
H6087B.portee: This word reminds us that God has formed us with intention and care, like an artist creates his work. For the believer, this invites recognition of the value and dignity that God has given to our bodies and lives. It also invites a distinction between forming and honoring the true God and the false cults that attempt to imitate Him: only the true God deserves our devotion.

sens: Experiencing pain, sorrow, or moral grief
Expressing melancholy, affliction, or disappointment
H6088.detail:
1. Experiencing pain, sorrow, or moral grief — This is the inner state of one who suffers emotionally, carrying a weight on the heart. In Daniel 6:20, King Darius approaches the lion's den with a "sad" voice: he is anxious, worried for Daniel and for himself, fearing that Daniel's God may not have been able to save him.
2. Expressing melancholy, affliction, or disappointment — This is the external manifestation of that inner pain, visible in tone, gaze, and words. The sad voice of the king reveals his emotional turmoil in the face of a serious and uncertain situation.
H6088.origine: The Hebrew word עֲצַב (a.tsav) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to shape" or "to mold," but which has taken on the meaning of "to grieve" or "to sadden," as if pain "shapes" or "marks" a person. The Aramaic form of the text in Daniel (נִצְטַּב in Aramaic) is closely related and denotes one who is grieved or afflicted. This image of pain shaping a person reflects a biblical view where emotions are not light: they transform the one who feels them.
H6088.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament Greek and here in the Aramaic texts of Daniel — it is an infrequent term in Scripture. Its unique use in Daniel 6:20 places it in a context of royal concern: King Darius, although powerful, is moved and troubled at the thought that Daniel might have perished at the hands of the lions. This usage shows that sadness can affect even the great of this world, and that it can arise in the face of uncertainty and fear of losing someone.
H6088.portee: This word reminds readers that true emotions — sadness, worry, grief — are recognized and named in Scripture. King Darius, a figure of power, is not ashamed to reveal his affliction. This encourages the believer to acknowledge their own pains as real and legitimate, while entrusting them to God who sees and can deliver, as He did for Daniel.

sens: Intense physical or moral suffering
Hard work, laborious effort
Heartache, sorrow of the heart
That which causes pain or irritation
H6089A.detail:
1. Pain is primarily intense suffering, whether physical or moral. In Genesis 3:16, it is the pain of childbirth that accompanies a woman's labor — a deep suffering linked to the body and sin.
2. The word also designates hard and tiring work, that which costs and exhausts. In Proverbs 10:22, "all toil brings abundance": it is the laborious effort required to earn one's bread, as in Psalms 127:2 where eating "the bread of pain" means feeding on the fruit of difficult and anxious labor.
3. Pain is also the heartache, the sadness that weighs on the soul. In Proverbs 10:22, God's blessing enriches "without sorrow," meaning without the wealth being gnawed by worry or regret.
4. Finally, the word can refer to that which causes pain, that which wounds or irritates: in Proverbs 15:1, a "harsh" word "stirs up" anger, provoking a moral wound that inflames fury.
H6089A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of working, laboring, and by extension suffering. It describes both the pain of work and the suffering it engenders. It is a concrete word that evokes the sweat of the brow, the effort that tires the body and mind, but also the moral pain that results from it.
H6089A.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Proverbs and Psalms, with a few occurrences in Genesis. Its meaning varies according to the context: in Genesis 3:16, it is the physical suffering of childbirth, a consequence of sin. In Psalms and Proverbs, it mainly denotes the painful work and anxious fatigue of daily labor (Psalms 127:2, Proverbs 5:10, 14:23), but also the heartache and worry that accompany wealth or anger (Proverbs 10:22, 15:1). The word always retains this dual dimension: the pain of the body and that of the heart.
H6089A.portee: This word reminds the believer that pain and labor are part of the human condition since the original sin (Genesis 3:16). But it also invites them to see that work, even difficult, can be blessed by God and bear fruit (Proverbs 10:22 and 14:23). Pain is not in vain if it is accepted and leads to trust in God rather than anxiety: it is the contrast between eating "the bread of pain" and receiving "the blessing of the Lord."

sens: Container, object shaped to hold or serve a purpose
H6089B.detail: 1. A vessel is a manufactured container, an object created to serve a purpose — here, to hold or transport. Jeremiah 22:28 uses it in the literal sense: King Jeconiah is compared to a despised and broken vessel, an object thrown away because it is no longer pleasing or useful.
H6089B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to form" or "to shape" — the idea of creating something with one's hands. A vessel is a creation, a human creation; it is always shaped, molded, made to last and serve. The biblical context contrasts it with what is natural or living: it is wood, stone, or clay that has been worked.
H6089B.emploi: This word appears only once in Jeremiah 22:28, in a word of judgment addressed to King Jeconiah. The prophecy compares him to a vessel that is thrown away because he is worthless — a fragile, despicable object destined for exile. The image of the broken or rejected vessel represents the king's fate: a creation that is abandoned.
H6089B.portee: This image of the broken vessel reminds the believer that all human power, even royal, is as fragile as an earthen object — destined to be judged and rejected if it opposes God. It invites one not to place their trust in the princes of this world, but to seek the eternal King.

sens: Objet fabriqué de main d'homme, taillé ou coulé, représentant un dieu ou un être divin
Représentation matérielle d'une divinité destinée à être adorée
Ce qu'on vénère à la place du vrai Dieu
H6090B.detail: 1. Le mot désigne d'abord un objet concret, façonné par l'humain — taillé dans la pierre ou le bois, ou coulé en métal — qui prend la forme d'un dieu ou d'une puissance divine. En Ésaïe 48:5, Dieu reproche au peuple d'Israël de créditer son idole de ce que Dieu lui-même a accompli : ils vénéraient une image façonnée de leurs mains au lieu de reconnaître l'action du Seigneur. 2. Par extension, le mot désigne tout ce qu'on adore en place du vrai Dieu — non seulement les statues, mais aussi tout ce à quoi on donne son cœur et son obéissance. C'est l'objet de dépendance spirituelle, celui vers lequel se tourne le culte humain au lieu de se tourner vers le Seigneur.
H6090B.origine: Le mot hébreux ֹצֶב (otsev) vient de la racine יצב ou צבה qui signifie « tailler, façonner » ou « sculpter ». Le mot renvoie essentiellement à l'idée de quelque chose de façonné, taillé, travaillé de main. C'est pourquoi le terme souligne le caractère fabriqué de l'idole : c'est une création humaine, non un dieu véritable. La racine évoque le labeur, l'effort, l'intention de celui qui façonne.
H6090B.emploi: Le mot apparaît une seule fois dans l'Ancien Testament hébreu, dans le passage où Ésaïe présente la controverse entre le vrai Dieu et les idoles. Dieu accuse le peuple de confondre son idole taillée ou fondue avec le Dieu vivant qui contrôle l'histoire. Le contexte montre que l'idole est un objet d'adoration erroné, une créature dépourvue de pouvoir réel, contrairement au Dieu qui annonce et accomplit les événements. Ce passage critique radicalement la confiance en des représentations matérielles de divinités.
H6090B.portee: Ce mot rappelle aux croyants que l'adoration véritable ne se porte pas sur des objets matériels façonnés par l'humain, mais sur le Dieu vivant seul. Il invite à examiner nos cœurs : qu'adorons-nous réellement ? Pouvons-nous attribuer à des créations humaines ou à des choses matérielles le pouvoir et la domination qui n'appartiennent qu'à Dieu ? Le passage d'Ésaïe nous appelle à reconnaître la souveraineté de Dieu sur l'histoire et à nous détourner de tout ce qui prétend à la divinité sans en avoir le pouvoir.

sens: objet sculpté en bois, pierre ou métal, représentant un dieu ou un être divin
représentation matérielle d'une puissance surnaturelle, destinée au culte et à l'adoration
ce qui remplace Dieu dans le cœur et les actes d'un croyant infidèle
H6091.detail:
1. Le mot désigne d'abord l'objet physique façonné par les mains : une statue, un bloc taillé, en argent, or, bois ou pierre, qui figure une divinité. En 1 Samuel 31:9, les Philistins annonçaient la défaite de Saül « dans les maisons de leurs idoles », montrant que ces objets occupaient une place centrale dans leurs sanctuaires. Les Psaumes décrivent ces idoles comme fabriquées par l'homme : « Leurs idoles sont de l'argent et de l'or, elles sont l'ouvrage de la main des hommes » (Psaumes 115:4).
2. Au-delà du simple objet, une idole est une puissance religieuse : ce qu'on honore, ce devant quoi on se prosterne, ce qu'on pense capable d'intercéder ou de protéger. En Psaumes 106:36, le psalmiste dit que les idoles « furent pour eux un piège », suggérant qu'elles captivent ceux qui les servent. Jérémie proclame que « Babylone est prise, Bel est confondu, Merodac est brisé, ses idoles sont confondues » (Jérémie 50:2) : détruire les idoles, c'est anéantir la puissance qu'on croyait y résider.
3. Pour la foi biblique, une idole représente un mensonge spirituel : tout ce qui prétend à la place de Dieu dans la conscience et la vie d'une personne. C'est pourquoi les prophètes d'Israël combattent non seulement la fabrication d'idoles, mais l'idolâtrie elle-même, qui est le détournement de l'âme vers du néant.
H6091.origine: La racine hébreu « atzav » évoque l'action de tailler, de sculpter, de façonner. Une idole est donc littéralement « ce qui est taillé » ou « ce qui est formé ». Le nom partage cette racine avec des verbes signifiant travailler le bois ou la pierre. Ce terme neutre d'« ouvrage taillé » est devenu le mot biblique pour désigner l'objet du culte idolâtre, charge de toute sa condamnation religieuse.
H6091.emploi: Le mot apparaît dix-sept fois dans la Bible hébraïque, principalement dans les prophètes (Jérémie, Ésaïe, Osée) et les Psaumes. Il désigne les idoles des nations païennes (Philistins, Babyloniens, Cananéens) et celles qu'Israël a adoptées dans son infidélité. Dans les récits historiques (1 Samuel, 2 Chroniques), on le rencontre lors des batailles ou des réformes religieuses, notamment le détail que David et ses guerriers recueillaient « les idoles » de leurs ennemis (2 Samuel 5:21), les détruisant pour signifier la victoire du vrai Dieu. En Osée et Michée, le terme souligne la vanité et la gravité de l'idolâtrie : Osée rappelle qu'Israël « a fait des idoles », et Michée annonce que Dieu en fera « un monceau » (Michée 1:7). Le contexte montre toujours que l'idole est une abomination aux yeux du Seigneur.
H6091.portee: Comprendre ce qu'était une idole bibliquement aide le croyant à identifier ce qui usurpe la place de Dieu dans sa vie : non seulement les statues ou les faux dieux des autres religions, mais aussi la richesse, le prestige, le plaisir ou soi-même. La Bible enseigne que l'idole est un mensonge : elle promet ce qu'elle ne peut jamais tenir. Reconnaître sa propre idolâtrie devient alors une étape de conversion authentique.

sens: The backbone, the vertebral column of the animal
The region of the back or the loins, particularly in an animal intended for sacrifice
H6096.detail:
1. The spine is the backbone of an animal, that is, the entire set of vertebrae that form the vertebral column. This term also refers to the region of the sacrum (the bone at the base of the spine). In Leviticus 3:9, during the peace offering, the priest separates the fat "near the spine," which shows that the word can refer to the area all around this bony structure.
2. In the context of animal sacrifices, the spine represents the region of the back and the loins where a particular fat accumulates, related to the fat tail of the sheep. This part was offered to God as a special portion of the sacrifice, emphasizing that the spine is not just an anatomical bone, but a region of the animal rich in sacrificial fat.
H6096.origine: The Hebrew word עָצֶה (a.tseh) comes from a root expressing the idea of strength and solidity, since the backbone is the central support of the body. The word literally designates the "support" of the animal. In ancient Hebrew culture, solid and central bony parts had symbolic importance for sacrifices, as they represented the strength and vitality of the offered body.
H6096.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 3:9. It is found in the detailed description of peace offerings, where God commands that certain specific fats be burned as an offering. The spine is mentioned as an anatomical landmark to identify the fatty region of the sacrifice, particularly that which surrounds the fat tail of the sheep. The uniqueness of this usage shows that the term is a technical word in the sacrificial vocabulary, precise and specialized.
H6096.portee: This word reminds us that biblical sacrifices were not vague or symbolic from afar: they involved concrete knowledge of the body of the offered animal, demonstrating the seriousness and precision of worship. For the believer, this invites consideration that giving to God requires true knowledge and awareness of what is being offered, not an automatic gesture.

sens: Woody plant with a trunk, branches, and leaves
Wood or material obtained from the trunk and branches of a tree
Element of fortification (in biblical Hebrew)
H6097.detail:
1. A tree is a living plant, generally large and robust, with a woody trunk from which branches grow. It is the most visible plant creature in the natural world in Israel.

2. The word also designates the wood or material provided by the tree, which has been cut down or shaped from a tree. In Jeremiah 6:6, the command "cut down the trees" means to cut the trees around Jerusalem to build siege ramps: it is not the trees as plants that interest the assailant, but the wood they provide.

3. These "trees" have here a concrete military function: transformed into construction wood, they serve to build siege works against the besieged city. The verse shows how a simple word designates both the plant and its military use.
H6097.origine: The Hebrew word עֵצָה (etsah) comes from an ancient root that primarily designates the standing tree, a being of nature. In biblical Hebrew, it covers both the living tree and the worked wood, as the Hebrews saw the tree as the primary source of wood. This polysemy is natural: even in French, "wood" means both the forest of trees and the construction material.
H6097.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament (Jeremiah 6:6), in a context of military siege. The Lord commands the Babylonians to cut down the trees around Jerusalem to build ramps and war machines. This unique usage shows that the word designates a concrete reality of the agricultural and military world: trees as a resource for construction wood. The prophet Jeremiah uses this stark image to show the reality of divine punishment: destruction will not be abstract, but physical and material.
H6097.portee: This verse teaches the believer that God's judgment on the sin of a city is not vague, but manifests itself visibly and concretely. The details of the siege—down to the cutting down of trees—remind us that God sees and orchestrates all historical events, including the most material. For the reader of Jeremiah, this confirms the certainty of the prophet's word.

sens: Advice given to someone to enlighten them on what they should do
Plan or project that a person or God forms in their mind
Wisdom, ability to judge well and decide rightly
Decision made after deliberation
Consultation, action of seeking the opinion of others
Intention, God's purpose regarding His plan of salvation
H6098.detail:
1. Counsel is primarily advice given to someone: it is telling another person how to act, what is good or bad for them. When David rejects the "counsel of the wicked" (Job 21:16), he rejects their advice that would lead him away from God. A king who rejects good counsel exposes himself to error: Rehoboam did not listen to the counsel of the elders and tore his kingdom apart (1 Kings 12:8, 13, 14).
2. Counsel can also be a plan that someone forms—what they have decided to do. Ahithophel gave counsel to Absalom to kill David (2 Samuel 15:31, 34). Here, the word designates the intention, strategy, or design that one conceives.
3. It is also the wisdom and judgment that allow one to give good counsel: the Spirit resting on the Messiah includes the "Spirit of counsel" (Isaiah 11:2), that is, the wisdom to see clearly and decide rightly.
4. Counsel can be a resolution, a decision made after common reflection: the princes of the Philistines "consulted" (1 Chronicles 12:19), meaning they deliberated together before sending David away.
5. It is the action of asking for or giving advice: to consult someone is to seek their counsel.
6. Finally, the word designates God's eternal purpose or plan: "No counsel will stand against the Lord" (Proverbs 21:30), for God's project cannot be thwarted. Isaiah proclaims that God will accomplish His "purpose" and execute His "resolution" (Isaiah 46:11).
H6098.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of deliberating, reflecting together. It belongs to the family of Hebrew words that deal with judgment and decision. The central notion is that of a carefully weighed intention, an opinion rendered after reflection. In biblical Hebrew, this word appears mainly in historical narratives and wisdom literature, where the question of good judgment is central.
H6098.emploi: The word appears 85 times in the Old Testament. It is very frequent in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Psalms), where it designates either the good counsel to follow or the folly of those who despise it. In historical narratives (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), it often takes on a more political or military sense: it is the counsel of an advisor (Ahithophel, Hushai) or the result of deliberation. In Isaiah particularly, the word rises in generality: it speaks of the divine purpose, God's eternal plan that surpasses all human projects. The contrast is constant in the Bible: the counsel of man is weak and perishable, the counsel of God is wise, unshakeable, and will certainly be accomplished.
H6098.portee: This word reminds the believer that wisdom is not an individual matter: it arises from counsel, exchange, and listening. Rejecting good counsel is a sign of spiritual folly. But more profoundly, the Bible invites us to discover that God has a purpose for the world and for each person, a plan that holds firm against all obstacles. Trusting in God's counsel means renouncing the illusion of a life left to chance or fragile human judgment.

sens: Having great strength, great power
Numerous, abundant, formidable in number or quantity
Superior, dominant, insurmountable
H6099.detail:
1. The word primarily describes one who possesses formidable strength, capable of acting with authority and imposing their will. God is called "powerful" in His actions: in Joel 2:11, "the executor of His word is powerful," meaning capable of accomplishing all that He decrees. It also refers to military or political strength: Joshua 23:9 speaks of "great and powerful nations" that the Lord has driven out before Israel.
2. The word also designates what is considerable in number or mass. In Exodus 1:9, the Egyptians say that Israel has become "a great and powerful people" — the word emphasizes the magnitude of the population, its imposing character. Joel 2:2 describes a swarm of locusts whose "multitude is immense."
3. By extension, it refers to what dominates, what prevails or surpasses others. Proverbs 18:18 mentions "the powerful" in speaking of those who settle disputes, as if they have superior authority. Daniel 8:24 describes someone who "will destroy the powerful," meaning the dominant political and military actors.
H6099.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of strength and solidity. It is related to the notion of active or manifest power, not just potential. In the Old Testament, this term applies to both men and God, armies and populations, reflecting the importance of visible and concrete strength in Semitic culture.
H6099.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Pentateuch, Joshua), the Psalms, and the prophets. It regularly describes the nations that the Israelites must confront or that threaten them: Deuteronomy 7:1 lists seven nations "more powerful" than Israel, a theme echoed in Joshua 23:9 and Deuteronomy 4:38. The word also qualifies God Himself and the manifestation of His power (Joel 2:11). In Isaiah 53:12, the suffering Servant will be associated "with the powerful," suggesting a final victory despite the appearance of defeat. The context is often one of contrast between human strength and divine sovereignty.
H6099.portee: This word reminds us that true power does not primarily belong to empires or strong men, but to God and His word. It invites the believer not to fear seemingly "powerful" adversaries, but to trust in the God who will defeat them. It is also an invitation to recognize in God's promises (like the one made to Abraham in Genesis 18:18) a real, active power, not just a future one.

sens: Souffrance physique ou morale intense
Peine, affliction du cœur
Travail pénible, fatigue
Voie, chemin difficile ou mauvais
H6090A.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes intense physical or emotional suffering, the pain that overwhelms a person. When Jabez's mother names him thus, she expresses the intense pain she felt in giving birth to him (1 Chronicles 4:9).
2. It also refers to the grief, the affliction that weighs on the heart and mind — the burden of sadness or sorrow. The psalmist asks God to see if there is a "wicked way" in him, meaning a painful or contrary direction to His will (Psalms 139:24).
3. The word can denote hard and exhausting work, the fatigue resulting from prolonged effort. Isaiah promises Israel rest after their "labors" and agitations, evoking the weariness caused by servitude (Isaiah 14:3).
4. By extension, it can qualify a way or situation marked by pain and difficulty — what is "bad" in the sense that it brings suffering.
H6090A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally expresses the idea of hard work, effort that tires. It is linked to the image of labor and pain. In Hebrew, this root appears in several forms that all evoke physical or emotional fatigue. It is a concrete word that paints the reality of human suffering in work and life.
H6090A.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible translated by Segond, always to express a difficult reality. It qualifies the pain of childbirth (1 Chronicles 4:9), where it is at the very heart of the proper name given to a child as a mark of what it cost. It can describe a wicked, difficult way (Psalms 139:24), where man asks God to keep him from this path of pain. It also evokes the fatigue and weariness caused by servitude and oppression (Isaiah 14:3), painting the condition of the enslaved people. Each use shows a facet of human suffering: physical, emotional, or related to condition.
H6090A.portee: This word reminds the reader that pain and fatigue are deeply human realities and that God sees them. For Jabez, being named according to the pain of his birth does not condemn him — he even becomes more esteemed than his brothers, showing that God can transform what begins in pain. For the believer, recognizing pain in his name invites him to confess the reality to God and seek the rest He promises after trials.

sens: worker who works for a wage
one who acts out of self-interest rather than conviction
H6092.detail:
1. The mercenary is a worker, a laborer hired for pay. It is someone who rents their services to earn a living. In Isaiah 58:3, the context speaks of mistreating "all your hired workers": these are the salaried workers employed for household or field tasks, who are oppressed instead of being treated justly.
2. Figuratively, it refers to one who acts solely out of personal interest, without sincere devotion. The word carries the idea of someone who can only be counted on if they are paid, unlike the faithful servant who obeys out of true attachment.
H6092.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to work, to toil." It literally designates one who performs work for a wage, the laborer or day laborer. It is a concrete word that evokes the sweat of daily work.
H6092.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 58:3. The prophet denounces the hypocrisy of the people who fast while oppressing their hired workers: the fast that claims to honor God has no value if, at the same time, they mistreat those they employ. The context emphasizes social justice: a true fast must be accompanied by respect and kindness towards all, especially the most vulnerable, like the hired workers who depend on their wages to survive.
H6092.portee: This word reminds us that God cares about those who work to earn their bread and that He calls us to respect and treat them justly. True faith is not reduced to visible religious practices; it must transform our relationship with others, especially the economically weaker.

sens: Intense physical or emotional pain
Continuous painful effort
Difficult and tiring work
H6093.detail:
1. Suffering is the vivid experience of pain, whether physical or emotional. Eve receives the command: "I will greatly increase your pains in childbirth" (Genesis 3:16), which refers to the pains of labor and the emotional weight of motherhood.
2. It is also the constant effort required by an exhausting task. Man must eat "by the sweat of his brow," meaning through painful and daily work (Genesis 3:17): each day brings its burden.
3. More broadly, it is the hard work that wears down the body and mind. Noah receives his name because he "will comfort us concerning our work and the toil of our hands" (Genesis 5:29), as if all human labor carries this mark of difficulty.
H6093.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes fatigue and pain. The suffix "on" in Hebrew forms a concrete noun. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often describes what is difficult, painful, or produces sadness. It is a reality of the world after the Fall: work becomes suffering, motherhood becomes pain.
H6093.emploi: This word appears three times in Genesis, in the first three chapters. It first denotes the suffering inflicted on Eve as a consequence of sin (Genesis 3:16), then the hard work imposed on Adam (Genesis 3:17). Finally, it describes human labor in general, of which Noah is announced as the one who will bring rest (Genesis 5:29). The three uses show a progression: from personal punishment to ordinary work, then to the hope of consolation.
H6093.portee: This word reminds the believer that suffering and difficult work are not a cosmic curse, but a consequence of original sin. However, they also become the place where faith is exercised: accepting suffering, transforming work into service, awaiting a promised consolation. It is an invitation to see in daily pains a fundamental biblical reality, and to hope for future rest and redemption.

sens: Fermer les yeux ou la bouche
Clore volontairement pour garder secret ou méditer un projet
H6095.detail:
1. Fermer les yeux ou la bouche : c'est l'action physique de clore une ouverture du visage. En Proverbes 16:30, celui qui « ferme les yeux » les plisse volontairement pour mieux se concentrer sur ses pensées, comme quelqu'un qui veut éloigner les distractions du monde extérieur.
2. Clore volontairement pour garder secret ou méditer un projet : fermer les yeux signifie aussi se détourner délibérément de la vérité ou de la justice pour laisser germer dans l'ombre une intention cachée. Dans ce passage, l'homme ferme les yeux, se mord les lèvres (geste de retenue) et prépare déjà le mal en silence : il isole son esprit pour ruminer ses mauvais desseins.
H6095.origine: Le verbe hébreu עָצָה (atsah) exprime l'idée de fermer, de clore. Son image de base est celle des yeux ou des lèvres qui se ferment. La racine évoque une fermeture physique, mais elle s'applique aussi à celui qui se ferme intérieurement, qui refuse la lumière ou la parole juste. C'est un mot simple et concret de la langue hébraïque.
H6095.emploi: Le mot n'apparaît qu'une fois dans la Bible hébraïque, en Proverbes 16:30. Il décrit un personnage au cœur malveillant qui ferme les yeux pour méditer le mal — geste qui révèle l'état de son âme. Cet emploi unique montre comment la fermeture physique des yeux devient le signe d'une fermeture morale et spirituelle : on ne veut plus voir le bien, on se concentre sur le mal.
H6095.portee: Ce verset nous avertit que les gestes du corps révèlent l'état du cœur. Fermer les yeux volontairement peut sembler innocent, mais la Bible nous invite à surveiller nos pensées et nos intentions : quand on commence à se détourner de la vérité pour ruminer le mal en secret, on emprunte déjà le chemin du péché. C'est un appel à la vigilance sur nos pensées cachées.
